It is also possible that the pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to mockery and polytheism, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, so the two pronouns differ in their reference on this view. End of quote.

Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid: "naslukuh" means "We insert the denial." On this reading the "bā'" in "bihi" is causal.

What appears most likely is that the pronoun refers to the mockery understood from "yastahzi'ūn" (they mock), and the "bā'" in "bihi" is causal.

The guilty (al-mujrimūn) here are the Quraysh disbelievers and those whom the Messenger invited to faith. If "lā yu'minūna" is a new independent statement, it is a general expression intended in a specific sense, referring to those upon whose hearts a seal was set, since a whole world of people did believe, even among those who had denied the Messenger.

"Wa-qad khalat sunnatu al-awwalīn" (though the way of the former peoples has passed) means the practice of the former peoples in denying their messengers, or in their destruction when they denied their messengers and mocked them. This is a threat to the polytheists of Quraysh.

The pronoun in "'alayhim" (for them) refers to the polytheists, and this is because of the extreme extent of their denial and their distance from faith, to the point that they deny what is sensed and witnessed with the eyes, touched by bodies in motion and movement. This is in accordance with the complete exaggeration in denying the truth.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" (and they kept) refers to the one referred to in "'alayhim." That is: even if a gate were opened for them from the sky, and a ladder were made for them on which they climbed, they would say: "This is something we imagine, with no reality, and we have been bewitched by it." The word "fa-ẓallū" (and they kept), which indicates that this happens during the day, so that they would be clearly aware of what they witnessed. Also, "ẓalla" can come with the meaning of "ṣāra" (became).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" refers to the angels, in reference to their statement: ﴿Why do you not bring the angels to us?﴾. That is: even if they saw the angels ascending and descending through an open gate in the sky, they would not believe.

Al-A'mash and Abu Haywa read "ya'rijūna" with a kasra on the rā' (ya'rijūna), which is the dialect of Hudhayl for "ascending," meaning climbing up.

The word "innamā" (only) suggests restriction, as if He said: "That is nothing but the dazzling of the eyes."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir read "suккirat" with a light kāf, in the passive voice. The remaining seven read it with a doubled kāf in the passive voice. Al-Zuhri read it with a fatḥa on the sīn and a kasra on the kāf, lightened, in the active voice, comparing the seeing of their eyes to the seeing of a drunkard because of the weakness of his perception of what he sees.

As for the doubled reading, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "We have been prevented from seeing reality by intoxication (sukr), with a kasra on the sīn," which means binding and restraining. It is also said: "shudda" (bound); from Jawhar: "jud'at" (cut off); from Mujahid: "ḥubisat" (held back); from al-Kalbi: "'amiyat" (blinded); from Abu 'Amr: "ghuṭṭiyat" (covered); from Qatada also: "ukhidhat" (seized); from Abu 'Ubayd: "ghushiyat" (overcome).

As for the light reading, it was said that it has the meaning of the doubled form, but the lightened form conveys the same meaning. It was also said: the doubled form means "seized," and the lightened form means "bewitched." It is well known that "sakira" is not transitive. Abu 'Ali said: "It is possible that it was heard as transitive in Basra." Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Abu 'Ubayda that it is said: "suккirat abṣāruhum" (their eyes were stopped) when sleeplessness covers them so that they cannot see.

It was also said: the doubled form is from "sukkira al-mā'" (the water was blocked), and the lightened form is from "sakira al-sharāb" (the drink intoxicated). The Arabs say: "sakarat al-rīḥ taskuru sakaran" (the wind became still) when it settles and does not pass on as it was previously going. "Sakira al-rajulu min al-sharāb sukran" (the man became intoxicated) when his state changes, becomes still, and does not pass through what it was meant to pass through. From this meaning comes "sakrān yabitt" (a drunkard who cannot decide), meaning one who does not carry out a matter. The Arabs say: "sukkirat fī majārī al-mā'" (the water courses were blocked) when they are obstructed, and the water is turned back so that it does not flow in its direction.

If it is from "sukkira al-sharāb" or "sukkirat al-rīḥ," then the doubling is for transitivity. If it is from "sakkara majārī al-mā'," then the doubling is for intensity, because its lightened form is transitive. As for "sakarat" in the lightened form: if it is from "sakara al-mā'," its verb is transitive; if it is from "sakara al-sharāb" or "al-rīḥ," then it belongs to the pattern of "wajia Zayd" and "wajjaha ghayruhu" (Zayd was in pain and another caused him pain), so one says: "sakira al-rajul" and "sakkarahu ghayruhu" (someone else made him drunk), and "sakarat al-rīḥ" and "sakkarahā ghayruhā," just as "sa'ida Zayd" and "sa'-ddahu ghayruhu" (Zayd was made happy and another made him happy).

Al-Zamakhshari summarized this and said: "wa-suккirat" means "ḥuyyirat" (bewildered) or "ḥubisat" (held back), from the word for intoxication (sukr) or the word for blockage (sakar). It was read with the lightened form, meaning: held back as a river is held back from flowing. End of quote.

Aban ibn Tha'lab read: "suḥirat abṣāruna" (our eyes have been bewitched).

The statement "bal naḥnu qawmun masḥūrūn" (rather, we are a people bewitched) comes as a move to a greater level of bewitchment of the mind. It is appropriate to take this reading as an explanation of meaning and not as a recited text, since it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf.

The answer to "law" (even if) is "laqālū" (they would say), meaning that they witness what they witness and do not doubt the seeing of what is sensed. But they say what they do not believe, by agreement in obstinacy, rejecting the proof, pure arrogance, and preferring to win, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

﴿And We have certainly placed constellations in the sky and adorned it for the observers.﴾ ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil.﴾ ﴿Except one who eavesdrops, and he is pursued by a clear flame.﴾

When He mentioned the state of those who deny prophethood, and this was based on the oneness of Allah, He mentioned the signs of divine unity in the heavens, beginning with them and then following them with the signs on earth.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: When He, exalted is He, mentioned that if they saw the aforementioned sign in the sky they would still be obstinate about it, He followed that with this verse, as if He said: "Indeed in the sky there are lessons," placed in contrast to the aforementioned, and their disbelief in them and their turning away from them is a persistence and a rebellion on their part. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that "ja'alnā" (We placed) means "khalaqnā" (We created), and "fī al-samā'" (in the sky) is related to "ja'alnā." It is also possible that it means "ṣayyarnā" (We made), and "fī al-samā'" is the second object, so it relates to an omitted element.

"Al-burūj" is the plural of "burj" (constellation), whose linguistic meaning was discussed earlier. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: they are the stars. Abu Salih said: the wandering planets. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: they are twelve constellations (Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces), and they are the stations of the sun and the moon.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: they are palaces in the sky, in which there are guards, and these are the ones mentioned in His saying: ﴿It has been filled with a severe guard and meteors﴾ [al-Jinn: 8]. It was also said: the sphere has twelve constellations, each constellation being two and a half miles.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "wa-zayyannāhā" (and We adorned it) refers to the constellations, since they are what is spoken about and are nearest in wording. It was said that it refers to the sky, and this is the view of the majority. They are specified as "for the observers" because they are among the sensible things that are perceived only by the sight of the eye. It is possible that it is by the sight of the heart, because of the spiritual adornment in them, which is the excellence of their wisdom, the wonders of their craftsmanship and the strange wonders of divine power.

The pronoun in "ḥafiẓnāhā" (We guarded it) refers to the sky. For this reason the majority said that the pronoun in "wa-zayyannāhā" refers to the sky, so that the pronouns do not differ. The guarding of the sky is by pelting with meteors, as contained in the authentic hadiths. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The devils approach the sky in groups; a rebellious one among them separates off and listens, then he is struck by a meteor, and he tells his companions while it is burning: 'Such and such a matter has occurred.' So the devils add to that, and they pass it on to the soothsayers, who add a hundred words to the one word." And other hadiths similar to this one.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meteors come out and cause harm, but they do not kill. Al-Hasan said: they kill. In the hadiths there is evidence that the pelting occurred in the pre-Islamic period, but it became more intense at the time of Islam. The sky was guarded with complete protection.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "They were not barred from the heavens. When 'Isa was born they were barred from three heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was born they were barred from all the heavens."

The apparent meaning is that His saying "illā man istaraqa" (except one who eavesdrops) is an exception of the connected type (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: then it was not guarded from him. This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi and others, and the meaning is: he heard some of its news and threw it to the devils. It was also said that it is a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), meaning: it was guarded from him. On both interpretations, "man" is in the accusative position.

Al-Hawfi said: "man" is a substitute (badal) for "kulli shayṭān" (every devil). Abu al-Baqa' said similarly: it is genitive as a substitute, meaning: except for the one who eavesdrops. This grammatical analysis is not valid, because what precedes it is affirmative, so exclusion (tafrīgh) is not possible, and therefore it cannot be a substitute. But it is possible that "illā man istaraqa" is a qualifier (na't), with some disagreement on this.

Abu al-Baqa' also said: "man" may be in the nominative position as a subject, and "fa-atba'ahu" (then he was pursued) is the predicate. The entry of "fa" is allowed because "man" carries the meaning of "alladhī" (the one who) or the conditional. End of quote.

"Al-istirāq" is a reflexive form derived from "al-sariqa" (theft), which is taking something secretly, namely snatching speech with a quick brief snatch. "Al-sam'" (hearing) is the thing heard. The meaning of "mubīn" (clear) is evident to those who see.

[p. 448] [p. 449] [p. 450]

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 1–25 (part 4 of 4)**

﴿And the earth — We spread it out, and cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow in it every thing in balanced measure.﴾ ﴿And We made for you in it means of livelihood, and [also] for those whom you do not provide for.﴾ ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.﴾ ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing, then sent down water from the sky and gave it to you to drink, and you are not its keepers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors.﴾ ﴿And We have known those of you who go forward, and We have known those who remain behind.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord — it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, Knowing.﴾

*Madadnaha* (مَدَدْناها): *basatnaha*, we spread it out, so that benefit may be obtained from it by those who dwell on it. Al-Hasan said: Allah took a clump of clay and said to it, "Spread out," and it spread out. It was also said: it was spread out from beneath the Ka'bah.

Since the clause that follows this phrase is a verbal clause (*jumla fi'liyya*), the accusative reading (*al-nasb*) is preferable to the nominative reading on the basis of inchoative (*al-ibtida'*) construction, which is why (*wal-ard*) is in the accusative. [Here *al-nasb 'ala al-ishtighal* (النصب على الاشتغال), the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun placed first, is preferred over *al-raf' 'ala al-ibtida'* (الرفع على الابتداء), the nominative on the basis of inchoative construction.]

*Al-rawasi* (الرَّواسِي): the mountains. In a hadith: "Indeed the earth used to shake with its inhabitants as a ship shakes, so Allah made it firm with the mountains."

The *min* (مِن) in ﴿min kulli﴾ is partitive (*li-l-tab'idh*, indicating a part of the whole). According to al-Akhfash, it is extra (*za'ida*, redundant), meaning *kull shay'* (every thing).

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (*fiha*) refers to the earth that was spread out. It was also said that it refers to the mountains, and it was also said that it refers to both of them together.

Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: *mawzun* means measured by a measure. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this, saying: it was weighed by the scale of wisdom and measured by a measure which requires that there be no addition or deficiency in it. Ibn Atiyya said: the majority said its meaning is *muqaddar* (determined), *muharrar* (precisely arranged) by intention and will, so the weighing (*al-wazn*) in this sense is metaphorical. Ibn Zayd said: what is intended is that which is literally weighed, such as gold and silver and other things that are weighed. Qatada said: *mawzun* means divided (*maqsum*). Mujahid said: *ma'dud* (counted). Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it has weight and measure in the matters of blessing and benefit. Another expounded it, saying: it has a standing, as you say, "he has no weight," meaning he has no worth and standing. It is also said: "this is *kalam mawzun*," meaning versified, not scattered. On this view, *anbatna fiha* (we caused to grow in it) includes what is weighed of jewels, minerals and animals.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He caused it to grow a good growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. The intended meaning of *inbat* (causing to grow) is creation and bringing into existence.

Al-A'raj and Kharija from Nafi' read *ma'ayish* (مَعائِشَ) with a hamza. Ibn Atiyya said: the correct form is to omit the hamza, and he gave a reason for that which is well known in grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ma'ayish*, with a clear *ya'* (ياء), unlike *al-shama'il* and *al-khaba'ith*, for making the *ya'* clear in them is an error, and the correct form is the hamza, or else the *ya'* is pronounced in an intermediate way (*bayn bayn*, between the hamza and the *ya'*).

The explanation of *ma'ayish* has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf. The apparent reading is that *man* (مَن) refers to rational beings, and what is intended by it is dependants, slaves and servants, whom you think you provide for, and you are mistaken, for Allah is the Provider who provides for you and for them. Al-Farra said this too. What is included with them by way of predominance (*al-taghlib*) is what is not rational, such as livestock and beasts. *Ma* (ما) in this sense is among those whom Allah provides for, and their thought has already gone to the idea that they are the providers. Al-Zajjaj also said this. Mujahid said: the beasts, livestock and cattle. It was said: wild animals, predators and birds. On these two views, *man* refers to what is not rational.

The apparent reading is that *man* is in the genitive position (*fi mawdi' jarr*), in coordination (*'atf*) with the genitive pronoun in *lakum*. This is the view of the Kufis, Yunus and al-Akhfash. The one who holds this view has used as evidence for its soundness the verse in al-Baqarah: ﴿and disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

Al-Zajjaj said: *man* is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted whose estimate is: "and We gave life to whom you do not provide for," i.e., other nations than you, because the meaning is "We gave you life." It was also said: it is in coordination with *ma'ayish*, meaning: "and We made for you, and for those whom you do not provide for, of slaves and craftsmen, means of livelihood." It was also said: and animals. It was said: in coordination with the place (*mahall*) of *lakum*. It was also said: *man* is the subject of an inchoative clause whose predicate is omitted, being indicated by the meaning, i.e.: "and for whom you do not provide, We made for him means of livelihood in it." This is not objectionable, for they permitted: "I struck Zayd, and 'Amr" with the nominative on the basis of inchoative construction, meaning: "and as for 'Amr, I struck him," the predicate being omitted because what came before indicates it.

The explanation of the treasuries (*khaza'in*) has already been given. *In* (إنْ) is negative, and *min* is extra. The apparent meaning is: there is nothing that the servants benefit from except that We are capable of bringing it into existence, creating it, and bestowing it. Thus the treasuries, which are the places in which things are kept, are used metaphorically, from the sensible (the physical body) to the intelligible.

Some people said: what is meant is the treasuries literally, which are the places in which things are kept; that the wind has a place, the rain has a place, and every place has an angel and guardians. When Allah commands that something be brought out of it, the guardians bring it out. It was also said: what is meant by *shay'* here is rain. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Al-A'mash read: (*wa-ma nursiluhu*) in place of ﴿wa-ma nunazziluhu﴾. *Al-irsal* (sending) is more general. This is a reading for explanation of meaning, not a reading of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (*sawad al-mushaf*). From Ibn Abbas and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna: there is no year with more rain than another, but Allah the Exalted sends it down in some places and not in others.

*Lawaqih* (لَواقِحُ) is the plural of *laqih* (لاقِحٌ). It is said: *rih laqih*, meaning winds bringing good by producing rain-bearing clouds, just as the one that brings no good but evil is called *rih 'aqim* (a barren wind). Or *mala'iq*, meaning bearers of rain. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari: *lawaqih* means *mala'ih* (fertilizing), *mulaqqaha* (made to fertilize).

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Allah sends the *mubashshira* (the bearer of good tidings), which sweeps the earth with a sweep, then the *muthira* (the stirring one), which stirs up the clouds, then the *mu'allifa* (the gathering one), which gathers them together. Then Allah sends the *lawaqih*, which fertilize the trees.

As for the one who reads *al-rih* in the singular, it is according to the interpretation of the genus (*ta'wil al-jins*), as they say: "The yellow dinar destroyed the people," and "the white dirham." *Saqa* (سَقى) and *asqa* (أسْقى) may both have the same meaning. Abu 'Ubayda said: whoever gives drink to the mouth uses *saqa* only, while for giving drink to land and fruit trees he uses *asqa*, and for calling someone to drink from land or other things, he uses *asqa* only. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs say of everything that is from the bellies of livestock, or from the sky, or from a flowing river: *asqaytuhu*, meaning I made it a drink for him, and I made for him a place to drink from it. When it is for the mouth, they say *saqa* and do not say *asqa*. Abu 'Ali said: *saqaytuhu* means until he was satisfied, and *asqaytuhu* nahran means I made it a drink for him (from a river).

The pronoun here comes connected after another connected pronoun, as was mentioned earlier in the verse: ﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾ [Hud: 28]. It has already been stated that the view of Sibawayh regarding this is that connection is obligatory.

*Wa-ma antum lahu bi-khazinin*: that is, you are not capable of bringing it into existence, as an indication of His great power and a demonstration of your incapacity. *Hum* (هم): that is, you are not capable of it at the time you need it. Sufyan said: *bi-khazinin* means not withholding the rain.

*Nuhyi* (نُحْيِـي): We bring it out from pure non-existence into life. *Numit* (نُمِيتُ): We remove its life. *Wa-nahnu al-warithun* (وَنَحْنُ الوارِثُونَ): the ones who remain after the passing away of the creation.

As for *al-mustaqdimin* (المُسْتَقْدِمِينَ), Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they are the dead, and *al-musta'khirin* (المُسْتَأْخِرِينَ) are the living. Qatada, Ikrima and others said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who came earlier in creation, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who have not yet been created.

Mujahid said: *al-mustaqdimin* are the earlier nations, and *al-musta'khirin* are the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan and Qatada also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who advanced in obedience and goodness, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lagged behind in disobedience and evil.

Ibn Jubayr said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those in the front rows of battle, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lag behind in it. It was also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who were killed in jihad, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who were not killed. It was said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those in the front rows of prayer, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lag behind because of women, in order to look at them. Qatada also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who hastened to Islam, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who held back from it.

The better view is to take these statements as examples (*al-tamthil*), not as exhaustive limitation (*al-hasr*). The meaning is that His knowledge encompasses those who went before and those who came after, and their circumstances. Then the Exalted informed that He will gather them.

Al-A'mash read *yahshirhum* (يَحْشِرُهم) with a kasra on the *shin*. Ibn Abbas, Marwan ibn al-Hakam and Abu al-Hawra' said: a beautiful woman used to pray behind the Messenger (ﷺ). Some would move forward so as not to be tempted by her, and some would lag behind in order to steal a glance at her during the prayer, so the verse was revealed concerning them.

The Exalted concluded this verse with these two attributes, wisdom and knowledge, in the utmost appropriateness.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book, and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved will often wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without it having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾ ﴿They said: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely possessed!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿We send down the angels only with truth, and then they would not be granted respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and We Ourselves will surely preserve it.﴾ ﴿We sent messengers before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has passed before them.﴾ ﴿Even if We opened to them a gate from the sky and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people under sorcery!"﴾ ﴿We have placed constellations in the sky and adorned it for the beholders.﴾ ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil.﴾ ﴿Except one who steals a hearing, and a clear flaming meteor pursues him.﴾ ﴿As for the earth, We spread it out, cast firmly set mountains upon it, and caused every kind of thing to grow in it in due measure.﴾ ﴿We made for you therein means of livelihood, and for those whom you do not provide for.﴾ ﴿There is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure.﴾ ﴿We send the winds fertilizing, then We send down water from the sky and give you drink from it, though you are not its keepers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritor.﴾ ﴿We certainly know those of you who go forward, and We certainly know those who hold back.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will gather them; He is Wise, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿We certainly created man from clay of dry ringing mud, shaped from black molded clay.﴾ [al-Hijr: 26] ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind.﴾ [al-Hijr: 27] (p. 442)

*Rubba*: a particle of jarr (governing, a preposition), not a noun, contrary to the Kufans, al-Akhfash in one of his two opinions, and Ibn al-Tarawah. Its meaning, according to the well-known view, is diminution (*taqlil*) rather than multiplication (*takthir*), contrary to the claim of the one who asserts this and attributes it to Sibawayh, and contrary to the one who says it conveys neither diminution nor multiplication but is a particle of affirmation. The claim of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi that there is consensus that it is set for diminution is baseless. The statement of al-Zajjaj that *rubba* is for multiplication, the opposite of what the people of the language know, is not correct. It has several dialects, and its rules are numerous and are mentioned in grammar. It occurs in the Qur'an only in this surah, despite how frequently it occurs in the speech of the Arabs.

*Dhar*: an imperative that has largely dispensed with its past tense by using *tark* (leaving). In a hadith: "Leave the Abyssinians as long as they leave you."

*Lawma*: a particle of exhortation (*tahdid*), followed by a verb, explicit or implied; and a particle of prohibition (*imtina'*) for the existence of something, followed by a noun as its subject according to the Basran school. From it is the verse of the poet:

Had it not been for shame, and had it not been for religion, I would have reproached you both for some of what is in you, since you have reproached me for my faults.

Some have said that the *mim* in *lawma* is a substitute for the *lam* in *lawla*. Similar is *istawla 'ala al-shay'* and *istawma*; *khallaltuhu* and *khalamtuhu*, so that *khilli* and *khilmi* mean "my friend."

Al-Zamakhshari said: *law* is combined with *la* and *ma* for two meanings. As for *hal*, it is combined only with *la* alone, for exhortation, and that is the end of his statement. What I choose is that both are simple, not compound, and that *ma* is not a substitute for *la*.

*Salaka al-khayt fi al-ibra* and *aslakaha*: he inserted it into it and strung it. The poet said:

Until, when they drove them into a narrow place, scattering them as the driver drives the stray herd.

Another said:

And I was the wrangler of your opponent, not having been accustomed; and they have led you into a grievous day.

*Al-shihab*: a flame of fire, and it is also applied to a star because of its brightness, being likened to fire. Abu Tammam said:

And the banner amid the spear-shafts is gleaming, between the two armies, not among the seven shining stars.

*Al-lawaqih*: the apparent meaning is that it is the plural of *laqih*, meaning those possessing fertilization (*liqah*), like *labin* and *tamir*, because the wind passes over water, then passes over the clouds and trees, and so there is fertilization in it. This was said by al-Farra'. Al-Azhari said: they are carriers that bear the clouds and direct them. A she-camel is *laqih*, and female camels are *lawaqih* when they carry foetuses in their wombs. Zuhayr said:

When a fierce, harmful war is fertilized, a biting one, its teeth are bared, and it frightens the people.

Abu 'Ubayda said: it means *malaqih*, the plural of *mulaqqiha*, because it fertilizes the clouds by casting water. He said:

And one struck, by what the calamities cast down.

That is, *al-matawih*, the plural of *mutih*.

*Al-salsal*: Abu 'Ubayda said it is clay when mixed with sand and dried. Abu al-Haytham said: *al-salsal* is the sound of a bridle and the like, like the rattling in a garment. It was also said: finely crumbled dust. *Salsala al-raml* means the sand sounded. *Salsal* means *musalsil*, like *qadqad*, meaning *muqadqid*, and this kind of doubled form is abundant. This pattern, when it is a verbal noun, is such that you say *zulzila zalzalan* (with fatha) and *zilzalan* (with kasra). Its measure according to the Basrans is *fi'lal*, and likewise all doubled roots, whose letters are all radicals, not *qa'qa'*, contrary to al-Farra' and many grammarians. Nor is it *fa'fal*, contrary to some Basrans and some Kufans, nor that its origin is *fa''al* with a doubled 'ayn, a letter of the same type as the first being substituted for the second, contrary to some Kufans. From these views follows: *wa-rubba salsal*.

*Al-hama'*: black, foul-smelling mud. Its singular is *hama'a* with the *mim* vowelled; al-Layth said this but erred in it. They said: we do not know in the speech of the Arabs *hama'a* except with the *mim* quiescent. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda and most of the scholars, as Abu al-Aswad said:

He comes to you with its fullness at times, and at times it comes with mud and little water.

On this view, *hama'* does not have the *ta' marbuta* between it and its singular, because the patterns differ.

*Al-samum*: the extreme of heat that penetrates the pores until it kills, from fire, sun or wind. It was said: *al-samum* is at night and the heat is by day.

[The Qur'anic verses at the head of the next section:] ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book, and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved will often wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without it having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾: This surah is Meccan without disagreement. Its connection to what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned at the end of the previous surah some matters of the conditions of the Resurrection, such as the changing of the heavens and the earth, and the state of the disbelievers on that day, and that what he brought was in accordance with conveying and warning, He began this surah by mentioning the Qur'an, which is a message to mankind, and the state of the unbelievers and their desire that they had been Muslims.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the Book" here means the scriptures revealed before the Qur'an, and on their view "those" is a reference to the verses of the Book. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that "the Book" means the Qur'an, and the attribute is conjoined to it. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned only that this demonstrative refers to what the surah contains of verses. He said: "the Book and a clear Qur'an" is the surah. The indefiniteness of "Qur'an" is for magnification. The meaning: these are the verses of the Book that is perfect in being a Book, and the verses of a clear Qur'an, as if it were said: and the Book comprehensive of perfection and of wonder in its matter.

The apparent view is that *ma* in *rubba* is a preparatory (*muhayyi'a*) particle, because *rubba* as a preposition is only followed by nouns, so *ma* was brought as a preparation for the verb's coming after it. They allowed *ma* to be an indefinite relative (*nakira mawsufa*), with *rubba* as the governing preposition, and the returning pronoun in the attributive clause is omitted, its estimate being: "*rubba* of a thing that those who disbelieved desire." And "*law kanu muslimin*" is an apposition to *ma* on the view that *law* is verbal (*masdariyya*). On the first view it is in the accusative position as the object of *yawaddu*, and whoever does not consider *law* to come as verbal makes the object of *yawaddu* omitted.

*Law* in "*law kanu muslimin*" is a particle for what would have happened because something else happened. Its answer is omitted, meaning: "Those who disbelieved will often wish for Islam, if they had been Muslims; they would be delighted by that and be saved from the punishment." Since *rubba*, according to most, does not enter upon the future, they interpreted *yawaddu* as meaning *waddu* (past). Since the future in God's report is as the past for the certainty of its occurrence, it is as if it were said *waddu*. This is not necessary; it may enter upon the future, but that is rare compared with its entering upon the past. Among what occurs with it for the future is the verse of Sulaym al-Qushayri:

And one who clings to cowardice out of fear of death, he will surely perish; and one who fights, fearful, will surely return.

And the saying of Hind, mother of Mu'awiya:

O many a speaker tomorrow, alas for the mother of Mu'awiya!

And the saying of Jahdar:

So if I perish, many a youth will weep over me, refined, with soft fingers.

in several verses. As for the statement of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi that they agreed that the word *rubba* (perhaps, "many a time") is specific to entering upon the past tense, this is not sound. On this basis, *yawaddu* ("they will wish") would not need interpretation. As for the one who interpreted it by supplying *kāna* (was), meaning "perhaps they were wishing," his view is weak, and this is not one of the places where *kāna* is supplied. Since, according to al-Zamakhshari and others, *rubba* denotes diminution, they needed an interpretation for the occurrence of *rubba* here, and al-Zamakhshari extended his discussion of this interpretation. As for the one who said that it denotes abundance, then abundance is evident here, because their wishing for that is great. As for the one who said that diminution and abundance are understood only from the context of the speech and not from the meaning of *rubba* itself, he said: the context of the speech indicates abundance.

It was said: the terrors of that Day will bewilder them, so they will remain stunned. If, at some moments, they regain some awareness from their intoxication, they will wish for it, and therefore it is expressed as diminution.

ʿĀṣim and Nāfiʿ read *rubbamā* with a light *bāʾ* (rubba, shortened), and the rest of the seven read it with a doubled *bāʾ*. From Abū ʿAmr there are both readings. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *rubbatamā*, with an added *tāʾ*.

When will they wish that? It was said: in this world. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: at the moment of witnessing death. Ibn Masʿūd said: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, who wished for that on the Day of Badr when they saw the victory of the Muslims. It was said: when there befell them what befell them of the Muslims taking possession of their land, their wealth and their women, they wished for that before what befell them had befallen them. It was said: they will wish for that in the Hereafter, when the sinful among the Muslims are brought out of the Fire. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas ibn Mālik, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and Ibrāhīm, and Abū Mūsā related it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who recited this verse. It was said: when the Messenger intercedes and intercession is granted, until he says: "Whoever among the Muslims is in it, let him enter Paradise." Mujāhid related it from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was said: when they see the Resurrection; this was mentioned by al-Zajjāj. It was said: at every state in which the disbeliever is punished and the believer is safe; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbārī.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to warn them. This is a command of threat and menace toward them; that is, they are not among those who refrain from the disbelief and denial they are in, nor among those who benefit from advice and reminder. Their portion is only the portion of the cattle: eating, enjoying the present life, and hoping to attain it. This is what distracts them and occupies them from belief in Allah and His Messenger.

In His words *yaʾkulū wa-yatamattaʿū* ("let them eat and enjoy themselves") there is an indication that luxury, indulgence, and not preparing for death and not readying oneself for it are not among the traits of one who seeks salvation from the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter. It is reported from some scholars: enjoyment in this world is among the traits of the doomed. al-Ḥasan said: no servant prolongs hope except that he does evil in deed.

*Yaʾkulū* is in the jussive mood, as is what is conjoined to it, as an answer to the imperative. It appears that He commanded leaving them alone, letting them go their way, and making truce and peace with them. For this reason it is correctly placed as an answer, because if he occupied them with fighting and the clashing of swords and the waging of war, eating and enjoying would not be pleasant for them. What supports this is that the surah is Meccan. And if you make *dharhum* ("leave them") an imperative to abandon advising them and to busy oneself with them, then the answer does not follow from it, because they eat and enjoy themselves whether or not he abandoned advising them.

*Fa-sawfa yaʿlamūn* ("but they will come to know"): a threat and menace, that is, they will come to know the outcome of their affair and what they will come to in this world of humiliation, killing and captivity, and in the Hereafter of everlasting punishment.

When He threatened them with what would befall them, He followed that with what indicates their destruction, and that it is not to be hastened, for it has a term it does not exceed. The meaning is: no community [*qarya*] of disbelievers. The apparent meaning is that the destruction intended is the total destruction of those who denied the messengers, and this is more forceful in deterrence. It was said: the intended meaning is destruction by death. The *wāw* in His words *wa-lahā* is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*). Some said: it is an intrusive *wāw* (*muqḥama*), that is, superfluous, but this is nothing. Ibn Abī ʿAblah read it without it.

al-Zamakhsharī said: the sentence is situated as a description of *qarya*, and the analogical rule is that *lā* should come between the *wāw* and the two, as in His words: ﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had warners﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 208]. It came in the middle only to emphasize the attachment of the description to the described, as one says of the circumstantial clause: "Zayd came to me, upon him a garment," and "Zayd came to me while upon him a garment." End of quotation. Abū al-Baqāʾ agreed with him, saying: the sentence is an adjective to *qarya*, like your saying: "I did not meet a man except a scholar." He said: We have already mentioned the status of the *wāw* in such a case in al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿Perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. End of quotation.

What al-Zamakhsharī said, which Abū al-Baqāʾ followed, we do not know anyone among the grammarians to have said. It is based on the premise that what comes after *illā* may be a description, and they have prohibited that. al-Akhfash said: one should not separate the description and the described by the exception (*ithm*). He said: and a sentence like "No man came to me except a rider" is taken as "except a man, a rider," and there is ugliness in making the description like the noun. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: you say "I did not pass by anyone except standing," so *qāʾiman* is a circumstantial accusative of *aḥad*, and it is not permissible to say *illā qāʾimun*, because *illā* does not intervene between the description and the described. Ibn Mālik said: as for what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, in sentences like "I did not pass by anyone except that Zayd is better than him," that the clause after *illā* is a description of *aḥad*, this is a view not known from any Basran or Kufan, so one should not turn to it. Ibn Mālik refuted al-Zamakhsharī's claim that the *wāw* came in the middle to emphasize the attachment of the description to the described.

al-Qāḍī Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: this *wāw* is the one that indicates that the state that follows it in wording is, in time, before the state that precedes the *wāw*. From it is His saying: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that the Book known (*kitāb maʿlūm*) is the term written in the Preserved Tablet and specified. This is indicated by what follows it. It was said: in it are written their deeds, their lifespans and the terms of their destruction. al-Māwardī mentioned: *kitābun maʿlūm* means an obligatory decree that is fixed. The *min* (from) is superfluous, denoting the totality of the genus, that is: no community precedes its term. He made the term feminine (*ajalahā*) according to the wording of *ummah* (community), and He made it plural and masculine in *wa-mā yastakhirūn* ("nor do they delay") according to the meaning, and He omitted something from it because the context indicates it.

﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad!"﴾ ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you should be of the truthful?﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. Muqātil said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Umayyah, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *nazala ʿalayhi al-dhikr* (the past tense, light, active): "that the Reminder came down upon him." He also read: *yā ayyuhā alladhī ulqiya ilayhi al-dhikr* ("O you to whom the Reminder was cast"). It should be taken that this reading is an explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (*sawād al-muṣḥaf*).

This description, "the one upon whom the Reminder was sent down," they said mockingly and disparagingly, because they do not acknowledge that the Reminder was sent down upon him, and they attribute him to madness, since if he were a believer in the message of Mūsā, he would not have reported about him as madness. Then they proposed to him that he bring them the angels as witnesses to your truthfulness and the soundness of your claim and your warning, as He said: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he might be with him a warner?﴾ [al-Furqān: 7]; or that they be punishers for your denial, as the angels used to come to the denying nations.

The two Ḥarams and the two Arabs read *mā tanazzalu*, the present of *tanazzala*, meaning *mā tatanazzalu al-malāʾikah* ("the angels do not descend"), with the nominative. Abū Bakr and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read *mā tunazzalu* with a *tāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma*, a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and the *zāy*, and *al-malāʾikatu* in the nominative. The two brothers (ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah?), Ḥafṣ and Ibn Muṣarrif read *mā nunazzilu* with a *ḍamma* on the first *nūn*, a *fatḥa* on the second, a *kasra* on the *zāy*, and *al-malāʾikata* in the accusative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *mā nazala*, the past tense, light, active, with *al-malāʾikatu* in the nominative.

The truth (*al-ḥaqq*) here is the punishment; so said al-Ḥasan. Or it is the message; so said Mujāhid. Or it is the seizing of souls at death; so said Ibn al-Sāʾib. Or it is the Qurʾān; mentioned by al-Māwardī. al-Zamakhsharī said: "Unless We send them down while accompanied by wisdom and benefit, and there is no wisdom in their coming to you visibly, which you would see and they would bear witness for you to the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), for then you would be believers out of compulsion." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the apparent meaning is that its sense is: as it is necessary and due from the revelation and the benefits that Allah, exalted is He, intended for His servants, not according to the proposal of a disbeliever, nor by the choice of an objector. Then He mentioned Allah's custom with the nations: that He never came to them with a sign of proposal except that the punishment came after it ﴿if they do not believe﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. So the statement means: We do not send down the angels except with a due truth, not by your proposal. Also, if they were sent down, you would not be given respite thereafter from the punishment; that is, you would not be delayed. And this does not happen, since it is in Allah's knowledge that among them is one who will believe, or that there will be born one who will believe.

al-Zamakhsharī said: *wa-idhan* is an answer and a condition, because it is an answer to them, and a conditional response to the condition that is presumed, its presumed form being: "And if We had sent down the angels, they would not have been respited, and He would not have delayed their punishment."

When they said mockingly: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾, He answered them that he is the one upon whom it was sent down, so it is not from him or from anyone's side, but from Allah, exalted is He, who sent Jibrīl (peace be upon him) with it to His Messenger. He emphasized that with His words: ﴿Indeed, it is We﴾, by the entry of *inna* and by the phrase *naḥnu* ("We"). *Naḥnu* is either a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) or an emphasis of the noun of *inna*. Then He said: ﴿and indeed We will be its guardian﴾, that is, guardians of it from the devils. At all times Allah, exalted is He, has undertaken its preservation, so no addition or subtraction befalls it, nor any distortion or alteration, unlike the other earlier books, for He, exalted is He, did not undertake to preserve them; rather He said, exalted is He: "the rabbis and the scholars were entrusted with preserving them," and for that reason disagreement occurred in them.

His preserving it is evidence that it is from His own speech, exalted is He, since if it were the speech of humans it would have been subject to what befalls the speech of humans. al-Ḥasan said: He preserved it by keeping His law until the Day of Resurrection. It was said: He preserves it in the hearts of those for whom He intends good, so that if anyone changes a single dot, the children will say to him: "You lied, and its correct form is such-and-such," and this has not happened to any other book besides it. On this basis, the apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *lahu* ("for it") refers to the Reminder, because it is the one explicitly mentioned in the verse, and this is the view of the majority: Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others. A group said: the pronoun in *lahu* refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that is, He preserves him from your harm and protects him from your plotting, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 67]. Within this verse is the good tidings of the life of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), until Allah makes the religion prevail through him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 1–25 (part 3 of 4):

﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿Yet no messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the guilty.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has passed.﴾ ﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the mockery of the disbelievers toward him (peace be upon him), their attributing madness to him, and their demand for the descent of angels, He consoled him by saying that those sent before him were met by the same practice of the messengers' peoples as the practice of these people toward you. The meaning of "shiya'" (sects, factions) was already explained at the end of Surat al-An'am. The object of "arsalna" (We sent) is omitted; the sense is "messengers from before you."

Al-Farra' said: "fī shiya'i al-awwalīn" (among the sects of the former peoples) is an instance of the attribute being attached to what it describes, like "ḥaqq al-yaqīn" (the certainty of certainty) and "bi-janibi al-gharbī" (on the western side). That is, "shiya'" is described by the attribute: among the sects of the former nations. "Al-awwalūn" are the most ancient.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿wa-mā ya'tīhim﴾ (yet ... came to them)" is a narration in the past tense, because "mā" does not enter upon a present-tense verb except when it refers to the present circumstance (ḥāl, the clause describing the state at the time of the action), and does not enter upon a past-tense verb except when it is close to the present circumstance. End of quote. This that he mentioned is the view of most grammarians, that "mā" makes the present tense specific to the present and determines it for that. Others held that "mā" often enters upon the present tense with the meaning of the present, and also enters upon it with the meaning of the future. They cited as evidence the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Sorrows left me bereft of my sons and bequeathed me grief,
at the time of sleep, and a tear that does not cease."

And the verse of al-A'sha praising the Messenger (peace be upon him):

"He has gifts whose bestowal never stops,
and today's giving does not prevent him tomorrow."

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for me to change it on my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15].

The pronoun in "naslukuhu" (We insert it) refers to the Reminder (al-dhikr), as al-Zamakhshari said: "The pronoun refers to the Reminder, meaning: like that insertion." A similar statement is: "We insert the Reminder into the hearts of the guilty," in the sense that He casts it into their hearts as something denied and mocked, not accepted. This is like when you bring a need to a miser and he does not grant it, and you say: "Thus I bring it to the miserly," meaning: in this same manner I bring it to them, returned and not welcomed.

The position of "lā yu'minūna" (they do not believe) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: not believing in it. Or it is an explanation of "kadhālika naslukuhu" (thus We insert it). End of quote.

What he (al-Zamakhshari) said, that the pronoun refers to the Reminder, was also cited by al-Gharnawi from al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: "Its meaning is: We insert the Reminder as a way of establishing the proof."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to the mockery and polytheism and the like. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd. The pronoun in "bihi" (in it) also refers to that same thing, and the "bi" is causal (bā' al-sabab), meaning: they do not believe because of their polytheism and mockery. The phrase "lā yu'minūna bihi" is then in the position of a circumstantial clause. It is also possible that the pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to the previously mentioned Preserved Reminder, which is the Qur'an, meaning: denied, rejected and mocked, He causes it to enter the hearts of the guilty; and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to it. It is also possible that the pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to mockery and polytheism, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, so the two pronouns differ in their reference on this view. End of quote.

Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid: "naslukuh" means "We insert the denial." On this reading the "bā'" in "bihi" is causal.

What appears most likely is that the pronoun refers to the mockery understood from "yastahzi'ūn" (they mock), and the "bā'" in "bihi" is causal.

The guilty (al-mujrimūn) here are the Quraysh disbelievers and those whom the Messenger invited to faith. If "lā yu'minūna" is a new independent statement, it is a general expression intended in a specific sense, referring to those upon whose hearts a seal was set, since a whole world of people did believe, even among those who had denied the Messenger.

"Wa-qad khalat sunnatu al-awwalīn" (though the way of the former peoples has passed) means the practice of the former peoples in denying their messengers, or in their destruction when they denied their messengers and mocked them. This is a threat to the polytheists of Quraysh.

The pronoun in "'alayhim" (for them) refers to the polytheists, and this is because of the extreme extent of their denial and their distance from faith, to the point that they deny what is sensed and witnessed with the eyes, touched by bodies in motion and movement. This is in accordance with the complete exaggeration in denying the truth.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" (and they kept) refers to the one referred to in "'alayhim." That is: even if a gate were opened for them from the sky, and a ladder were made for them on which they climbed, they would say: "This is something we imagine, with no reality, and we have been bewitched by it." The word "fa-ẓallū" (and they kept), which indicates that this happens during the day, so that they would be clearly aware of what they witnessed. Also, "ẓalla" can come with the meaning of "ṣāra" (became).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the pronoun in "fa-ẓallū" refers to the angels, in reference to their statement: ﴿Why do you not bring the angels to us?﴾. That is: even if they saw the angels ascending and descending through an open gate in the sky, they would not believe.

Al-A'mash and Abu Haywa read "ya'rijūna" with a kasra on the rā' (ya'rijūna), which is the dialect of Hudhayl for "ascending," meaning climbing up.

The word "innamā" (only) suggests restriction, as if He said: "That is nothing but the dazzling of the eyes."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir read "suккirat" with a light kāf, in the passive voice. The remaining seven read it with a doubled kāf in the passive voice. Al-Zuhri read it with a fatḥa on the sīn and a kasra on the kāf, lightened, in the active voice, comparing the seeing of their eyes to the seeing of a drunkard because of the weakness of his perception of what he sees.

As for the doubled reading, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: "We have been prevented from seeing reality by intoxication (sukr), with a kasra on the sīn," which means binding and restraining. It is also said: "shudda" (bound); from Jawhar: "jud'at" (cut off); from Mujahid: "ḥubisat" (held back); from al-Kalbi: "'amiyat" (blinded); from Abu 'Amr: "ghuṭṭiyat" (covered); from Qatada also: "ukhidhat" (seized); from Abu 'Ubayd: "ghushiyat" (overcome).

As for the light reading, it was said that it has the meaning of the doubled form, but the lightened form conveys the same meaning. It was also said: the doubled form means "seized," and the lightened form means "bewitched." It is well known that "sakira" is not transitive. Abu 'Ali said: "It is possible that it was heard as transitive in Basra." Abu 'Ubayd narrated from Abu 'Ubayda that it is said: "suккirat abṣāruhum" (their eyes were stopped) when sleeplessness covers them so that they cannot see.

It was also said: the doubled form is from "sukkira al-mā'" (the water was blocked), and the lightened form is from "sakira al-sharāb" (the drink intoxicated). The Arabs say: "sakarat al-rīḥ taskuru sakaran" (the wind became still) when it settles and does not pass on as it was previously going. "Sakira al-rajulu min al-sharāb sukran" (the man became intoxicated) when his state changes, becomes still, and does not pass through what it was meant to pass through. From this meaning comes "sakrān yabitt" (a drunkard who cannot decide), meaning one who does not carry out a matter. The Arabs say: "sukkirat fī majārī al-mā'" (the water courses were blocked) when they are obstructed, and the water is turned back so that it does not flow in its direction.

If it is from "sukkira al-sharāb" or "sukkirat al-rīḥ," then the doubling is for transitivity. If it is from "sakkara majārī al-mā'," then the doubling is for intensity, because its lightened form is transitive. As for "sakarat" in the lightened form: if it is from "sakara al-mā'," its verb is transitive; if it is from "sakara al-sharāb" or "al-rīḥ," then it belongs to the pattern of "wajia Zayd" and "wajjaha ghayruhu" (Zayd was in pain and another caused him pain), so one says: "sakira al-rajul" and "sakkarahu ghayruhu" (someone else made him drunk), and "sakarat al-rīḥ" and "sakkarahā ghayruhā," just as "sa'ida Zayd" and "sa'-ddahu ghayruhu" (Zayd was made happy and another made him happy).

Al-Zamakhshari summarized this and said: "wa-suккirat" means "ḥuyyirat" (bewildered) or "ḥubisat" (held back), from the word for intoxication (sukr) or the word for blockage (sakar). It was read with the lightened form, meaning: held back as a river is held back from flowing. End of quote.

Aban ibn Tha'lab read: "suḥirat abṣāruna" (our eyes have been bewitched).

The statement "bal naḥnu qawmun masḥūrūn" (rather, we are a people bewitched) comes as a move to a greater level of bewitchment of the mind. It is appropriate to take this reading as an explanation of meaning and not as a recited text, since it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf.

The answer to "law" (even if) is "laqālū" (they would say), meaning that they witness what they witness and do not doubt the seeing of what is sensed. But they say what they do not believe, by agreement in obstinacy, rejecting the proof, pure arrogance, and preferring to win, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

﴿And We have certainly placed constellations in the sky and adorned it for the observers.﴾ ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil.﴾ ﴿Except one who eavesdrops, and he is pursued by a clear flame.﴾

When He mentioned the state of those who deny prophethood, and this was based on the oneness of Allah, He mentioned the signs of divine unity in the heavens, beginning with them and then following them with the signs on earth.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: When He, exalted is He, mentioned that if they saw the aforementioned sign in the sky they would still be obstinate about it, He followed that with this verse, as if He said: "Indeed in the sky there are lessons," placed in contrast to the aforementioned, and their disbelief in them and their turning away from them is a persistence and a rebellion on their part. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that "ja'alnā" (We placed) means "khalaqnā" (We created), and "fī al-samā'" (in the sky) is related to "ja'alnā." It is also possible that it means "ṣayyarnā" (We made), and "fī al-samā'" is the second object, so it relates to an omitted element.

"Al-burūj" is the plural of "burj" (constellation), whose linguistic meaning was discussed earlier. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: they are the stars. Abu Salih said: the wandering planets. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: they are twelve constellations (Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces), and they are the stations of the sun and the moon.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: they are palaces in the sky, in which there are guards, and these are the ones mentioned in His saying: ﴿It has been filled with a severe guard and meteors﴾ [al-Jinn: 8]. It was also said: the sphere has twelve constellations, each constellation being two and a half miles.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "wa-zayyannāhā" (and We adorned it) refers to the constellations, since they are what is spoken about and are nearest in wording. It was said that it refers to the sky, and this is the view of the majority. They are specified as "for the observers" because they are among the sensible things that are perceived only by the sight of the eye. It is possible that it is by the sight of the heart, because of the spiritual adornment in them, which is the excellence of their wisdom, the wonders of their craftsmanship and the strange wonders of divine power.

The pronoun in "ḥafiẓnāhā" (We guarded it) refers to the sky. For this reason the majority said that the pronoun in "wa-zayyannāhā" refers to the sky, so that the pronouns do not differ. The guarding of the sky is by pelting with meteors, as contained in the authentic hadiths. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The devils approach the sky in groups; a rebellious one among them separates off and listens, then he is struck by a meteor, and he tells his companions while it is burning: 'Such and such a matter has occurred.' So the devils add to that, and they pass it on to the soothsayers, who add a hundred words to the one word." And other hadiths similar to this one.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meteors come out and cause harm, but they do not kill. Al-Hasan said: they kill. In the hadiths there is evidence that the pelting occurred in the pre-Islamic period, but it became more intense at the time of Islam. The sky was guarded with complete protection.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "They were not barred from the heavens. When 'Isa was born they were barred from three heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was born they were barred from all the heavens."

The apparent meaning is that His saying "illā man istaraqa" (except one who eavesdrops) is an exception of the connected type (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: then it was not guarded from him. This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi and others, and the meaning is: he heard some of its news and threw it to the devils. It was also said that it is a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), meaning: it was guarded from him. On both interpretations, "man" is in the accusative position.

Al-Hawfi said: "man" is a substitute (badal) for "kulli shayṭān" (every devil). Abu al-Baqa' said similarly: it is genitive as a substitute, meaning: except for the one who eavesdrops. This grammatical analysis is not valid, because what precedes it is affirmative, so exclusion (tafrīgh) is not possible, and therefore it cannot be a substitute. But it is possible that "illā man istaraqa" is a qualifier (na't), with some disagreement on this.

Abu al-Baqa' also said: "man" may be in the nominative position as a subject, and "fa-atba'ahu" (then he was pursued) is the predicate. The entry of "fa" is allowed because "man" carries the meaning of "alladhī" (the one who) or the conditional. End of quote.

"Al-istirāq" is a reflexive form derived from "al-sariqa" (theft), which is taking something secretly, namely snatching speech with a quick brief snatch. "Al-sam'" (hearing) is the thing heard. The meaning of "mubīn" (clear) is evident to those who see.

[p. 448] [p. 449] [p. 450]

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 1–25 (part 4 of 4)**

﴿And the earth — We spread it out, and cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow in it every thing in balanced measure.﴾ ﴿And We made for you in it means of livelihood, and [also] for those whom you do not provide for.﴾ ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.﴾ ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing, then sent down water from the sky and gave it to you to drink, and you are not its keepers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors.﴾ ﴿And We have known those of you who go forward, and We have known those who remain behind.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord — it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, Knowing.﴾

*Madadnaha* (مَدَدْناها): *basatnaha*, we spread it out, so that benefit may be obtained from it by those who dwell on it. Al-Hasan said: Allah took a clump of clay and said to it, "Spread out," and it spread out. It was also said: it was spread out from beneath the Ka'bah.

Since the clause that follows this phrase is a verbal clause (*jumla fi'liyya*), the accusative reading (*al-nasb*) is preferable to the nominative reading on the basis of inchoative (*al-ibtida'*) construction, which is why (*wal-ard*) is in the accusative. [Here *al-nasb 'ala al-ishtighal* (النصب على الاشتغال), the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun placed first, is preferred over *al-raf' 'ala al-ibtida'* (الرفع على الابتداء), the nominative on the basis of inchoative construction.]

*Al-rawasi* (الرَّواسِي): the mountains. In a hadith: "Indeed the earth used to shake with its inhabitants as a ship shakes, so Allah made it firm with the mountains."

The *min* (مِن) in ﴿min kulli﴾ is partitive (*li-l-tab'idh*, indicating a part of the whole). According to al-Akhfash, it is extra (*za'ida*, redundant), meaning *kull shay'* (every thing).

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (*fiha*) refers to the earth that was spread out. It was also said that it refers to the mountains, and it was also said that it refers to both of them together.

Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: *mawzun* means measured by a measure. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this, saying: it was weighed by the scale of wisdom and measured by a measure which requires that there be no addition or deficiency in it. Ibn Atiyya said: the majority said its meaning is *muqaddar* (determined), *muharrar* (precisely arranged) by intention and will, so the weighing (*al-wazn*) in this sense is metaphorical. Ibn Zayd said: what is intended is that which is literally weighed, such as gold and silver and other things that are weighed. Qatada said: *mawzun* means divided (*maqsum*). Mujahid said: *ma'dud* (counted). Al-Zamakhshari also said: or it has weight and measure in the matters of blessing and benefit. Another expounded it, saying: it has a standing, as you say, "he has no weight," meaning he has no worth and standing. It is also said: "this is *kalam mawzun*," meaning versified, not scattered. On this view, *anbatna fiha* (we caused to grow in it) includes what is weighed of jewels, minerals and animals.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He caused it to grow a good growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. The intended meaning of *inbat* (causing to grow) is creation and bringing into existence.

Al-A'raj and Kharija from Nafi' read *ma'ayish* (مَعائِشَ) with a hamza. Ibn Atiyya said: the correct form is to omit the hamza, and he gave a reason for that which is well known in grammar. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ma'ayish*, with a clear *ya'* (ياء), unlike *al-shama'il* and *al-khaba'ith*, for making the *ya'* clear in them is an error, and the correct form is the hamza, or else the *ya'* is pronounced in an intermediate way (*bayn bayn*, between the hamza and the *ya'*).

The explanation of *ma'ayish* has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf. The apparent reading is that *man* (مَن) refers to rational beings, and what is intended by it is dependants, slaves and servants, whom you think you provide for, and you are mistaken, for Allah is the Provider who provides for you and for them. Al-Farra said this too. What is included with them by way of predominance (*al-taghlib*) is what is not rational, such as livestock and beasts. *Ma* (ما) in this sense is among those whom Allah provides for, and their thought has already gone to the idea that they are the providers. Al-Zajjaj also said this. Mujahid said: the beasts, livestock and cattle. It was said: wild animals, predators and birds. On these two views, *man* refers to what is not rational.

The apparent reading is that *man* is in the genitive position (*fi mawdi' jarr*), in coordination (*'atf*) with the genitive pronoun in *lakum*. This is the view of the Kufis, Yunus and al-Akhfash. The one who holds this view has used as evidence for its soundness the verse in al-Baqarah: ﴿and disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217].

Al-Zajjaj said: *man* is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted whose estimate is: "and We gave life to whom you do not provide for," i.e., other nations than you, because the meaning is "We gave you life." It was also said: it is in coordination with *ma'ayish*, meaning: "and We made for you, and for those whom you do not provide for, of slaves and craftsmen, means of livelihood." It was also said: and animals. It was said: in coordination with the place (*mahall*) of *lakum*. It was also said: *man* is the subject of an inchoative clause whose predicate is omitted, being indicated by the meaning, i.e.: "and for whom you do not provide, We made for him means of livelihood in it." This is not objectionable, for they permitted: "I struck Zayd, and 'Amr" with the nominative on the basis of inchoative construction, meaning: "and as for 'Amr, I struck him," the predicate being omitted because what came before indicates it.

The explanation of the treasuries (*khaza'in*) has already been given. *In* (إنْ) is negative, and *min* is extra. The apparent meaning is: there is nothing that the servants benefit from except that We are capable of bringing it into existence, creating it, and bestowing it. Thus the treasuries, which are the places in which things are kept, are used metaphorically, from the sensible (the physical body) to the intelligible.

Some people said: what is meant is the treasuries literally, which are the places in which things are kept; that the wind has a place, the rain has a place, and every place has an angel and guardians. When Allah commands that something be brought out of it, the guardians bring it out. It was also said: what is meant by *shay'* here is rain. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Al-A'mash read: (*wa-ma nursiluhu*) in place of ﴿wa-ma nunazziluhu﴾. *Al-irsal* (sending) is more general. This is a reading for explanation of meaning, not a reading of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (*sawad al-mushaf*). From Ibn Abbas and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna: there is no year with more rain than another, but Allah the Exalted sends it down in some places and not in others.

*Lawaqih* (لَواقِحُ) is the plural of *laqih* (لاقِحٌ). It is said: *rih laqih*, meaning winds bringing good by producing rain-bearing clouds, just as the one that brings no good but evil is called *rih 'aqim* (a barren wind). Or *mala'iq*, meaning bearers of rain. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari: *lawaqih* means *mala'ih* (fertilizing), *mulaqqaha* (made to fertilize).

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Allah sends the *mubashshira* (the bearer of good tidings), which sweeps the earth with a sweep, then the *muthira* (the stirring one), which stirs up the clouds, then the *mu'allifa* (the gathering one), which gathers them together. Then Allah sends the *lawaqih*, which fertilize the trees.

As for the one who reads *al-rih* in the singular, it is according to the interpretation of the genus (*ta'wil al-jins*), as they say: "The yellow dinar destroyed the people," and "the white dirham." *Saqa* (سَقى) and *asqa* (أسْقى) may both have the same meaning. Abu 'Ubayda said: whoever gives drink to the mouth uses *saqa* only, while for giving drink to land and fruit trees he uses *asqa*, and for calling someone to drink from land or other things, he uses *asqa* only. Al-Azhari said: the Arabs say of everything that is from the bellies of livestock, or from the sky, or from a flowing river: *asqaytuhu*, meaning I made it a drink for him, and I made for him a place to drink from it. When it is for the mouth, they say *saqa* and do not say *asqa*. Abu 'Ali said: *saqaytuhu* means until he was satisfied, and *asqaytuhu* nahran means I made it a drink for him (from a river).

The pronoun here comes connected after another connected pronoun, as was mentioned earlier in the verse: ﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾ [Hud: 28]. It has already been stated that the view of Sibawayh regarding this is that connection is obligatory.

*Wa-ma antum lahu bi-khazinin*: that is, you are not capable of bringing it into existence, as an indication of His great power and a demonstration of your incapacity. *Hum* (هم): that is, you are not capable of it at the time you need it. Sufyan said: *bi-khazinin* means not withholding the rain.

*Nuhyi* (نُحْيِـي): We bring it out from pure non-existence into life. *Numit* (نُمِيتُ): We remove its life. *Wa-nahnu al-warithun* (وَنَحْنُ الوارِثُونَ): the ones who remain after the passing away of the creation.

As for *al-mustaqdimin* (المُسْتَقْدِمِينَ), Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: they are the dead, and *al-musta'khirin* (المُسْتَأْخِرِينَ) are the living. Qatada, Ikrima and others said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who came earlier in creation, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who have not yet been created.

Mujahid said: *al-mustaqdimin* are the earlier nations, and *al-musta'khirin* are the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan and Qatada also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who advanced in obedience and goodness, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lagged behind in disobedience and evil.

Ibn Jubayr said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those in the front rows of battle, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lag behind in it. It was also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who were killed in jihad, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who were not killed. It was said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those in the front rows of prayer, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who lag behind because of women, in order to look at them. Qatada also said: *al-mustaqdimin* are those who hastened to Islam, and *al-musta'khirin* are those who held back from it.

The better view is to take these statements as examples (*al-tamthil*), not as exhaustive limitation (*al-hasr*). The meaning is that His knowledge encompasses those who went before and those who came after, and their circumstances. Then the Exalted informed that He will gather them.

Al-A'mash read *yahshirhum* (يَحْشِرُهم) with a kasra on the *shin*. Ibn Abbas, Marwan ibn al-Hakam and Abu al-Hawra' said: a beautiful woman used to pray behind the Messenger (ﷺ). Some would move forward so as not to be tempted by her, and some would lag behind in order to steal a glance at her during the prayer, so the verse was revealed concerning them.

The Exalted concluded this verse with these two attributes, wisdom and knowledge, in the utmost appropriateness.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book, and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieved will often wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without it having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾ ﴿They said: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely possessed!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿We send down the angels only with truth, and then they would not be granted respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and We Ourselves will surely preserve it.﴾ ﴿We sent messengers before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has passed before them.﴾ ﴿Even if We opened to them a gate from the sky and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people under sorcery!"﴾ ﴿We have placed constellations in the sky and adorned it for the beholders.﴾ ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil.﴾ ﴿Except one who steals a hearing, and a clear flaming meteor pursues him.﴾ ﴿As for the earth, We spread it out, cast firmly set mountains upon it, and caused every kind of thing to grow in it in due measure.﴾ ﴿We made for you therein means of livelihood, and for those whom you do not provide for.﴾ ﴿There is not a thing but its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure.﴾ ﴿We send the winds fertilizing, then We send down water from the sky and give you drink from it, though you are not its keepers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritor.﴾ ﴿We certainly know those of you who go forward, and We certainly know those who hold back.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will gather them; He is Wise, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿We certainly created man from clay of dry ringing mud, shaped from black molded clay.﴾ [al-Hijr: 26] ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the scorching wind.﴾ [al-Hijr: 27] (p. 442)

*Rubba*: a particle of jarr (governing, a preposition), not a noun, contrary to the Kufans, al-Akhfash in one of his two opinions, and Ibn al-Tarawah. Its meaning, according to the well-known view, is diminution (*taqlil*) rather than multiplication (*takthir*), contrary to the claim of the one who asserts this and attributes it to Sibawayh, and contrary to the one who says it conveys neither diminution nor multiplication but is a particle of affirmation. The claim of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi that there is consensus that it is set for diminution is baseless. The statement of al-Zajjaj that *rubba* is for multiplication, the opposite of what the people of the language know, is not correct. It has several dialects, and its rules are numerous and are mentioned in grammar. It occurs in the Qur'an only in this surah, despite how frequently it occurs in the speech of the Arabs.

*Dhar*: an imperative that has largely dispensed with its past tense by using *tark* (leaving). In a hadith: "Leave the Abyssinians as long as they leave you."

*Lawma*: a particle of exhortation (*tahdid*), followed by a verb, explicit or implied; and a particle of prohibition (*imtina'*) for the existence of something, followed by a noun as its subject according to the Basran school. From it is the verse of the poet:

Had it not been for shame, and had it not been for religion, I would have reproached you both for some of what is in you, since you have reproached me for my faults.

Some have said that the *mim* in *lawma* is a substitute for the *lam* in *lawla*. Similar is *istawla 'ala al-shay'* and *istawma*; *khallaltuhu* and *khalamtuhu*, so that *khilli* and *khilmi* mean "my friend."

Al-Zamakhshari said: *law* is combined with *la* and *ma* for two meanings. As for *hal*, it is combined only with *la* alone, for exhortation, and that is the end of his statement. What I choose is that both are simple, not compound, and that *ma* is not a substitute for *la*.

*Salaka al-khayt fi al-ibra* and *aslakaha*: he inserted it into it and strung it. The poet said:

Until, when they drove them into a narrow place, scattering them as the driver drives the stray herd.

Another said:

And I was the wrangler of your opponent, not having been accustomed; and they have led you into a grievous day.

*Al-shihab*: a flame of fire, and it is also applied to a star because of its brightness, being likened to fire. Abu Tammam said:

And the banner amid the spear-shafts is gleaming, between the two armies, not among the seven shining stars.

*Al-lawaqih*: the apparent meaning is that it is the plural of *laqih*, meaning those possessing fertilization (*liqah*), like *labin* and *tamir*, because the wind passes over water, then passes over the clouds and trees, and so there is fertilization in it. This was said by al-Farra'. Al-Azhari said: they are carriers that bear the clouds and direct them. A she-camel is *laqih*, and female camels are *lawaqih* when they carry foetuses in their wombs. Zuhayr said:

When a fierce, harmful war is fertilized, a biting one, its teeth are bared, and it frightens the people.

Abu 'Ubayda said: it means *malaqih*, the plural of *mulaqqiha*, because it fertilizes the clouds by casting water. He said:

And one struck, by what the calamities cast down.

That is, *al-matawih*, the plural of *mutih*.

*Al-salsal*: Abu 'Ubayda said it is clay when mixed with sand and dried. Abu al-Haytham said: *al-salsal* is the sound of a bridle and the like, like the rattling in a garment.
