He, exalted is He, when He had alerted [us] to the final end of creation, which is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, to where they will settle, alerted them to the origin of their root, Adam, and to what took place with his enemy Iblis in the dialogue with Allah, exalted is He. Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. It was also said: it means "poured," from "sanantu al-turab wa al-ma'a," when you pour them one after another; so the meaning is: "I pour out the form of a human as forms are poured out from molten substances in their moulds." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿hama'in masnun﴾ in the sense of "shaped" may be a descriptor of ﴿salsal﴾, as if He poured out the black mud and shaped from it an image of a hollow human; it dried until, when struck, it rang (salsala), then He changed it after that into another substance; end of quote. It was also said: *al-masnun* means "shaped" from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. The poet said:

*It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

*Al-jann* is the father of the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-jann* for the jinn is like Adam for mankind. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is Iblis, who was created before Adam. Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

﴿Sawwaytuhu﴾ means "I completed its creation," and *al-taswiyah* is an expression for perfection and making its parts balanced in what they were created for. ﴿Wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi﴾ means: I brought life into it. There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. Issues concerning ﴿minha﴾ have been discussed previously in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf, and the exegetes repeated them here. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. It is described as "appointed" either because Allah alone knows it, as He said: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]; ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]; or because the end of the world is known to occur at it. Thus He expressed it as the Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time, with what was near to that Day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of His misguiding him is attributing to him [the responsibility] for his error, in that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, and that led to his error. The command to prostrate is not the best [thing]; it is an opportunity for reward through humility and submission to the command of Allah [p. 454], but Iblis chose refusal and arrogance, so he perished, while Allah, exalted is He, is free of his error, of his will, and of approval of it; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (al-I'tizal, a rationalist theological school). The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ refers to something not mentioned but understood from the context, namely the descendants of Adam. For this reason, in another verse He said: ﴿If You reprieve me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. The adornment (al-tazyin) is making sins appear good to them and his whispering until they fall into them. "On earth" means: in this world, which is the abode of delusion, due to His saying: ﴿He inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. Or he meant: "I am able to scheme against Adam and to make [eating from] the tree appealing to him, although that was in heaven; so I am more able to adorn it for his offspring." Or he meant: "I will make the place of adornment with them the earth, and I will raise my rank in it," i.e., "I will adorn it in their eyes, and I will tell them that the adornment is in this world alone, until they prefer it over the Hereafter and feel content with it instead," and similar to this is: "it wounds in its hamstrings, we pray," as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿Illa 'ibadaka﴾ (except Your servants) is an exception of a few from many, since the sincere ones are few in comparison to the deviators. His exception of them [from the scope of his misguidance] means that Iblis knew that his adornment would not affect them. In this there is evidence for the high rank of this attribute, and that it is the best quality that the obedient one can possess.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. The Arabs say: "Your course in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning that the consideration of your affair belongs to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a true path that it is incumbent upon me to observe, which is that you have no authority over My servants except those who choose to follow you from among them for their own misguidance," end of quote. Thus he made this a reference to the negation of Iblis's adornment and seduction, and to his having no authority over them. It seems he took the demonstrative as referring to what Iblis excepted and to what God affirmed with His words ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ (Indeed My servants). His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

The author of al-Lawami' said: that is, "This is a path whose uprightness is entrusted to Me," and "in its preservation," meaning its preservation is upon Me, and it is straight and not crooked. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ is "towards Me." It was also said: ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ means that whoever passes along it passes towards Me, that is, towards My good pleasure and My honour.

Al-Dahhak, Ibrahim, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Humayd, 'Amr ibn Maymun, 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, Abu Sharaf (client of Kindah), and Ya'qub read ﴿عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾: meaning "exalted," because of the highness of its status. This reading confirms that the reference is to sincerity, and it is closer to it. The annexation in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ is an annexation of honour, meaning: those specially devoted to My worship. On this view, ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ (except those who follow you) is not a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because whoever followed him is not included in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾. However, if by ﴿عِبَادِي﴾ the whole of creation is meant, then ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from a general category, and it would indicate the exclusion of the majority and the remainder of the excepted group being fewer. This is a question on which the grammarians differed. The Kufans permitted it, and following them among our companions was the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf; the proofs for this are recorded in the books of grammar.

What appears evident is that when Iblis excepted the sincere servants, the attribute was intended in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾; that is, "My sincere servants whom I have mentioned: you have no authority over them." The ﴿مِنْ﴾ in ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾ is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), meaning: those who are the misguided.

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of those who claim that Satan and the jinn are able to cause people to fall (*sar') and to remove their intellects, as the common people say, and as they sometimes attribute to sorcerers. He said: this contradicts what God has explicitly stated. ﴿وَلِمَوْعِدِهِمْ﴾ (and for their appointed meeting) is the place of the promised meeting, and the pronoun refers to ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ is an emphatic, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial state (*hal*), end of quote. This is an inclination towards the view of those who claim that ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ indicates the unity of time, whereas the correct view is that its meaning is the same as the meaning of ﴿كُلِّهِمْ﴾ (all of them). (p-455)

It was said: the gates of the Fire are its layers and its levels: the highest is for the monotheists, the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. *It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. Something different is reported from al-Zuhri. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah it says: "Ibn Shihab read with a damma on the zay," and this is probably a copyist's error, because I found in al-Tahrir: "Ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on both, with hamza." In the book of al-Zamakhshari and the book of al-Lawami', it is reported that he read with the shadda; in al-Lawami' it is said he and Abu Ja'far (did so as well).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

He, exalted is He, when He had alerted [us] to the final end of creation, which is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, to where they will settle, alerted them to the origin of their root, Adam, and to what took place with his enemy Iblis in the dialogue with Allah, exalted is He. Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. It was also said: it means "poured," from "sanantu al-turab wa al-ma'a," when you pour them one after another; so the meaning is: "I pour out the form of a human as forms are poured out from molten substances in their moulds." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿hama'in masnun﴾ in the sense of "shaped" may be a descriptor of ﴿salsal﴾, as if He poured out the black mud and shaped from it an image of a hollow human; it dried until, when struck, it rang (salsala), then He changed it after that into another substance; end of quote. It was also said: *al-masnun* means "shaped" from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. The poet said:

*It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

*Al-jann* is the father of the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-jann* for the jinn is like Adam for mankind. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is Iblis, who was created before Adam. Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

﴿Sawwaytuhu﴾ means "I completed its creation," and *al-taswiyah* is an expression for perfection and making its parts balanced in what they were created for. ﴿Wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi﴾ means: I brought life into it. There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. Issues concerning ﴿minha﴾ have been discussed previously in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf, and the exegetes repeated them here. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. It is described as "appointed" either because Allah alone knows it, as He said: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]; ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]; or because the end of the world is known to occur at it. Thus He expressed it as the Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time, with what was near to that Day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of His misguiding him is attributing to him [the responsibility] for his error, in that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, and that led to his error. The command to prostrate is not the best [thing]; it is an opportunity for reward through humility and submission to the command of Allah [p. 454], but Iblis chose refusal and arrogance, so he perished, while Allah, exalted is He, is free of his error, of his will, and of approval of it; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (al-I'tizal, a rationalist theological school). The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ refers to something not mentioned but understood from the context, namely the descendants of Adam. For this reason, in another verse He said: ﴿If You reprieve me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. The adornment (al-tazyin) is making sins appear good to them and his whispering until they fall into them. "On earth" means: in this world, which is the abode of delusion, due to His saying: ﴿He inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. Or he meant: "I am able to scheme against Adam and to make [eating from] the tree appealing to him, although that was in heaven; so I am more able to adorn it for his offspring." Or he meant: "I will make the place of adornment with them the earth, and I will raise my rank in it," i.e., "I will adorn it in their eyes, and I will tell them that the adornment is in this world alone, until they prefer it over the Hereafter and feel content with it instead," and similar to this is: "it wounds in its hamstrings, we pray," as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿Illa 'ibadaka﴾ (except Your servants) is an exception of a few from many, since the sincere ones are few in comparison to the deviators. His exception of them [from the scope of his misguidance] means that Iblis knew that his adornment would not affect them. In this there is evidence for the high rank of this attribute, and that it is the best quality that the obedient one can possess.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. The Arabs say: "Your course in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning that the consideration of your affair belongs to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a true path that it is incumbent upon me to observe, which is that you have no authority over My servants except those who choose to follow you from among them for their own misguidance," end of quote. Thus he made this a reference to the negation of Iblis's adornment and seduction, and to his having no authority over them. It seems he took the demonstrative as referring to what Iblis excepted and to what God affirmed with His words ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ (Indeed My servants). His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

The author of al-Lawami' said: that is, "This is a path whose uprightness is entrusted to Me," and "in its preservation," meaning its preservation is upon Me, and it is straight and not crooked. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ is "towards Me." It was also said: ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ means that whoever passes along it passes towards Me, that is, towards My good pleasure and My honour.

Al-Dahhak, Ibrahim, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Humayd, 'Amr ibn Maymun, 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, Abu Sharaf (client of Kindah), and Ya'qub read ﴿عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾: meaning "exalted," because of the highness of its status. This reading confirms that the reference is to sincerity, and it is closer to it. The annexation in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ is an annexation of honour, meaning: those specially devoted to My worship. On this view, ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ (except those who follow you) is not a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because whoever followed him is not included in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾. However, if by ﴿عِبَادِي﴾ the whole of creation is meant, then ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from a general category, and it would indicate the exclusion of the majority and the remainder of the excepted group being fewer. This is a question on which the grammarians differed. The Kufans permitted it, and following them among our companions was the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf; the proofs for this are recorded in the books of grammar.

What appears evident is that when Iblis excepted the sincere servants, the attribute was intended in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾; that is, "My sincere servants whom I have mentioned: you have no authority over them." The ﴿مِنْ﴾ in ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾ is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), meaning: those who are the misguided.

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of those who claim that Satan and the jinn are able to cause people to fall (*sar') and to remove their intellects, as the common people say, and as they sometimes attribute to sorcerers. He said: this contradicts what God has explicitly stated. ﴿وَلِمَوْعِدِهِمْ﴾ (and for their appointed meeting) is the place of the promised meeting, and the pronoun refers to ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ is an emphatic, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial state (*hal*), end of quote. This is an inclination towards the view of those who claim that ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ indicates the unity of time, whereas the correct view is that its meaning is the same as the meaning of ﴿كُلِّهِمْ﴾ (all of them). (p-455)

It was said: the gates of the Fire are its layers and its levels: the highest is for the monotheists, the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. *It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. Something different is reported from al-Zuhri. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah it says: "Ibn Shihab read with a damma on the zay," and this is probably a copyist's error, because I found in al-Tahrir: "Ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on both, with hamza." In the book of al-Zamakhshari and the book of al-Lawami', it is reported that he read with the shadda; in al-Lawami' it is said he and Abu Ja'far (did so as well).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

He, exalted is He, when He had alerted [us] to the final end of creation, which is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, to where they will settle, alerted them to the origin of their root, Adam, and to what took place with his enemy Iblis in the dialogue with Allah, exalted is He. Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. It was also said: it means "poured," from "sanantu al-turab wa al-ma'a," when you pour them one after another; so the meaning is: "I pour out the form of a human as forms are poured out from molten substances in their moulds." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿hama'in masnun﴾ in the sense of "shaped" may be a descriptor of ﴿salsal﴾, as if He poured out the black mud and shaped from it an image of a hollow human; it dried until, when struck, it rang (salsala), then He changed it after that into another substance; end of quote. It was also said: *al-masnun* means "shaped" from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. The poet said:

*It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

*Al-jann* is the father of the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-jann* for the jinn is like Adam for mankind. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is Iblis, who was created before Adam. Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

﴿Sawwaytuhu﴾ means "I completed its creation," and *al-taswiyah* is an expression for perfection and making its parts balanced in what they were created for. ﴿Wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi﴾ means: I brought life into it. There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. Issues concerning ﴿minha﴾ have been discussed previously in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf, and the exegetes repeated them here. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. It is described as "appointed" either because Allah alone knows it, as He said: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]; ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]; or because the end of the world is known to occur at it. Thus He expressed it as the Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time, with what was near to that Day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of His misguiding him is attributing to him [the responsibility] for his error, in that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, and that led to his error. The command to prostrate is not the best [thing]; it is an opportunity for reward through humility and submission to the command of Allah [p. 454], but Iblis chose refusal and arrogance, so he perished, while Allah, exalted is He, is free of his error, of his will, and of approval of it; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (al-I'tizal, a rationalist theological school). The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ refers to something not mentioned but understood from the context, namely the descendants of Adam. For this reason, in another verse He said: ﴿If You reprieve me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. The adornment (al-tazyin) is making sins appear good to them and his whispering until they fall into them. "On earth" means: in this world, which is the abode of delusion, due to His saying: ﴿He inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. Or he meant: "I am able to scheme against Adam and to make [eating from] the tree appealing to him, although that was in heaven; so I am more able to adorn it for his offspring." Or he meant: "I will make the place of adornment with them the earth, and I will raise my rank in it," i.e., "I will adorn it in their eyes, and I will tell them that the adornment is in this world alone, until they prefer it over the Hereafter and feel content with it instead," and similar to this is: "it wounds in its hamstrings, we pray," as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿Illa 'ibadaka﴾ (except Your servants) is an exception of a few from many, since the sincere ones are few in comparison to the deviators. His exception of them [from the scope of his misguidance] means that Iblis knew that his adornment would not affect them. In this there is evidence for the high rank of this attribute, and that it is the best quality that the obedient one can possess.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. The Arabs say: "Your course in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning that the consideration of your affair belongs to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a true path that it is incumbent upon me to observe, which is that you have no authority over My servants except those who choose to follow you from among them for their own misguidance," end of quote. Thus he made this a reference to the negation of Iblis's adornment and seduction, and to his having no authority over them. It seems he took the demonstrative as referring to what Iblis excepted and to what God affirmed with His words ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ (Indeed My servants). His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

The author of al-Lawami' said: that is, "This is a path whose uprightness is entrusted to Me," and "in its preservation," meaning its preservation is upon Me, and it is straight and not crooked. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ is "towards Me." It was also said: ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ means that whoever passes along it passes towards Me, that is, towards My good pleasure and My honour.

Al-Dahhak, Ibrahim, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Humayd, 'Amr ibn Maymun, 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, Abu Sharaf (client of Kindah), and Ya'qub read ﴿عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾: meaning "exalted," because of the highness of its status. This reading confirms that the reference is to sincerity, and it is closer to it. The annexation in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ is an annexation of honour, meaning: those specially devoted to My worship. On this view, ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ (except those who follow you) is not a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because whoever followed him is not included in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾. However, if by ﴿عِبَادِي﴾ the whole of creation is meant, then ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from a general category, and it would indicate the exclusion of the majority and the remainder of the excepted group being fewer. This is a question on which the grammarians differed. The Kufans permitted it, and following them among our companions was the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf; the proofs for this are recorded in the books of grammar.

What appears evident is that when Iblis excepted the sincere servants, the attribute was intended in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾; that is, "My sincere servants whom I have mentioned: you have no authority over them." The ﴿مِنْ﴾ in ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾ is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), meaning: those who are the misguided.

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of those who claim that Satan and the jinn are able to cause people to fall (*sar') and to remove their intellects, as the common people say, and as they sometimes attribute to sorcerers. He said: this contradicts what God has explicitly stated. ﴿وَلِمَوْعِدِهِمْ﴾ (and for their appointed meeting) is the place of the promised meeting, and the pronoun refers to ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ is an emphatic, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial state (*hal*), end of quote. This is an inclination towards the view of those who claim that ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ indicates the unity of time, whereas the correct view is that its meaning is the same as the meaning of ﴿كُلِّهِمْ﴾ (all of them). (p-455)

It was said: the gates of the Fire are its layers and its levels: the highest is for the monotheists, the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. *It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. Something different is reported from al-Zuhri. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah it says: "Ibn Shihab read with a damma on the zay," and this is probably a copyist's error, because I found in al-Tahrir: "Ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on both, with hamza." In the book of al-Zamakhshari and the book of al-Lawami', it is reported that he read with the shadda; in al-Lawami' it is said he and Abu Ja'far (did so as well).

Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

Its basis is that he dropped the hamza, transferred its vowel to the zay, then stopped with the shadda, as in ﴿هَذَا فَرَجٌ﴾, and then applied the pause form to the continuous reading. Something different is reported from al-Zuhri. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah it says: "Ibn Shihab read with a damma on the zay," and this is probably a copyist's error, because I found in al-Tahrir: "Ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on both, with hamza." Al-Zuhri read with a shadda on the zay without hamza, and this is the reading of Ibn al-Qa'qa'. A group read it with the shadda, among them Ibn al-Qa'qa'. In the book of al-Zamakhshari and the book of al-Lawami', it is reported that he read with the shadda; in al-Lawami' it is said he and Abu Ja'far (did so as well).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 15, verses 26–46 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And We certainly created man from clay, from black mud altered in form.﴾ ﴿And the jinn We had created before from the fire of scorching wind.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will create a human from clay, from black mud altered in form."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, fall down to him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely.﴾ ﴿Except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"﴾ ﴿He said, "I would never prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered in form."﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are expelled.﴾ ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the time appointed."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will certainly make [wrongdoing] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾ ﴿except Your sincere servants among them."﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "This is a straight path to Me.﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants – you will have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators."﴾ ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all.﴾ ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate is a portion designated [for them]."﴾

He, exalted is He, when He had alerted [us] to the final end of creation, which is the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, to where they will settle, alerted them to the origin of their root, Adam, and to what took place with his enemy Iblis in the dialogue with Allah, exalted is He. Part of this story has already been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah, following the mention of death, life, and return to Him, exalted is He. It is also [mentioned] in al-A'raf after the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the mention of the scales on it. In al-Kahf, it comes after the mention of the gathering, and likewise in Surah Sad, after the mention of what He has prepared of Paradise and Hellfire for His creation. So when He mentioned the final end of this creation, He mentioned its beginning [p. 453] and its story with his enemy Iblis, so that they might be warned against his scheming and consider what happened to him with Him, until He expelled him from Paradise, the abode of happiness and ease, to the earth, the abode of obligation and hardship, so that they would guard themselves against his scheming.

As for ﴿min hama'in﴾ (from black mud), al-Hawfi said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿min salsalin﴾ (from clay), with the preposition repeated. Abu al-Baqa' said that ﴿min hama'in﴾ is in a genitive position as a descriptive (sifah) of ﴿salsal﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-masnun* means clay, and its meaning is "poured," because it is not poured unless it is wet; so he referred to "poured" by describing it, because it is placed for that purpose. Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ma'mar said: *al-masnun* means "foul-smelling." Al-Zamakhshari said: [it derives] from "sanantu al-hajar 'ala al-hajar," when you rub one stone against another, so what flows between them is *sanin*, and it is only foul-smelling. Others said: [it derives] from "asana al-ma'u," when water changes. This is not valid because the two roots differ. It was also said: it means "poured," from "sanantu al-turab wa al-ma'a," when you pour them one after another; so the meaning is: "I pour out the form of a human as forms are poured out from molten substances in their moulds." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿hama'in masnun﴾ in the sense of "shaped" may be a descriptor of ﴿salsal﴾, as if He poured out the black mud and shaped from it an image of a hollow human; it dried until, when struck, it rang (salsala), then He changed it after that into another substance; end of quote. It was also said: *al-masnun* means "shaped" from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form. The poet said:

*It shows you the form (sunnat) of a face, not disgraced.*

It was also said: *al-masnun* means "attributed," i.e., his descendants are attributed to him.

*Al-jann* is the father of the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-jann* for the jinn is like Adam for mankind. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is Iblis, who was created before Adam. Ibn Bahr said: it is a name for the species of jinn, and "the human" intended is Adam; and "min qabl" means: before the creation of the human.

Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read *wa al-ja'n* with a hamzah. As for *al-samum*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the hot wind that kills. He also said: it is a fire with no smoke, from which thunderbolts come. Al-Hasan said: it is a fire with a barrier beyond it. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the breath of fire; and from him also: it is the flame of fire. It was said: the fire of blazing flame is *al-samum*. It was said: the described (*mawsuf*) was attributed to its description, i.e., "the fire, the scorching [wind]."

﴿Sawwaytuhu﴾ means "I completed its creation," and *al-taswiyah* is an expression for perfection and making its parts balanced in what they were created for. ﴿Wa nafakhtu fihi min ruhi﴾ means: I brought life into it. There is no blowing there, and nothing is literally blown; it is only an image (tamthil) for achieving what He gives life with. He attributed the spirit to Himself, exalted is He, as a form of honour, like "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah"; or [it means] ownership, since He is the one who disposes of the creation of the spirit and places it wherever He wills.

﴿Waqa'u lahu﴾ means: fall upon the earth. The preposition is omitted from *an* (i.e., "that"): "what is for you in not being...?" and "what call summoned you to refuse prostration?" As for ﴿li-asjuda﴾, the *lam* is *lam al-juhud* (the lam of denial), and the meaning is: "It is not suitable for my state to prostrate to him."

In al-Baqarah, He alerted to the cause that prevents it, which is arrogance, meaning he saw himself as too great to prostrate. In al-A'raf He stated explicitly the direction of arrogance, which is claiming superiority and excellence by claiming the substance from which each of them was created. Here He alerted only to the substance of Adam alone, and here [it says] ﴿fakhruj minha﴾ (get out of it), while in al-A'raf it is ﴿fahbut minha﴾ (descend from it) [al-A'raf: 13]. The disagreement about what the pronoun in *minha* refers back to was mentioned earlier. Issues concerning ﴿minha﴾ have been discussed previously in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf, and the exegetes repeated them here. We refer to what was mentioned earlier, except for what has a particular feature in this surah, and we mention that.

So we say: The Day of Recompense was set as the limit for the curse, either because it is the furthest limit by which people are harmed in their speech, or it may mean that you are blameworthy and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Recompense, without being punished. When that Day comes, you will be punished with what makes one forget the curse. The Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time are one and the same. It is the time of the first blast, until creation dies. It is described as "appointed" either because Allah alone knows it, as He said: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]; ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]; or because the end of the world is known to occur at it. Thus He expressed it as the Day of Recompense, the Day they are resurrected, and the Day of the appointed time, with what was near to that Day.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of His misguiding him is attributing to him [the responsibility] for his error, in that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, and that led to his error. The command to prostrate is not the best [thing]; it is an opportunity for reward through humility and submission to the command of Allah [p. 454], but Iblis chose refusal and arrogance, so he perished, while Allah, exalted is He, is free of his error, of his will, and of approval of it; end of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (al-I'tizal, a rationalist theological school). The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ refers to something not mentioned but understood from the context, namely the descendants of Adam. For this reason, in another verse He said: ﴿If You reprieve me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. The adornment (al-tazyin) is making sins appear good to them and his whispering until they fall into them. "On earth" means: in this world, which is the abode of delusion, due to His saying: ﴿He inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. Or he meant: "I am able to scheme against Adam and to make [eating from] the tree appealing to him, although that was in heaven; so I am more able to adorn it for his offspring." Or he meant: "I will make the place of adornment with them the earth, and I will raise my rank in it," i.e., "I will adorn it in their eyes, and I will tell them that the adornment is in this world alone, until they prefer it over the Hereafter and feel content with it instead," and similar to this is: "it wounds in its hamstrings, we pray," as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿Illa 'ibadaka﴾ (except Your servants) is an exception of a few from many, since the sincere ones are few in comparison to the deviators. His exception of them [from the scope of his misguidance] means that Iblis knew that his adornment would not affect them. In this there is evidence for the high rank of this attribute, and that it is the best quality that the obedient one can possess.

The Kufans, Nafi', al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَخْلَصْتَهُ﴾ with a fatha on the lam (*al-lam*). Its meaning is: "except those whom You have made sincere to obedience, so my adornment has no effect on them." The rest of the seven readers and the majority read it with a kasra: "except those who made their deed sincere for God and did not associate anyone else with Him in it." The verb ﴿وَلَا رَأَى بِهِ﴾ and the subject of ﴿قَالَ﴾ is God: "God said." The demonstrative ﴿هَذَا﴾ refers to what is implied by the word "the sincere ones" (*al-mukhlasin*) as a verbal noun, meaning: sincerity that occurs among My servants is ﴿صِرَاطٌ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ (a straight path) that no one treads and then strays or slips from, because whomever I have chosen, or who has made his deed sincere for Me, you have no authority over him. It was also said: when Iblis divided the descendants of Adam into the misguided and the sincere, God said: "This is a matter whose outcome returns to Me," and described it as uprightness; that is, it is true, and their ending in these two categories is not up to you. The Arabs say: "Your course in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning that the consideration of your affair belongs to him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a true path that it is incumbent upon me to observe, which is that you have no authority over My servants except those who choose to follow you from among them for their own misguidance," end of quote. Thus he made this a reference to the negation of Iblis's adornment and seduction, and to his having no authority over them. It seems he took the demonstrative as referring to what Iblis excepted and to what God affirmed with His words ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ (Indeed My servants). His statement contains the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school).

The author of al-Lawami' said: that is, "This is a path whose uprightness is entrusted to Me," and "in its preservation," meaning its preservation is upon Me, and it is straight and not crooked. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ is "towards Me." It was also said: ﴿عَلَيَّ﴾ means that whoever passes along it passes towards Me, that is, towards My good pleasure and My honour.

Al-Dahhak, Ibrahim, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Humayd, 'Amr ibn Maymun, 'Imarah ibn Abi Hafsah, Abu Sharaf (client of Kindah), and Ya'qub read ﴿عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾: meaning "exalted," because of the highness of its status. This reading confirms that the reference is to sincerity, and it is closer to it. The annexation in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾ is an annexation of honour, meaning: those specially devoted to My worship. On this view, ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ (except those who follow you) is not a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because whoever followed him is not included in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾. However, if by ﴿عِبَادِي﴾ the whole of creation is meant, then ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from a general category, and it would indicate the exclusion of the majority and the remainder of the excepted group being fewer. This is a question on which the grammarians differed. The Kufans permitted it, and following them among our companions was the teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf; the proofs for this are recorded in the books of grammar.

What appears evident is that when Iblis excepted the sincere servants, the attribute was intended in ﴿إِنَّ عِبَادِي﴾; that is, "My sincere servants whom I have mentioned: you have no authority over them." The ﴿مِنْ﴾ in ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾ is explanatory of the kind (*li-bayan al-jins*), meaning: those who are the misguided.

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of those who claim that Satan and the jinn are able to cause people to fall (*sar') and to remove their intellects, as the common people say, and as they sometimes attribute to sorcerers. He said: this contradicts what God has explicitly stated. ﴿وَلِمَوْعِدِهِمْ﴾ (and for their appointed meeting) is the place of the promised meeting, and the pronoun refers to ﴿الْغَاوِينَ﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ is an emphatic, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial state (*hal*), end of quote. This is an inclination towards the view of those who claim that ﴿أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ indicates the unity of time, whereas the correct view is that its meaning is the same as the meaning of ﴿كُلِّهِمْ﴾ (all of them). (p-455)

The apparent meaning is that Hell (*jahannam*) is one, and it has seven gates. It was said: the gates of the Fire are its layers and its levels: the highest is for the monotheists, the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites.

Ibn al-Qa'qa' read ﴿جَزٌّ﴾ with a shadda on the zay without hamza. Its basis is that he dropped the hamza, transferred its vowel to the zay, then stopped with the shadda, as in ﴿هَذَا فَرَجٌ﴾, and then applied the pause form to the continuous reading. Something different is reported from al-Zuhri. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah it says: "Ibn Shihab read with a damma on the zay," and this is probably a copyist's error, because I found in al-Tahrir: "Ibn Wathhab read it with a damma on both, with hamza." Al-Zuhri read with a shadda on the zay without hamza, and this is the reading of Ibn al-Qa'qa'. A group read it with the shadda, among them Ibn al-Qa'qa'. In the book of al-Zamakhshari and the book of al-Lawami', it is reported that he read with the shadda; in al-Lawami' it is said he and Abu Ja'far (did so as well).
