"Fa-bima tubashshirun" (then of what do you give good news) is an emphasis of incredulity and wonder, and it is as if he did not know that they were angels sent by God to him, and so he asked, and found it strange that a son be born to him. Had he known that they were messengers of God, he would not have marvelled or found it strange, especially since he had seen with his own eyes the signs of God, how He gave life to the dead.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is as if he said: "Then by what wonder do you give me good news?" Or he meant: you give me good news of what is not conceivable in habit, so by what thing do you give good news? That is: you do not in reality give me good news of anything, since the good news of such a thing is good news of nothing. It is permissible that it not be a complement of "basar" (human), and that it be a question about the manner and method, meaning: by what manner do you give me good news of a son, when good news of such has no manner in custom? End quote. It is as if he said: "Is it on account of my being described as old, or because I am being returned to youth?" It was also said: when he found the good news pleasant, he repeated the question. This is weakened by their saying to him: ﴿We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing﴾.

Al-Hasan read "tubashshirunni" with a doubled nun and the ya' of the first person, assimilating the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya). Ibn Kathir read it with the nun doubled and kasra, without a ya'. Nafi' read it with a kasra and single nun, and Abu Hatim criticised him as a mistake, and said: this occurs only in poetry out of necessity. It was explained that he dropped the nun of protection and vowelled the nun of the nominative with a kasra for the ya', then the ya' was dropped because the kasra indicates it. They said it is like the saying of the poet:

"Yasu'u al-qalibat idha qalayni" (It grieves the [women] who forsake when they have forsaken me)

and the saying of another:

"La abaki tukhawwifini" (By your father, you do not frighten me)

The remaining seven read it with a fatha (p. 459), which is the sign of the nominative.

Al-Hasan said: "Fa-bima tubashshirun" is in the manner of belittling and little concern for the good news, because of the passing of age and the dominance of old age. Mujahid said: he marvelled at his own old age and the old age of his wife, and his age at the time of the good news had been mentioned earlier.

"Bil-haqq" (in truth): that is, with the certainty in which there is no doubt, or by the way which is truth, and it is the word of God and His promise, and that He is able to bring about a child without two parents, so how much more from an aged old man and a barren old woman. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, and it is related from Abu Amr, read "min al-qanitin" (of those who despair), from "qanita, yaqnatu". The two grammarians (al-nahwiyyan) and al-A'mash read "wa-man yaqnatu" (and who despairs). It is an interrogative which contains negation within it, and for this reason "illa" (except) entered in His saying: ﴿except the astray﴾. Their saying to him: ﴿So do not be of the despairing﴾ is a prohibition, and a prohibition against something does not indicate that the one prohibited is engaged in it or accompanied by it. His saying ﴿And who despairs﴾ is a rejection of them, and that the dialogue about the good news does not indicate despair, rather that is by way of astonishment regarding what custom has established. In that there is an indication that the giving of a child in old age is from the mercy of God, since it strengthens the arm of his father by him and supports him in a state where he is not self-sufficient, and he inherits from him his knowledge and his religion.

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,"﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all﴾ ﴿except his wife. We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾ ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot,﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown."﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to dispute."﴾ ﴿And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night and follow behind them, and let not one of you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.﴾ ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree: that the last remnant of those would be cut off by morning.﴾

When they gave him good news of the son and debated with him about it, he knew that they were the angels of God and His messengers, and so he asked with His saying: ﴿Then what is your business?﴾ The word "khatb" (business) is hardly said except of a grave matter, so he attributed it to them, in that they were the bearers of it to those tormented people. He made "qawman" (a people) and its description indefinite, to diminish them and to show contempt for them, and they were the people of Lot, the inhabitants of the city of Sodom (p. 460). The meaning: we have been sent with destruction.

"Illa al-Lut" (except the family of Lot): it is possible that it is an exception from the pronoun concealed in "mujrimin" (criminals), and the estimate is: "they all committed crime except the family of Lot," so it would be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning: except the family of Lot, for they did not commit crime. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them all" would be a resumed statement of information about their deliverance, because they did not commit crime, and the ruling of sending would extend to a criminal people and to the family of Lot: for the destruction of these and the saving of those. The apparent sense is that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because the family of Lot is not included in the general meaning by the indefiniteness of "qawmin mujrimin" (a criminal people), and because the description of crime is not in the family of Lot. And if it is an exception, then it is of the kind in which the accusative must be used, because it is an exception that cannot be governed by the operator upon the excepted item, since they were not sent to them at all; rather they were sent only to the criminal people. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them" operates in the manner of the predicate of "lakinna" (but) in its connection to the family of Lot, because the meaning is: "but the family of Lot will be saved." Some grammarians have claimed about the disconnected exception that is estimated as "lakin" (but), when there is nothing after it that could be a predicate, that the predicate is omitted, and that it is in the nominative position because of the operation of "illa" (except) and its estimate as "lakin".

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Regarding His saying "except his wife," what is it excepted from, and is it an exception from an exception? (I answer): It is excepted from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying "surely We will deliver them," and it has nothing to do with exception (istithna'), because exception occurs only where the ruling is the same, as if one said: "We destroyed them except the family of Lut, except his wife," just as the ruling is the same in the speech of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times, except two, except one," and in the speech of the one who acknowledges to someone: "I owe him ten dirhams except three, except one dirham." But in the verse the two rulings differ, because "except the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "criminals," while "except his wife" is connected to "surely We will deliver them," so how could it be an exception from an exception? End of quote.

When al-Zamakhshari had asserted that "except his wife" is excepted from the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them," he did not allow it to be an exception from an exception. Whoever says it is an exception can have his statement made sound in one of two ways. The first: since the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them" refers back to the family of Lut, and she has been excepted from it, it becomes as if she were excepted from the family of Lut, because the pronoun in meaning is the same as the noun it refers to. The second: when His saying "except the family of Lut" passes a ruling on them that differs from the ruling on the criminal people, this implies their deliverance, so His saying "surely We will deliver them all" comes as an emphasis of the meaning of the exception, since the meaning is: "except the family of Lut, upon whom We did not send the punishment," and their deliverance is consequent upon not sending the punishment to them. This is like your saying: "The people stood up except Zayd," for he did not stand, and "except Zayd did not stand." So this clause is an emphasis of what the exception contains of a ruling on what follows "except," the opposite of the ruling preceding the excepted-from term. Thus "except his wife," according to this explanation we have set out, is an exception from "the family of Lut," because an exception from what was brought for establishment (ta'sis) is preferable to an exception from what was brought for emphasis (ta'kid).

The two brothers (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) read "lamunajjuhum" with light stress (takhfif), and the rest of the seven read it with heavy stress (tashdid). Abu Bakr read "qadarna" with light stress, and the rest of the seven with heavy stress. "Inna" is read with a kasra because the verb of decreeing (taqdir) is treated as the verb of knowing (ilm), either because it has its meaning or because it leads to it. They attributed the decree to themselves and did not say "God decreed," because they are the ones commanded to destroy them, as one who takes refuge with a king and one who acts under his commands says: "We were commanded to do such-and-such," while the commander is the king. Al-Zamakhshari said: because of their closeness and special relationship to God, which none other than they have. End of quote. Thus he wove the Mu'tazilite doctrine of the superiority of the angels into the course of his speech.

"Munkarun" (unknown to him) is said of people because he found them strange and recoiled from them, and feared that they would visit him with evil. "Bal" (but) is a turning away from an implied statement, meaning: "We did not come to you with anything you fear; rather, We came to you with punishment for your people, since they were doubting it," that is, doubting its occurrence, or disputing with you about it, calling you a liar in what you promised them from God. It is possible that he found them strange because they were not known in this region, so he feared an attack from them upon him, or that someone of his people might confront them, since they appeared as handsome beardless youths.

"Wa-atayna-ka bil-haqq": that is, with certainty about their punishment. "Wa-inna la-sadiqun": truthful in the report, because it will descend upon them. The disagreement about the reading in "fa-asri" has already been mentioned. The author of al-Iqlid transmitted it as "fussira" from the journey (siyar), and Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Lawami' transmitted it from al-Yamani. Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id related that a group read "qit'in" with a fatha on the ta', and the discussion of qat' (cutting) and of iltifat (shift of person) was mentioned in Surat Hud.

Al-Zamakhshari here delivered a discourse, saying: (If you ask): What is the meaning of His command to follow behind them, and His prohibition against looking back? (I answer): God sent destruction upon his people, and saved him and his household, in answer to his supplication against them, and he went out as an emigrant. So there was no escape from striving in gratitude to God and continuing His remembrance and emptying his mind; for this reason he was commanded to put them ahead of him, so that his heart would not be occupied with those behind him, and so that he would observe them and their terrors, and no glance of concern nor other slip would escape him in that dreadful and feared situation, and so that none of them would lag behind for some purpose and be struck. And his journey would be that of the fugitive whose going forth precedes him and is lost to him.

"Haythu tu'marun": Ibn 'Abbas said: the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: a place of salvation not known. It was also said: Egypt. It was also said: to the land of Abraham, to a place called al-Yaqin. "Haythu" here retains its primary sense as a spatial adverb. The claim that it may be a temporal adverb, since in the verse there is no command except His saying "So travel with your household in a part of the night," and then it was said to him "where you are commanded," is weak. The wording "tu'marun" indicates otherwise, since the construction would have been "min haythu umirtum." "Haythu" is among the indefinite spatial adverbs, and for this reason the verb reaches it directly, as in "go," and you say: "I sat where Zayd sat." In poetry the particle "fi" has come before it. The poet said:

"So he woke in the place where we met their fugitive, freed, with his two hands bound and his nose bleeding."

When "qadayna" was made to include the sense of "awhayna" (We revealed), it took the preposition "ila" as its complement, meaning: "We revealed to Lut the matter decreed, decisively settled." The indication by "dhalika" refers to what God promised him of the destruction of his people. "Anna dabira" is for magnification and glorification of the matter, and it is in the accusative position as a substitute for "dhalika," as al-Akhfash said, or by dropping the preposition, meaning "bi-anna dabiran," as al-Farra' said, and al-Hawfi permitted it. "Anna dabira ha'ulai maqtu'un" is a metaphor for complete extermination. The explanation of a similar expression in His saying "so the root of the people who did wrong was cut off" [al-An'am: 45] has already been given. "Musbihin" means entering into morning, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in "maqtu'" according to meaning. For this reason al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd made it plural and estimated: "if they are entering morning," as you say: "You riding are better than you walking." If this is an explanation of meaning it is correct, but if it is meant as grammatical analysis, there is no necessity for this estimate.

Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza, since the verb "qadayna" includes the sense of "awhayna," so the meaning was "we informed," and the verb governed it so the particle "inna" took a kasra; or because the decree in the sense of revelation has the sense of saying, the two kasras agree. This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah. We say that "inna dabira" is a reading of interpretation, not of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the written text.

"Al-madina" is Sodom, the city whose judge was struck as a proverb for injustice.

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ [Al-Hijr: 45] ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [Al-Hijr: 46] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; they will be as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ ﴿No weariness will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it﴾ ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾

When God mentioned what He had prepared for the people of the Fire, He mentioned what He had prepared for the people of Paradise, to show the contrast between the two groups. Since the state of the believers is a matter of concern, He informed that they are in gardens and springs. He treated what they will settle in the Hereafter as though they were already settled in it in this world. For this reason it came as ﴿ṭ adkhulūhā﴾ ("enter it," imperative) in the reading of the imperative, because one who has already settled in a place is not said to be "made to enter" it. The state of the deviators came as a promise in His saying ﴿li-mawʿiduhum﴾ ("their appointed place"), because they had not entered it.

﴿al-ʿuyūn﴾ (the springs) is the plural of ʿayn. Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ and Hishām read ﴿wa-ʿUyūn﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, and the rest of the seven read it with a kasrah. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as a past tense verb in the passive voice, from the causative form (al-idkhāl). Yaʿqūb, in the transmission of Ruways, read it the same way, with a ḍammah on the tanwīn, and it is also reported from him that he read it with a fatḥah. What follows is an imperative under an assumed reading: "Cause them to enter it," from the causative form, meaning He commanded the angels to bring the God-fearing into Paradise, and the hamzah drops in both readings. The majority read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as an imperative from the verb "to enter." According to the two imperative readings, there is an elided element, i.e., "it is said to them," or "it is said to the angels."

﴿bi-salām﴾ (in peace) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It may mean "accompanied by safety," or it may mean "greeted," i.e., "those greeted with peace," as is related about the angels, that they enter upon the people of Paradise saying: "Peace be upon you."

﴿wa-nazaʿnā mā fī ṣudūrihim min ghill﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts). Its explanation was given in al-Aʿrāf. It has been said: ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and it is a state relating to the pronoun. A state relating to the genitive-governed noun (muḍāf ilayhi) is rare when it is not governed by the thing it is attached to, in either the nominative or accusative case. For this reason some said that when the first noun is a part of the second, as here (since "breasts" are part of the people), and is like a part, as in His saying ﴿wa-ittabaʿa millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfan﴾ [An-Nisa: 125], a state comes from the genitive-governed noun. We have established that this is not permissible. The evidence they cite has an interpretation other than what they mention. Its interpretation here is that it is in the accusative by way of praise, the sense being: "I praise [them as] brothers." Since it cannot be an adjective of the pronoun, it has been detached from its case and placed in the accusative for praise. Abū al-Baqāʾ has mentioned that it is a state relating to the pronoun in the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿fī jannāt﴾ (in gardens) [Al-Hijr: 45], and that it may be a state relating to the subject of ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ (enter it), or to the pronoun in ﴿āminīn﴾ (secure).

The meaning of ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is: people who have close ties and mutual affection. ﴿ʿalā sururin mutaqābilīn﴾ (upon couches, facing one another): these are two states. Sitting upon couches is a sign of exalted rank and complete honor, as He said: "They ride the back of this sea as kings upon thrones," or "like kings upon thrones." From Ibn ʿAbbās: "upon couches adorned with jacinth, emerald and pearls." Qatādah said: ﴿mutaqābilīn﴾ means "equal in mutual connection and visiting." From Mujāhid: "None of them looks at the back of another; the couches turn them wherever they turn, so that in all their states they are facing one another." End.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 47–66 (part 2 of 3)

Since this world (al-dunya) is a place of toil, with the strain of seeking a livelihood, the hardship of the obligations necessary for the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter, the company of opposites, the onset of calamities and illnesses, and a place of transition from it to another abode, its affairs are fearful for the believer. It is not a place of permanent residence. Almighty God informed that this is absent in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾. When touch is negated, perpetuity is established. He emphasized the negation of expulsion by the entry of the particle bi- (bi-) into: "bi-mukhrajin" (﴿nor shall they be expelled from it﴾).

It was said: reward has four conditions. It must be beneficial, and to this points His saying: ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ [al-Hijr: 45], accompanied by honour. To this points His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [al-Hijr: 46], free from the places of spiritual impurities, such as resentment and envy, and of bodily ones, such as weariness and toil. To this points His saying: "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾, as a lasting state. To this points His saying: ﴿Nor shall they be expelled from it﴾.

It is related from Ali ibn al-Husayn that His saying "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar, and that "al-ghill" (rancour) is the rancour of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance). It was also said: there had been enmities between the Banu Tamim, Adi and Hashim, and when they embraced Islam they came to love one another.

When the mention of what is in the Fire and what is in the Garden had preceded, Almighty God emphasized the alerting of people and the establishment of this in the soul by His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The mention of forgiveness and mercy fits with the connection of this to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ [al-Hijr: 45]. And in giving precedence to these two great attributes by which He described Himself, His saying ﴿and that My punishment﴾ came in the utmost gentleness, since He did not say it in the manner of a contrast, and that I am the one who punishes painfully. All of this is a preference for the aspect of pardon and mercy.

"Anna" (that) fills the place of the two objects of "nabbi'" (inform) if we say it takes three objects, and fills the place of one if we say it takes two. It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Forgiving" is for the one who repents, and His punishment is for the one who does not repent.

In His saying "nabbi'" (inform) up to the end of the verse, there is a preference for the aspect of good, from the aspect of His command to His Messenger with this proclamation. It is as if it were a testimony by Himself to His undertaking of forgiveness and mercy. His attributing the servants to Himself is an honour for them. And the emphasis of the name of "anna" (that) is by His saying "ana" (I). The prefixing of al- (the definite article) to these two attributes, and their coming in the form of intensive emphasis (mubalagha), and the beginning with the attribute that delights first, which is forgiveness, followed by the attribute from which forgiveness arises, which is mercy.

It is related in a hadith: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from the forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy his own soul." And in a hadith from Ibn al-Mubarak, with his chain of narration: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came out from the gate through which the Banu Shayba enter, and we were laughing. He said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, until when he reached al-Hijr, he came back to us backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, came and said: God says: Why do you despair, My servants?' [and he recited] ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾."

(p. 458) ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good news of a boy with much knowledge."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good news although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good news?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾

When Almighty God mentioned what He had prepared for the disobedient of the Fire and for the obedient of the Garden, He reminded the Arabs of the circumstances of those whom they know, from among those who disobeyed and denied the messengers, and upon whom the punishment of this world befell before the punishment of the Hereafter, so that they might desist from their disbelief and take warning from what befell others. So He began with the mention of their great forefather Abraham, peace be upon him, and what befell the people of his nephew Lot, then with the mention of the companions of al-Hijr, who were the people of Salih, then with the companions of al-Aykah, who were the people of Shu'ayb.

Abu Haywa read "wa-nabiyyuhum" with the hamza replaced by a ya'.

The guests of Abraham were the angels who gave him good news of a son and of the destruction of the people of Lot. They were attributed to Abraham although they were not guests, because they were in the appearance of those who used to come to him as guests, since none came to him without his hosting them, and he was called "Abu al-Diyfan" (father of guests). His palace had four gates, one on each side, so that no one would pass him by.

The word "dayf" (guest) is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and the more eloquent usage is that it is not made dual or plural for the dual or plural. There is no need to strain with an implied term, as al-Nahhas and others said, such as "companions of a guest" (ashab dayf).

"Salaman" (peace) is detached from a quoted sentence introduced by "qalu" (they said), so it is not governed by it. The estimate is: "I greet with a greeting of safety" (sallamtu salaman min al-salama), or "we greet with a greeting of salutation" (sallamna salaman min al-tahiyya). It was also said: "salaman" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "they said a word of peace" (fa-qalu qawlan salaman). Its explicit statement here that he was a man among them came after his bringing near to them what he hosted them with, namely the roasted calf, and their refraining from eating it. In Hud it is mentioned that he sensed fear in himself (awjasa fi nafsihi khifa). So it is possible that this explicit statement came after the sensing of fear. It is also possible that the saying here is metaphorical, in that signs of fear appeared upon him until he became like one who had explicitly said it.

(The sentence) ﴿Do not fear﴾ was read by the majority with the verb active (la tawjal). Al-Hasan read it with the taa' vowelled with a damma, passive, from "ijal" (causing fear). It was also read "la tajal" with the waw replaced by an alif, as they said "taba" in "tawba" (repentance). And it was read "la tuwajil", from "wajalahu," in the sense of "awjalahu" (caused him fear).

"Inna nubashshiruka" (Indeed, we give you good news) is a resumptive statement in the sense of the reason for the prohibition against fear, meaning: you are like one secure who brings good news, so do not fear. The one given good news of is Isaac, and that was after Ishmael had been born to him and had grown up. They gave him good news of two matters. The first: that he is a male. The second: they described him with knowledge by way of emphasis. It was said: the prophethood, as in His saying: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. And it was said: knowledgeable in religion.

Al-A'raj read "bashshartumuni" (have you given me good news) without the interrogative hamza, and taking "massani al-kibar" (old age has touched me) as in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Ibn Muhaysin read "al-kubr" with a damma on the kaf and a sukun on the ba'. Abraham, peace be upon him, found it strange that a child should be born to him in old age. "Fa-bima tubashshirun" (then of what do you give good news) is an emphasis of incredulity and wonder, and it is as if he did not know that they were angels sent by God to him, and so he asked, and found it strange that a son be born to him. Had he known that they were messengers of God, he would not have marvelled or found it strange, especially since he had seen with his own eyes the signs of God, how He gave life to the dead.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is as if he said: "Then by what wonder do you give me good news?" Or he meant: you give me good news of what is not conceivable in habit, so by what thing do you give good news? That is: you do not in reality give me good news of anything, since the good news of such a thing is good news of nothing. It is permissible that it not be a complement of "basar" (human), and that it be a question about the manner and method, meaning: by what manner do you give me good news of a son, when good news of such has no manner in custom? End quote. It is as if he said: "Is it on account of my being described as old, or because I am being returned to youth?" It was also said: when he found the good news pleasant, he repeated the question. This is weakened by their saying to him: ﴿We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing﴾.

Al-Hasan read "tubashshirunni" with a doubled nun and the ya' of the first person, assimilating the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya). Ibn Kathir read it with the nun doubled and kasra, without a ya'. Nafi' read it with a kasra and single nun, and Abu Hatim criticised him as a mistake, and said: this occurs only in poetry out of necessity. It was explained that he dropped the nun of protection and vowelled the nun of the nominative with a kasra for the ya', then the ya' was dropped because the kasra indicates it. They said it is like the saying of the poet:

"Yasu'u al-qalibat idha qalayni" (It grieves the [women] who forsake when they have forsaken me)

and the saying of another:

"La abaki tukhawwifini" (By your father, you do not frighten me)

The remaining seven read it with a fatha (p. 459), which is the sign of the nominative.

Al-Hasan said: "Fa-bima tubashshirun" is in the manner of belittling and little concern for the good news, because of the passing of age and the dominance of old age. Mujahid said: he marvelled at his own old age and the old age of his wife, and his age at the time of the good news had been mentioned earlier.

"Bil-haqq" (in truth): that is, with the certainty in which there is no doubt, or by the way which is truth, and it is the word of God and His promise, and that He is able to bring about a child without two parents, so how much more from an aged old man and a barren old woman. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, and it is related from Abu Amr, read "min al-qanitin" (of those who despair), from "qanita, yaqnatu". The two grammarians (al-nahwiyyan) and al-A'mash read "wa-man yaqnatu" (and who despairs). It is an interrogative which contains negation within it, and for this reason "illa" (except) entered in His saying: ﴿except the astray﴾. Their saying to him: ﴿So do not be of the despairing﴾ is a prohibition, and a prohibition against something does not indicate that the one prohibited is engaged in it or accompanied by it. His saying ﴿And who despairs﴾ is a rejection of them, and that the dialogue about the good news does not indicate despair, rather that is by way of astonishment regarding what custom has established. In that there is an indication that the giving of a child in old age is from the mercy of God, since it strengthens the arm of his father by him and supports him in a state where he is not self-sufficient, and he inherits from him his knowledge and his religion.

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,"﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all﴾ ﴿except his wife. We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾ ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot,﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown."﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to dispute."﴾ ﴿And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night and follow behind them, and let not one of you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.﴾ ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree: that the last remnant of those would be cut off by morning.﴾

When they gave him good news of the son and debated with him about it, he knew that they were the angels of God and His messengers, and so he asked with His saying: ﴿Then what is your business?﴾ The word "khatb" (business) is hardly said except of a grave matter, so he attributed it to them, in that they were the bearers of it to those tormented people. He made "qawman" (a people) and its description indefinite, to diminish them and to show contempt for them, and they were the people of Lot, the inhabitants of the city of Sodom (p. 460). The meaning: we have been sent with destruction.

"Illa al-Lut" (except the family of Lot): it is possible that it is an exception from the pronoun concealed in "mujrimin" (criminals), and the estimate is: "they all committed crime except the family of Lot," so it would be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning: except the family of Lot, for they did not commit crime. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them all" would be a resumed statement of information about their deliverance, because they did not commit crime, and the ruling of sending would extend to a criminal people and to the family of Lot: for the destruction of these and the saving of those. The apparent sense is that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because the family of Lot is not included in the general meaning by the indefiniteness of "qawmin mujrimin" (a criminal people), and because the description of crime is not in the family of Lot. And if it is an exception, then it is of the kind in which the accusative must be used, because it is an exception that cannot be governed by the operator upon the excepted item, since they were not sent to them at all; rather they were sent only to the criminal people. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them" operates in the manner of the predicate of "lakinna" (but) in its connection to the family of Lot, because the meaning is: "but the family of Lot will be saved." Some grammarians have claimed about the disconnected exception that is estimated as "lakin" (but), when there is nothing after it that could be a predicate, that the predicate is omitted, and that it is in the nominative position because of the operation of "illa" (except) and its estimate as "lakin".

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Regarding His saying "except his wife," what is it excepted from, and is it an exception from an exception? (I answer): It is excepted from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying "surely We will deliver them," and it has nothing to do with exception (istithna'), because exception occurs only where the ruling is the same, as if one said: "We destroyed them except the family of Lut, except his wife," just as the ruling is the same in the speech of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times, except two, except one," and in the speech of the one who acknowledges to someone: "I owe him ten dirhams except three, except one dirham." But in the verse the two rulings differ, because "except the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "criminals," while "except his wife" is connected to "surely We will deliver them," so how could it be an exception from an exception? End of quote.

When al-Zamakhshari had asserted that "except his wife" is excepted from the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them," he did not allow it to be an exception from an exception. Whoever says it is an exception can have his statement made sound in one of two ways. The first: since the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them" refers back to the family of Lut, and she has been excepted from it, it becomes as if she were excepted from the family of Lut, because the pronoun in meaning is the same as the noun it refers to. The second: when His saying "except the family of Lut" passes a ruling on them that differs from the ruling on the criminal people, this implies their deliverance, so His saying "surely We will deliver them all" comes as an emphasis of the meaning of the exception, since the meaning is: "except the family of Lut, upon whom We did not send the punishment," and their deliverance is consequent upon not sending the punishment to them. This is like your saying: "The people stood up except Zayd," for he did not stand, and "except Zayd did not stand." So this clause is an emphasis of what the exception contains of a ruling on what follows "except," the opposite of the ruling preceding the excepted-from term. Thus "except his wife," according to this explanation we have set out, is an exception from "the family of Lut," because an exception from what was brought for establishment (ta'sis) is preferable to an exception from what was brought for emphasis (ta'kid).

The two brothers (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) read "lamunajjuhum" with light stress (takhfif), and the rest of the seven read it with heavy stress (tashdid). Abu Bakr read "qadarna" with light stress, and the rest of the seven with heavy stress. "Inna" is read with a kasra because the verb of decreeing (taqdir) is treated as the verb of knowing (ilm), either because it has its meaning or because it leads to it. They attributed the decree to themselves and did not say "God decreed," because they are the ones commanded to destroy them, as one who takes refuge with a king and one who acts under his commands says: "We were commanded to do such-and-such," while the commander is the king. Al-Zamakhshari said: because of their closeness and special relationship to God, which none other than they have. End of quote. Thus he wove the Mu'tazilite doctrine of the superiority of the angels into the course of his speech.

"Munkarun" (unknown to him) is said of people because he found them strange and recoiled from them, and feared that they would visit him with evil. "Bal" (but) is a turning away from an implied statement, meaning: "We did not come to you with anything you fear; rather, We came to you with punishment for your people, since they were doubting it," that is, doubting its occurrence, or disputing with you about it, calling you a liar in what you promised them from God. It is possible that he found them strange because they were not known in this region, so he feared an attack from them upon him, or that someone of his people might confront them, since they appeared as handsome beardless youths.

"Wa-atayna-ka bil-haqq": that is, with certainty about their punishment. "Wa-inna la-sadiqun": truthful in the report, because it will descend upon them. The disagreement about the reading in "fa-asri" has already been mentioned. The author of al-Iqlid transmitted it as "fussira" from the journey (siyar), and Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Lawami' transmitted it from al-Yamani. Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id related that a group read "qit'in" with a fatha on the ta', and the discussion of qat' (cutting) and of iltifat (shift of person) was mentioned in Surat Hud.

Al-Zamakhshari here delivered a discourse, saying: (If you ask): What is the meaning of His command to follow behind them, and His prohibition against looking back? (I answer): God sent destruction upon his people, and saved him and his household, in answer to his supplication against them, and he went out as an emigrant. So there was no escape from striving in gratitude to God and continuing His remembrance and emptying his mind; for this reason he was commanded to put them ahead of him, so that his heart would not be occupied with those behind him, and so that he would observe them and their terrors, and no glance of concern nor other slip would escape him in that dreadful and feared situation, and so that none of them would lag behind for some purpose and be struck. And his journey would be that of the fugitive whose going forth precedes him and is lost to him.

"Haythu tu'marun": Ibn 'Abbas said: the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: a place of salvation not known. It was also said: Egypt. It was also said: to the land of Abraham, to a place called al-Yaqin. "Haythu" here retains its primary sense as a spatial adverb. The claim that it may be a temporal adverb, since in the verse there is no command except His saying "So travel with your household in a part of the night," and then it was said to him "where you are commanded," is weak. The wording "tu'marun" indicates otherwise, since the construction would have been "min haythu umirtum." "Haythu" is among the indefinite spatial adverbs, and for this reason the verb reaches it directly, as in "go," and you say: "I sat where Zayd sat." In poetry the particle "fi" has come before it. The poet said:

"So he woke in the place where we met their fugitive, freed, with his two hands bound and his nose bleeding."

When "qadayna" was made to include the sense of "awhayna" (We revealed), it took the preposition "ila" as its complement, meaning: "We revealed to Lut the matter decreed, decisively settled." The indication by "dhalika" refers to what God promised him of the destruction of his people. "Anna dabira" is for magnification and glorification of the matter, and it is in the accusative position as a substitute for "dhalika," as al-Akhfash said, or by dropping the preposition, meaning "bi-anna dabiran," as al-Farra' said, and al-Hawfi permitted it. "Anna dabira ha'ulai maqtu'un" is a metaphor for complete extermination. The explanation of a similar expression in His saying "so the root of the people who did wrong was cut off" [al-An'am: 45] has already been given. "Musbihin" means entering into morning, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in "maqtu'" according to meaning. For this reason al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd made it plural and estimated: "if they are entering morning," as you say: "You riding are better than you walking." If this is an explanation of meaning it is correct, but if it is meant as grammatical analysis, there is no necessity for this estimate.

Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza, since the verb "qadayna" includes the sense of "awhayna," so the meaning was "we informed," and the verb governed it so the particle "inna" took a kasra; or because the decree in the sense of revelation has the sense of saying, the two kasras agree. This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah. We say that "inna dabira" is a reading of interpretation, not of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the written text.

"Al-madina" is Sodom, the city whose judge was struck as a proverb for injustice.

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ [Al-Hijr: 45] ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [Al-Hijr: 46] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; they will be as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ ﴿No weariness will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it﴾ ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾

When God mentioned what He had prepared for the people of the Fire, He mentioned what He had prepared for the people of Paradise, to show the contrast between the two groups. Since the state of the believers is a matter of concern, He informed that they are in gardens and springs. He treated what they will settle in the Hereafter as though they were already settled in it in this world. For this reason it came as ﴿ṭ adkhulūhā﴾ ("enter it," imperative) in the reading of the imperative, because one who has already settled in a place is not said to be "made to enter" it. The state of the deviators came as a promise in His saying ﴿li-mawʿiduhum﴾ ("their appointed place"), because they had not entered it.

﴿al-ʿuyūn﴾ (the springs) is the plural of ʿayn. Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ and Hishām read ﴿wa-ʿUyūn﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, and the rest of the seven read it with a kasrah. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as a past tense verb in the passive voice, from the causative form (al-idkhāl). Yaʿqūb, in the transmission of Ruways, read it the same way, with a ḍammah on the tanwīn, and it is also reported from him that he read it with a fatḥah. What follows is an imperative under an assumed reading: "Cause them to enter it," from the causative form, meaning He commanded the angels to bring the God-fearing into Paradise, and the hamzah drops in both readings. The majority read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as an imperative from the verb "to enter." According to the two imperative readings, there is an elided element, i.e., "it is said to them," or "it is said to the angels."

﴿bi-salām﴾ (in peace) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It may mean "accompanied by safety," or it may mean "greeted," i.e., "those greeted with peace," as is related about the angels, that they enter upon the people of Paradise saying: "Peace be upon you."

﴿wa-nazaʿnā mā fī ṣudūrihim min ghill﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts). Its explanation was given in al-Aʿrāf. It has been said: ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and it is a state relating to the pronoun. A state relating to the genitive-governed noun (muḍāf ilayhi) is rare when it is not governed by the thing it is attached to, in either the nominative or accusative case. For this reason some said that when the first noun is a part of the second, as here (since "breasts" are part of the people), and is like a part, as in His saying ﴿wa-ittabaʿa millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfan﴾ [An-Nisa: 125], a state comes from the genitive-governed noun. We have established that this is not permissible. The evidence they cite has an interpretation other than what they mention. Its interpretation here is that it is in the accusative by way of praise, the sense being: "I praise [them as] brothers." Since it cannot be an adjective of the pronoun, it has been detached from its case and placed in the accusative for praise. Abū al-Baqāʾ has mentioned that it is a state relating to the pronoun in the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿fī jannāt﴾ (in gardens) [Al-Hijr: 45], and that it may be a state relating to the subject of ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ (enter it), or to the pronoun in ﴿āminīn﴾ (secure).

The meaning of ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is: people who have close ties and mutual affection. ﴿ʿalā sururin mutaqābilīn﴾ (upon couches, facing one another): these are two states. Sitting upon couches is a sign of exalted rank and complete honor, as He said: "They ride the back of this sea as kings upon thrones," or "like kings upon thrones." From Ibn ʿAbbās: "upon couches adorned with jacinth, emerald and pearls." Qatādah said: ﴿mutaqābilīn﴾ means "equal in mutual connection and visiting." From Mujāhid: "None of them looks at the back of another; the couches turn them wherever they turn, so that in all their states they are facing one another." End.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 47–66 (part 2 of 3)

Since this world (al-dunya) is a place of toil, with the strain of seeking a livelihood, the hardship of the obligations necessary for the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter, the company of opposites, the onset of calamities and illnesses, and a place of transition from it to another abode, its affairs are fearful for the believer. It is not a place of permanent residence. Almighty God informed that this is absent in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾. When touch is negated, perpetuity is established. He emphasized the negation of expulsion by the entry of the particle bi- (bi-) into: "bi-mukhrajin" (﴿nor shall they be expelled from it﴾).

It was said: reward has four conditions. It must be beneficial, and to this points His saying: ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ [al-Hijr: 45], accompanied by honour. To this points His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [al-Hijr: 46], free from the places of spiritual impurities, such as resentment and envy, and of bodily ones, such as weariness and toil. To this points His saying: "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾, as a lasting state. To this points His saying: ﴿Nor shall they be expelled from it﴾.

It is related from Ali ibn al-Husayn that His saying "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar, and that "al-ghill" (rancour) is the rancour of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance). It was also said: there had been enmities between the Banu Tamim, Adi and Hashim, and when they embraced Islam they came to love one another.

When the mention of what is in the Fire and what is in the Garden had preceded, Almighty God emphasized the alerting of people and the establishment of this in the soul by His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The mention of forgiveness and mercy fits with the connection of this to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ [al-Hijr: 45]. And in giving precedence to these two great attributes by which He described Himself, His saying ﴿and that My punishment﴾ came in the utmost gentleness, since He did not say it in the manner of a contrast, and that I am the one who punishes painfully. All of this is a preference for the aspect of pardon and mercy.

"Anna" (that) fills the place of the two objects of "nabbi'" (inform) if we say it takes three objects, and fills the place of one if we say it takes two. It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Forgiving" is for the one who repents, and His punishment is for the one who does not repent.

In His saying "nabbi'" (inform) up to the end of the verse, there is a preference for the aspect of good, from the aspect of His command to His Messenger with this proclamation. It is as if it were a testimony by Himself to His undertaking of forgiveness and mercy. His attributing the servants to Himself is an honour for them. And the emphasis of the name of "anna" (that) is by His saying "ana" (I). The prefixing of al- (the definite article) to these two attributes, and their coming in the form of intensive emphasis (mubalagha), and the beginning with the attribute that delights first, which is forgiveness, followed by the attribute from which forgiveness arises, which is mercy.

It is related in a hadith: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from the forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy his own soul." And in a hadith from Ibn al-Mubarak, with his chain of narration: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came out from the gate through which the Banu Shayba enter, and we were laughing. He said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, until when he reached al-Hijr, he came back to us backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, came and said: God says: Why do you despair, My servants?' [and he recited] ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾."

(p. 458) ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good news of a boy with much knowledge."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good news although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good news?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾

When Almighty God mentioned what He had prepared for the disobedient of the Fire and for the obedient of the Garden, He reminded the Arabs of the circumstances of those whom they know, from among those who disobeyed and denied the messengers, and upon whom the punishment of this world befell before the punishment of the Hereafter, so that they might desist from their disbelief and take warning from what befell others. So He began with the mention of their great forefather Abraham, peace be upon him, and what befell the people of his nephew Lot, then with the mention of the companions of al-Hijr, who were the people of Salih, then with the companions of al-Aykah, who were the people of Shu'ayb.

Abu Haywa read "wa-nabiyyuhum" with the hamza replaced by a ya'.

The guests of Abraham were the angels who gave him good news of a son and of the destruction of the people of Lot. They were attributed to Abraham although they were not guests, because they were in the appearance of those who used to come to him as guests, since none came to him without his hosting them, and he was called "Abu al-Diyfan" (father of guests). His palace had four gates, one on each side, so that no one would pass him by.

The word "dayf" (guest) is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and the more eloquent usage is that it is not made dual or plural for the dual or plural. There is no need to strain with an implied term, as al-Nahhas and others said, such as "companions of a guest" (ashab dayf).

"Salaman" (peace) is detached from a quoted sentence introduced by "qalu" (they said), so it is not governed by it. The estimate is: "I greet with a greeting of safety" (sallamtu salaman min al-salama), or "we greet with a greeting of salutation" (sallamna salaman min al-tahiyya). It was also said: "salaman" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "they said a word of peace" (fa-qalu qawlan salaman). Its explicit statement here that he was a man among them came after his bringing near to them what he hosted them with, namely the roasted calf, and their refraining from eating it. In Hud it is mentioned that he sensed fear in himself (awjasa fi nafsihi khifa). So it is possible that this explicit statement came after the sensing of fear. It is also possible that the saying here is metaphorical, in that signs of fear appeared upon him until he became like one who had explicitly said it.

(The sentence) ﴿Do not fear﴾ was read by the majority with the verb active (la tawjal). Al-Hasan read it with the taa' vowelled with a damma, passive, from "ijal" (causing fear). It was also read "la tajal" with the waw replaced by an alif, as they said "taba" in "tawba" (repentance). And it was read "la tuwajil", from "wajalahu," in the sense of "awjalahu" (caused him fear).

"Inna nubashshiruka" (Indeed, we give you good news) is a resumptive statement in the sense of the reason for the prohibition against fear, meaning: you are like one secure who brings good news, so do not fear. The one given good news of is Isaac, and that was after Ishmael had been born to him and had grown up. They gave him good news of two matters. The first: that he is a male. The second: they described him with knowledge by way of emphasis. It was said: the prophethood, as in His saying: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. And it was said: knowledgeable in religion.

Al-A'raj read "bashshartumuni" (have you given me good news) without the interrogative hamza, and taking "massani al-kibar" (old age has touched me) as in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Ibn Muhaysin read "al-kubr" with a damma on the kaf and a sukun on the ba'. Abraham, peace be upon him, found it strange that a child should be born to him in old age. "Fa-bima tubashshirun" (then of what do you give good news) is an emphasis of incredulity and wonder, and it is as if he did not know that they were angels sent by God to him, and so he asked, and found it strange that a son be born to him. Had he known that they were messengers of God, he would not have marvelled or found it strange, especially since he had seen with his own eyes the signs of God, how He gave life to the dead.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is as if he said: "Then by what wonder do you give me good news?" Or he meant: you give me good news of what is not conceivable in habit, so by what thing do you give good news? That is: you do not in reality give me good news of anything, since the good news of such a thing is good news of nothing. It is permissible that it not be a complement of "basar" (human), and that it be a question about the manner and method, meaning: by what manner do you give me good news of a son, when good news of such has no manner in custom? End quote. It is as if he said: "Is it on account of my being described as old, or because I am being returned to youth?" It was also said: when he found the good news pleasant, he repeated the question. This is weakened by their saying to him: ﴿We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing﴾.

Al-Hasan read "tubashshirunni" with a doubled nun and the ya' of the first person, assimilating the nun of the nominative into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya). Ibn Kathir read it with the nun doubled and kasra, without a ya'. Nafi' read it with a kasra and single nun, and Abu Hatim criticised him as a mistake, and said: this occurs only in poetry out of necessity. It was explained that he dropped the nun of protection and vowelled the nun of the nominative with a kasra for the ya', then the ya' was dropped because the kasra indicates it. They said it is like the saying of the poet:

"Yasu'u al-qalibat idha qalayni" (It grieves the [women] who forsake when they have forsaken me)

and the saying of another:

"La abaki tukhawwifini" (By your father, you do not frighten me)

The remaining seven read it with a fatha (p. 459), which is the sign of the nominative.

Al-Hasan said: "Fa-bima tubashshirun" is in the manner of belittling and little concern for the good news, because of the passing of age and the dominance of old age. Mujahid said: he marvelled at his own old age and the old age of his wife, and his age at the time of the good news had been mentioned earlier.

"Bil-haqq" (in truth): that is, with the certainty in which there is no doubt, or by the way which is truth, and it is the word of God and His promise, and that He is able to bring about a child without two parents, so how much more from an aged old man and a barren old woman. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, and it is related from Abu Amr, read "min al-qanitin" (of those who despair), from "qanita, yaqnatu". The two grammarians (al-nahwiyyan) and al-A'mash read "wa-man yaqnatu" (and who despairs). It is an interrogative which contains negation within it, and for this reason "illa" (except) entered in His saying: ﴿except the astray﴾. Their saying to him: ﴿So do not be of the despairing﴾ is a prohibition, and a prohibition against something does not indicate that the one prohibited is engaged in it or accompanied by it. His saying ﴿And who despairs﴾ is a rejection of them, and that the dialogue about the good news does not indicate despair, rather that is by way of astonishment regarding what custom has established. In that there is an indication that the giving of a child in old age is from the mercy of God, since it strengthens the arm of his father by him and supports him in a state where he is not self-sufficient, and he inherits from him his knowledge and his religion.

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people,"﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all﴾ ﴿except his wife. We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾ ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot,﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown."﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to dispute."﴾ ﴿And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night and follow behind them, and let not one of you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.﴾ ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree: that the last remnant of those would be cut off by morning.﴾

When they gave him good news of the son and debated with him about it, he knew that they were the angels of God and His messengers, and so he asked with His saying: ﴿Then what is your business?﴾ The word "khatb" (business) is hardly said except of a grave matter, so he attributed it to them, in that they were the bearers of it to those tormented people. He made "qawman" (a people) and its description indefinite, to diminish them and to show contempt for them, and they were the people of Lot, the inhabitants of the city of Sodom (p. 460). The meaning: we have been sent with destruction.

"Illa al-Lut" (except the family of Lot): it is possible that it is an exception from the pronoun concealed in "mujrimin" (criminals), and the estimate is: "they all committed crime except the family of Lot," so it would be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning: except the family of Lot, for they did not commit crime. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them all" would be a resumed statement of information about their deliverance, because they did not commit crime, and the ruling of sending would extend to a criminal people and to the family of Lot: for the destruction of these and the saving of those. The apparent sense is that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), because the family of Lot is not included in the general meaning by the indefiniteness of "qawmin mujrimin" (a criminal people), and because the description of crime is not in the family of Lot. And if it is an exception, then it is of the kind in which the accusative must be used, because it is an exception that cannot be governed by the operator upon the excepted item, since they were not sent to them at all; rather they were sent only to the criminal people. And His saying "Indeed, We will save them" operates in the manner of the predicate of "lakinna" (but) in its connection to the family of Lot, because the meaning is: "but the family of Lot will be saved." Some grammarians have claimed about the disconnected exception that is estimated as "lakin" (but), when there is nothing after it that could be a predicate, that the predicate is omitted, and that it is in the nominative position because of the operation of "illa" (except) and its estimate as "lakin".

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Regarding His saying "except his wife," what is it excepted from, and is it an exception from an exception? (I answer): It is excepted from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying "surely We will deliver them," and it has nothing to do with exception (istithna'), because exception occurs only where the ruling is the same, as if one said: "We destroyed them except the family of Lut, except his wife," just as the ruling is the same in the speech of the one who divorces: "You are divorced three times, except two, except one," and in the speech of the one who acknowledges to someone: "I owe him ten dirhams except three, except one dirham." But in the verse the two rulings differ, because "except the family of Lut" is connected to "We sent" or to "criminals," while "except his wife" is connected to "surely We will deliver them," so how could it be an exception from an exception? End of quote.

When al-Zamakhshari had asserted that "except his wife" is excepted from the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them," he did not allow it to be an exception from an exception. Whoever says it is an exception can have his statement made sound in one of two ways. The first: since the pronoun in "surely We will deliver them" refers back to the family of Lut, and she has been excepted from it, it becomes as if she were excepted from the family of Lut, because the pronoun in meaning is the same as the noun it refers to. The second: when His saying "except the family of Lut" passes a ruling on them that differs from the ruling on the criminal people, this implies their deliverance, so His saying "surely We will deliver them all" comes as an emphasis of the meaning of the exception, since the meaning is: "except the family of Lut, upon whom We did not send the punishment," and their deliverance is consequent upon not sending the punishment to them. This is like your saying: "The people stood up except Zayd," for he did not stand, and "except Zayd did not stand." So this clause is an emphasis of what the exception contains of a ruling on what follows "except," the opposite of the ruling preceding the excepted-from term. Thus "except his wife," according to this explanation we have set out, is an exception from "the family of Lut," because an exception from what was brought for establishment (ta'sis) is preferable to an exception from what was brought for emphasis (ta'kid).

The two brothers (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) read "lamunajjuhum" with light stress (takhfif), and the rest of the seven read it with heavy stress (tashdid). Abu Bakr read "qadarna" with light stress, and the rest of the seven with heavy stress. "Inna" is read with a kasra because the verb of decreeing (taqdir) is treated as the verb of knowing (ilm), either because it has its meaning or because it leads to it. They attributed the decree to themselves and did not say "God decreed," because they are the ones commanded to destroy them, as one who takes refuge with a king and one who acts under his commands says: "We were commanded to do such-and-such," while the commander is the king. Al-Zamakhshari said: because of their closeness and special relationship to God, which none other than they have. End of quote. Thus he wove the Mu'tazilite doctrine of the superiority of the angels into the course of his speech.

"Munkarun" (unknown to him) is said of people because he found them strange and recoiled from them, and feared that they would visit him with evil. "Bal" (but) is a turning away from an implied statement, meaning: "We did not come to you with anything you fear; rather, We came to you with punishment for your people, since they were doubting it," that is, doubting its occurrence, or disputing with you about it, calling you a liar in what you promised them from God. It is possible that he found them strange because they were not known in this region, so he feared an attack from them upon him, or that someone of his people might confront them, since they appeared as handsome beardless youths.

"Wa-atayna-ka bil-haqq": that is, with certainty about their punishment. "Wa-inna la-sadiqun": truthful in the report, because it will descend upon them. The disagreement about the reading in "fa-asri" has already been mentioned. The author of al-Iqlid transmitted it as "fussira" from the journey (siyar), and Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of al-Lawami' transmitted it from al-Yamani. Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id related that a group read "qit'in" with a fatha on the ta', and the discussion of qat' (cutting) and of iltifat (shift of person) was mentioned in Surat Hud.

Al-Zamakhshari here delivered a discourse, saying: (If you ask): What is the meaning of His command to follow behind them, and His prohibition against looking back? (I answer): God sent destruction upon his people, and saved him and his household, in answer to his supplication against them, and he went out as an emigrant. So there was no escape from striving in gratitude to God and continuing His remembrance and emptying his mind; for this reason he was commanded to put them ahead of him, so that his heart would not be occupied with those behind him, and so that he would observe them and their terrors, and no glance of concern nor other slip would escape him in that dreadful and feared situation, and so that none of them would lag behind for some purpose and be struck. And his journey would be that of the fugitive whose going forth precedes him and is lost to him.

"Haythu tu'marun": Ibn 'Abbas said: the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: a place of salvation not known. It was also said: Egypt. It was also said: to the land of Abraham, to a place called al-Yaqin. "Haythu" here retains its primary sense as a spatial adverb. The claim that it may be a temporal adverb, since in the verse there is no command except His saying "So travel with your household in a part of the night," and then it was said to him "where you are commanded," is weak. The wording "tu'marun" indicates otherwise, since the construction would have been "min haythu umirtum." "Haythu" is among the indefinite spatial adverbs, and for this reason the verb reaches it directly, as in "go," and you say: "I sat where Zayd sat." In poetry the particle "fi" has come before it. The poet said:

"So he woke in the place where we met their fugitive, freed, with his two hands bound and his nose bleeding."

When "qadayna" was made to include the sense of "awhayna" (We revealed), it took the preposition "ila" as its complement, meaning: "We revealed to Lut the matter decreed, decisively settled." The indication by "dhalika" refers to what God promised him of the destruction of his people. "Anna dabira" is for magnification and glorification of the matter, and it is in the accusative position as a substitute for "dhalika," as al-Akhfash said, or by dropping the preposition, meaning "bi-anna dabiran," as al-Farra' said, and al-Hawfi permitted it. "Anna dabira ha'ulai maqtu'un" is a metaphor for complete extermination. The explanation of a similar expression in His saying "so the root of the people who did wrong was cut off" [al-An'am: 45] has already been given. "Musbihin" means entering into morning, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in "maqtu'" according to meaning. For this reason al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd made it plural and estimated: "if they are entering morning," as you say: "You riding are better than you walking." If this is an explanation of meaning it is correct, but if it is meant as grammatical analysis, there is no necessity for this estimate.

Al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza, since the verb "qadayna" includes the sense of "awhayna," so the meaning was "we informed," and the verb governed it so the particle "inna" took a kasra; or because the decree in the sense of revelation has the sense of saying, the two kasras agree. This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah. We say that "inna dabira" is a reading of interpretation, not of the Qur'an, because it contradicts the written text.

"Al-madina" is Sodom, the city whose judge was struck as a proverb for injustice.

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾ [Al-Hijr: 45] ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [Al-Hijr: 46] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; they will be as brothers, facing one another on couches﴾ ﴿No weariness will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it﴾ ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾

When God mentioned what He had prepared for the people of the Fire, He mentioned what He had prepared for the people of Paradise, to show the contrast between the two groups. Since the state of the believers is a matter of concern, He informed that they are in gardens and springs. He treated what they will settle in the Hereafter as though they were already settled in it in this world. For this reason it came as ﴿ṭ adkhulūhā﴾ ("enter it," imperative) in the reading of the imperative, because one who has already settled in a place is not said to be "made to enter" it. The state of the deviators came as a promise in His saying ﴿li-mawʿiduhum﴾ ("their appointed place"), because they had not entered it.

﴿al-ʿuyūn﴾ (the springs) is the plural of ʿayn. Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥafṣ and Hishām read ﴿wa-ʿUyūn﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn, and the rest of the seven read it with a kasrah. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as a past tense verb in the passive voice, from the causative form (al-idkhāl). Yaʿqūb, in the transmission of Ruways, read it the same way, with a ḍammah on the tanwīn, and it is also reported from him that he read it with a fatḥah. What follows is an imperative under an assumed reading: "Cause them to enter it," from the causative form, meaning He commanded the angels to bring the God-fearing into Paradise, and the hamzah drops in both readings. The majority read ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ as an imperative from the verb "to enter." According to the two imperative readings, there is an elided element, i.e., "it is said to them," or "it is said to the angels."

﴿bi-salām﴾ (in peace) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It may mean "accompanied by safety," or it may mean "greeted," i.e., "those greeted with peace," as is related about the angels, that they enter upon the people of Paradise saying: "Peace be upon you."

﴿wa-nazaʿnā mā fī ṣudūrihim min ghill﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts). Its explanation was given in al-Aʿrāf. It has been said: ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, and it is a state relating to the pronoun. A state relating to the genitive-governed noun (muḍāf ilayhi) is rare when it is not governed by the thing it is attached to, in either the nominative or accusative case. For this reason some said that when the first noun is a part of the second, as here (since "breasts" are part of the people), and is like a part, as in His saying ﴿wa-ittabaʿa millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfan﴾ [An-Nisa: 125], a state comes from the genitive-governed noun. We have established that this is not permissible. The evidence they cite has an interpretation other than what they mention. Its interpretation here is that it is in the accusative by way of praise, the sense being: "I praise [them as] brothers." Since it cannot be an adjective of the pronoun, it has been detached from its case and placed in the accusative for praise. Abū al-Baqāʾ has mentioned that it is a state relating to the pronoun in the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿fī jannāt﴾ (in gardens) [Al-Hijr: 45], and that it may be a state relating to the subject of ﴿udkhulūhā﴾ (enter it), or to the pronoun in ﴿āminīn﴾ (secure).

The meaning of ﴿ikhwānan﴾ (as brothers) is: people who have close ties and mutual affection. ﴿ʿalā sururin mutaqābilīn﴾ (upon couches, facing one another): these are two states. Sitting upon couches is a sign of exalted rank and complete honor, as He said: "They ride the back of this sea as kings upon thrones," or "like kings upon thrones." From Ibn ʿAbbās: "upon couches adorned with jacinth, emerald and pearls." Qatādah said: ﴿mutaqābilīn﴾ means "equal in mutual connection and visiting." From Mujāhid: "None of them looks at the back of another; the couches turn them wherever they turn, so that in all their states they are facing one another." End.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 15, verses 47–66 (part 2 of 3)

Since this world (al-dunya) is a place of toil, with the strain of seeking a livelihood, the hardship of the obligations necessary for the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter, the company of opposites, the onset of calamities and illnesses, and a place of transition from it to another abode, its affairs are fearful for the believer. It is not a place of permanent residence. Almighty God informed that this is absent in Paradise, by His saying: ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾. When touch is negated, perpetuity is established. He emphasized the negation of expulsion by the entry of the particle bi- (bi-) into: "bi-mukhrajin" (﴿nor shall they be expelled from it﴾).

It was said: reward has four conditions. It must be beneficial, and to this points His saying: ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ [al-Hijr: 45], accompanied by honour. To this points His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ [al-Hijr: 46], free from the places of spiritual impurities, such as resentment and envy, and of bodily ones, such as weariness and toil. To this points His saying: "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to ﴿No toil shall touch them therein﴾, as a lasting state. To this points His saying: ﴿Nor shall they be expelled from it﴾.

It is related from Ali ibn al-Husayn that His saying "wa-naza'na" (﴿and We will remove﴾) up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar, and that "al-ghill" (rancour) is the rancour of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance). It was also said: there had been enmities between the Banu Tamim, Adi and Hashim, and when they embraced Islam they came to love one another.

When the mention of what is in the Fire and what is in the Garden had preceded, Almighty God emphasized the alerting of people and the establishment of this in the soul by His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The mention of forgiveness and mercy fits with the connection of this to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ [al-Hijr: 45]. And in giving precedence to these two great attributes by which He described Himself, His saying ﴿and that My punishment﴾ came in the utmost gentleness, since He did not say it in the manner of a contrast, and that I am the one who punishes painfully. All of this is a preference for the aspect of pardon and mercy.

"Anna" (that) fills the place of the two objects of "nabbi'" (inform) if we say it takes three objects, and fills the place of one if we say it takes two. It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Forgiving" is for the one who repents, and His punishment is for the one who does not repent.

In His saying "nabbi'" (inform) up to the end of the verse, there is a preference for the aspect of good, from the aspect of His command to His Messenger with this proclamation. It is as if it were a testimony by Himself to His undertaking of forgiveness and mercy. His attributing the servants to Himself is an honour for them. And the emphasis of the name of "anna" (that) is by His saying "ana" (I). The prefixing of al- (the definite article) to these two attributes, and their coming in the form of intensive emphasis (mubalagha), and the beginning with the attribute that delights first, which is forgiveness, followed by the attribute from which forgiveness arises, which is mercy.

It is related in a hadith: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from the forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy his own soul." And in a hadith from Ibn al-Mubarak, with his chain of narration: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came out from the gate through which the Banu Shayba enter, and we were laughing. He said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, until when he reached al-Hijr, he came back to us backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, came and said: God says: Why do you despair, My servants?' [and he recited] ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾."

(p. 458) ﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good news of a boy with much knowledge."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good news although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good news?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾

When Almighty God mentioned what He had prepared for the disobedient of the Fire and for the obedient of the Garden, He reminded the Arabs of the circumstances of those whom they know, from among those who disobeyed and denied the messengers, and upon whom the punishment of this world befell before the punishment of the Hereafter, so that they might desist from their disbelief and take warning from what befell others. So He began with the mention of their great forefather Abraham, peace be upon him, and what befell the people of his nephew Lot, then with the mention of the companions of al-Hijr, who were the people of Salih, then with the companions of al-Aykah, who were the people of Shu'ayb.

Abu Haywa read "wa-nabiyyuhum" with the hamza replaced by a ya'.

The guests of Abraham were the angels who gave him good news of a son and of the destruction of the people of Lot.
