The pronoun in wa innaha refers to the destroyed city, meaning: it is on a clear and evident path for the one who takes warning. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. It was said that it may refer to the signs, and it may refer to the stones. As for His words, labisabilin, it means a established passageway, and it is in a place where people see it and take warning from it; it has not been effaced. This is an admonition to Quraysh, for you pass by them in the morning and at night.

It was also said that it refers to the shout, meaning: indeed the shout is lying in wait for whoever does their deeds, based on His words: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 11:83]. It was also said: muqim means known. It was said: it means lasting transgression. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a destruction whose path endures.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in what We did to the people of Lut, is indeed a sign and a proof for whoever believes in Allah.

﴿And indeed the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿So We took vengeance upon them, and indeed both [towns] are on a clear highway﴾: They are the people of Shu'ayb, and the thicket (al-ayka) to which they were attributed was a tree of doum palm. It was also said: it was the arfaj tree. It was also said: the sidr (lote tree). It was also said: al-Ayka is the name of the region, in which case it is a proper noun. This is strengthened by the reading of those who recited it in al-Shu'ara' and Sad as Layka, without tanwin. They disbelieved, so Allah sent upon them the heat, and they were destroyed by the punishment of the cloud. This will be discussed in full, Allah willing, in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

In (in) the view of the Basrans, it is the light form of the heavy form (in mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah, i.e., "indeed" with the emphatic particle omitted). According to al-Farra', it is a negation, and the lam means "except" (illa). A similar discussion occurred regarding ﴿And indeed it was a great [matter]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143] in al-Baqarah.

The apparent view is that of the majority: that the pronoun in wa innahuma refers to the two towns, the town of the people of Lut and the people of Shu'ayb, meaning: they are on the passageway of the traveller. It was said that it refers to Shu'ayb and Lut, meaning: both are on a clear path (imam mubin), that is, a path of truth that is evident. The imam is the path. It was said: wa innahuma, meaning the stone, that is, the destruction of the people of Lut and the companions of the thicket, is in a clear book (kitab mubin), that is, the Preserved Tablet. Mu'arrij said: the imam is the book in the dialect of Himyar. It was also said: it refers to the companions of the thicket and Madyan, for he was sent to both of them, so the mention of one indicates the other, and the pronoun refers to both.

﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, secure﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at dawn﴾ ﴿And what they used to earn did not avail them﴾: The companions of al-Hijr are Thamud, the people of Salih (peace be upon him). Al-Hijr is a land between the Hijaz and Syria. Its story was discussed fully in al-A'raf. "The messengers" refers to their denial of Salih, for whoever denies one of them is as if he denied them all. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he meant Salih and those believers with him, just as it was said: "the Khubaybiyyun" regarding Ibn al-Zubayr and his companions.

It is narrated from Jabir, who said: "We passed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by al-Hijr, and he said to us: 'Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest what befell them befall you.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged his mount on, and it hastened until he left it behind." In one of its chains it adds: "Then he said: 'These are the people of Salih, whom Allah destroyed, except for a man who was in the sanctuary of Allah, whom the sanctity of Allah protected from the punishment of Allah.'" It was said: "Who is he, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Abu Righal." And the Thaqif tribe is attributed to him.

﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾: It was said: verses from the Book of Allah were sent down to them. It was also said: it refers to the establishment of proofs, but they turned away from them. It was also said: there were five signs in the she-camel: her emergence from the rock, her gestation being near at the time of her emergence, her great size such that no other camel resembled her, the abundance of her milk sufficient for all of them, and it was also said that he had signs other than the she-camel.

Al-Jumhur read yanhitun with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read it with a fatha. He described them with intense focus on the world and on earning from it, and he mentioned as an example their hewing with axes and the like in the stones. As for "secure": it was said: from collapse. It was said: from the accidents of the world. It was said: from death, because of their deception by long lives. It was said: from thieves' breaking in and from enemies. It was said: from the punishment of Allah, they supposing that the mountains would protect them from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the most correct interpretation is that they felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter, so they did not act according to its requirements, but acted according to the security they felt from it.

Musbihin means entering upon the morning. The apparent meaning of ma in His words fa-ma aghna is a negation particle, though it may also be an interrogative intended to express astonishment. The ma in ma kanu may be a masdariyyah (verbal-noun particle, meaning "what they earned"), but the apparent meaning is that it is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," with an omitted pronoun, meaning: what they used to earn of sturdy houses, wealth, and equipment. Rather, they fell prostrate, dead.

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed the Hour is coming, so overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾ ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers﴾ ﴿And say, "Indeed I am the clear warner"﴾ ﴿Like what We sent down upon the dividers﴾ ﴿Who have made the Qur'an into parts﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿About what they used to do﴾ ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ ﴿Indeed We suffice you against the mockers﴾ ﴿Who set up with Allah another god. But they are going to know﴾ ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ ﴿So exalt your Lord with praise and be among the prostrators﴾ ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾:

Except with truth: that is, a creation intertwined with truth. Nothing of that was created in vain or purposelessly, but so that whoever obeys may obey through reflection on that great creation, and so that one may remember the Hereafter by this first creation. For this reason He alerted whoever is alert with His words: "And indeed the Hour is coming," so that He may reward whoever obeyed and whoever disobeyed. Then He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to pardon, and this implies a truce, which was abrogated (mansukhah, meaning subject to naskh, abrogation) by the verse of the sword, as said by Qatadah. Or it means making the ruling clear to them and overlooking them.

When He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the All-Creator﴾. He used the intensive form because of the abundance of what He created. Or al-Khallaq means: He who grants whatever He wills, for whatever He wills, of happiness or misery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Khallaq is He who created you and them, and He is the All-Knowing of your condition and their condition, so nothing of what passes between you is hidden from Him. Or: indeed your Lord is He who created you and knew what is most beneficial for you, and He knew that forgiveness today is better than the sword would be.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, and Malik ibn Dinar read: huwa al-Khaliq (with the form of the active participle). Likewise in the codices of Ubayy and 'Uthman. (And) from al-mathani (the oft-repeated).

Al-mathani (the oft-repeated ones) is the plural of mathnat, and al-muthanna is anything that is made into a pair. You say: thaniytu al-shay' thaniyan, meaning I bent the thing and joined another to it. From this the knees and elbows of a beast are called mathani, because it bends at the thigh and the upper arm. The mathani of a valley are its bends.

So the phrase "seven of the mathani" means seven things of the kind that are doubled or repeated. This is unspecified (mujmal), and it cannot be identified except by a separate indicator (dalil munfasil).

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: the seven here are the seven long surahs (al-Tiwal): al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal with Bara'ah, since the two are treated as one surah, and for this reason no basmalah separates them. The long surahs were called mathani because the hudud (prescribed punishments), the fara'id (obligatory duties) and the amthal (parables) are repeated in them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and on his view min is for specifying the genus (li-bayan al-jins).

It was also said: the seventh is Surah Yunus, said by Ibn Jubayr. It was said: Bara'ah alone, said by Abu Malik.

On the view of these and of Ibn 'Abbas in his earlier statement, al-mathani means the Qur'an, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A Book, consistent, oft-repeated﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. It was so named because its narratives and reports are repeated and reiterated within it.

It was also said: the seven are the family of Hamim (Al Hamim), or seven scrolls, which are the sab'at (sets).

It was also said: the seven are the meanings revealed in the Qur'an: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, the coining of parables, the enumeration of blessings, and the reporting of nations. This was said by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam.

'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also (in another report), al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Abi Mulaykah, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and a group said: the seven here are the verses of praise (ayat al-hamd), i.e. al-Fatihah.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they are seven, beginning with bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Others said: seven excluding the basmalah.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: this surah (al-Fatihah) was revealed, and none of the long surahs had been revealed. One should not depart from this view; indeed, departing from it is not permissible, because of the hadith of Ubayy, at the end of which is "it is the seven mathani," and the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is the seven mathani, the Mother of the Qur'an, and the Opening of the Book." It is so named because it is repeated (tuthanna) in every rak'ah.

It was also said: because praise of Allah the Exalted is repeated through it. Al-Zajjaj permitted this.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "In this view there is a problem from the standpoint of morphology (tasrif); (end)."

There is no problem in this, for it is the plural of muthni, with a damma on the mim, a form of af'ala from athna (the quadriliteral), meaning one who gives thanks (muqirr thana'an) to Allah the Exalted; that is, it contains praise of Allah the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas said: because Allah reserved it (istathnaha) for this Ummah and did not give it to any other.

Ibn Abi Mulaykah said something similar.

On this interpretation found in the hadith, min is for specifying the genus, as if it were said: the ones which are the mathani. The same applies to the view of those who made them the sets of the Qur'an, or the seven meanings.

As for those who made them the long surahs or the family of Hamim, min is partitive (lil-tab'id). Likewise for the view of those who made the seven al-Fatihah and the mathani the Qur'an.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that all the Books of Allah are mathani, because they praise Him and because of the repeated admonitions in them, and the Qur'an is part of them.

The majority read: wa al-Qur'an al-'azim, with the accusative (naṣb).

If by the seven he means al-Fatihah or the long surahs, then this is conjunction of the general to the specific (ʿatf al-'amm 'ala al-khass), and the specific is mentioned twice: once in terms of particularity and once in terms of generality. Or because what is less than al-Fatihah or the long surahs is still called Qur'an, since it is a name applied to a part of a thing as it is applied to its whole.

If by the seven he means the sets, then it is conjunction of a thing to itself, in that the meaning is: "We have given you what is called the seven mathani and the great Qur'an," that is, the one combining these two meanings, which are praise, admonition and greatness.

A group read: wa al-Qur'ani al-'azim, with the genitive (khafd), in conjunction with al-mathani.

Whoever went to the view that the waw is superfluous (muqhamah), with the sense "seven of the mathani, the great Qur'an," is far off the mark.

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the blessing He bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ) by giving him what He gave him, He forbade him.

We have said that the prohibition does not require actual engagement or proximity, such as the lifting of the eye toward something of the goods of this world. Although this is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), the meaning is that He forbade his Ummah from this, because whoever is given the Qur'an is occupied by reflecting upon it, by carrying out its obligations and understanding its meanings, away from preoccupation with the splendour of this world.

The extending of the eye toward a thing is only for admiring and preferring it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not wish for what We have favoured some of them with of the goods of this world, spouses among them, that is, men with their women, or similar blessings; and there are various opinions about the categories of Jews, Christians and polytheists.

He, the Exalted, forbade him from grieving over them if they did not believe. He was extremely compassionate toward those to whom he was sent, and he loved that they should all believe in Allah, so grief over them would overtake him.

He, the Exalted, forbade him from grieving over those who did not believe, and commanded him to lower his wing (khafd janahihi) toward those who believed. This is a metaphor for gentleness and kindness.

Its origin is that when a bird gathers its chick to itself, it spreads its wing over it and then folds it over its young. The two wings of a human being are his two sides.

Then He commanded him to convey that he is the warner, the clear one, revealing to you what I have brought to you of the punishment if you do not believe, and of the sending down of the terrifying vengeance of Allah upon you.

Al-Kaf (the "ka" of "ka-ma"), al-Zamakhshari said, has two possibilities:

One: that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you﴾, that is: "We sent down to you the like of what We sent down to the People of the Book, who are the muqtasimun (those who divided), ﴿who made the Qur'an into fragments﴾," for they said, out of their obstinacy and hostility: "Part of it is true, agreeing with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false, contradicting them." So they divided it into true and false, and disobeyed it.

It was also said: they used to mock it, and one of them would say: "Al-Baqarah is mine," and another would say: "Al 'Imran is mine."

It is also possible that by the Qur'an is meant what they recite from their books, which they divided by their distortion, and that the Jews acknowledged part of the Torah and denied part, and the Christians acknowledged part of the Gospel and denied part. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the conduct of his people toward the Qur'an, their denial, and their saying "magic," "poetry," and "fables," in that other disbelievers did the same with other books.

The second: that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And say: "I am indeed the clear warner"﴾, meaning: warn the Quraysh with the like of what We sent down of punishment upon the muqtasimin, meaning the Jews. This is what befell Qurayzah and al-Nadir. He made the expected (al-mutawaqqa') equal to the actual (al-waqi'), and this is among the signs of prophethood, for it is a report of what would be and what has been.

It is also possible that "those who made the Qur'an into fragments" is in the accusative governed by "the warner," meaning: "Warn the fragmenters, who divide the Qur'an into magic, poetry and fables, like what We sent down upon the muqtasimin," and they are the twelve who divided the entrances of Mecca during the season, sitting at each entrance dispersed, in order to repel people from believing in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). One of them would say: "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from among us, for he is a magician"; another would say: "He is a liar"; and another: "He is a poet." Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr, and before that by various calamities, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and others.

Or: "like what We sent down upon the group who swore together to attack Salih (peace be upon him) by night." Al-iqtisam here has the sense of al-taqasum (mutual swearing).

(If you say): If you connect His saying "as We sent down" with His saying "And We have certainly given you," then what is the meaning of the interposition of "Do not extend your eyes..." to the end between them? (I say): Since that was a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their denial and hostility, he interposed what supports the meaning of consolation: the prohibition against turning toward their worldly life and grieving over their disbelief, and the command to turn with all his attention toward the believers; end.

As for the first possibility, that "ka" is connected to "atayna-ka," Abu al-Baqa' mentioned it on the basis that it is in the position of the accusative as an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), the estimate being: "We gave you seven of the mathani" as a giving (iya'an) like what We sent down, or as a sending down (inzalan) like what We sent down, since atayna-ka means anzalna 'alayka. As for his saying that the muqtasimun are the People of the Book, this is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid, and al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. As for his saying "they divided the Qur'an," this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas as narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. As for his saying "they divided," some said "Al-Baqarah" and some "Al 'Imran," and so on: this was said by 'Ikrimah. Al-Suddi said they were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Walid, al-'As, and al-Harith ibn Qays, who spoke of the Qur'an, so one said "the gnat is mine," another "the ant is mine," another "the fly is mine," another "the spider is mine," mocking; so Allah destroyed them all.

As for his saying that the Qur'an is an expression for what they recite of their books, to the end, this was said by Mujahid.

As for his saying that "those who made the Qur'an into fragments" may be in the accusative governed by "the warner," meaning "warn the fragmenters," it cannot be in the accusative governed by "the warner" as was mentioned, because the warner is described as "the clear one," and it is not permissible for an adjective to govern a preceding object, according to the Basran school, which does not permit "this is a knowing brave one" in which one separates "knowing" from "knowledge of grammar" by the word "brave." The Kufans permitted it. This is a disputed matter whose proofs are discussed in the science of grammar.

As for his saying "who fragment the Qur'an into magic, poetry and fables," this is related from Qatadah, except that he said "kahanah" (soothsaying) instead of "poetry."

As for his saying "those who divided the entrances of Mecca," this is the saying of al-Sa'ib. In it, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said: "Let some of you say 'he is a soothsayer,' some 'he is a magician,' some 'he is a poet,' and some 'he is a madman'." They were: Hanzalah ibn Abi Sufyan, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl, al-'As ibn Hisham, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid, Qays ibn al-Fakih, Zuhayr ibn Umayyah, Hilal ibn 'Abd al-Aswad, al-Sa'ib ibn Sayfi, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham, Zam'ah ibn al-Hajjaj, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Aws ibn al-Mughirah. They swore together to deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were all destroyed.

As for his saying that they are those who swore together to attack Salih, this is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: [the text continues beyond this point].

I am the clear warner, [just as] We sent down [the punishment] upon the dividers (al-muqtasimin). These are far-fetched opinions and forced interpretations. What appears to me is that when Allah commanded him not to grieve over those who did not believe, and commanded him to lower his wing (khafd janah) to the believers, He commanded him to inform the believers and others that he is the clear warner, lest the believers suppose that, because he, peace be upon him, was commanded to lower his wing to them, they were released from the obligation of warning. So Allah commanded him to tell them: "Indeed, I am the clear warner to you and to others," as Allah said:

﴿Indeed, you are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:45]

The kaf (ك) in ﴿كَما أنْزَلْنا﴾ (as We sent down) is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), whose estimated sense is: "And say a statement like what We sent down upon the dividers, that you are a warner to them." Thus the warning to the believers is like the warning to the disbelieving dividers, lest it be thought that your warning to the disbelievers contradicts your warning to the believers. Rather, you are in the quality of warning to them on one level: you warn the believers just as you warn the disbelievers, as Allah said:

﴿a warner and a bringer of good news to a people who believe.﴾ [al-A'raf 7:188]

Apparently, alladhina (الَّذِينَ) is an adjective (sifah) of al-muqtasimin. Others allowed that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and it may be in the accusative as a dispraise (dhamm). The az-Zamakhshari permission for it to be the object of al-nadhir (the warner) was mentioned earlier.

Then: ﴿So by your Lord﴾: Allah swore by His own essence and His lordship, attributing it to His Messenger as a mark of honor. The pronoun in ﴿لَنَسْألَنَّهم﴾ (We will surely question them) apparently returns to the dividers; this is a threat of a questioning meant as reproach. It is also said that it returns to all of them, disbelievers and believers, since both have been mentioned before. The questioning is general for all creation. It is also permissible that the questioning is a metaphor (kinayah) for requital. And ﴿for what they used to do﴾ is general for all deeds.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: He will question the servants about two states: about what they used to worship, and about how they responded to the messengers. Ibn 'Abbas said: It will be said to them, "Why did you do such and such?"

Anas, Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid said: The questioning is about "There is no god but Allah." az-Zuhri mentioned this from the Prophet ﷺ. If that is established, then the meaning is: about fulfilling "There is no god but Allah," and being truthful to its statement, as al-Hasan said: "Faith is not by adornment, nor religion by wishful thinking, but what settles in the hearts and is confirmed by deeds."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ means: carry it out.

al-Kalbi said: Make it public and manifest it, from al-sadi' (صَدِيع), which is the dawn. A poet said:

*As if the whiteness of its blaze is a dawn.*

As-Suddi said: Speak what you are commanded. Ibn Zayd said: Inform [them] of the delivery. Ibn Bahr said: He made the statement clear in calling to faith. Abu 'Ubaydah reported from Ru'bah: "Nothing in the Qur'an is stranger than His saying ﴿فَاصْدَعْ بِما تُؤْمَرُ﴾." The ma (ما) in (بِما) (with what) means "that which," and the second object is omitted, its estimated form being: "what you are commanded it (bihi)." Its original form was tu'maru bihi (you are commanded with it) from the laws (shara'i'), then the preposition was dropped and the verb became transitive to it. al-Akhfash said: ma is a relative pronoun, and the estimate is: "proclaim what you are commanded with its proclaiming," so he omitted the genitive-governed noun, then the preposition, then the pronoun. az-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ma be a verbal particle (masdariyyah), i.e., "by your command," a masdar from the passive. [End of his words.] This is based on the position of those who permit that the masdar be expressed by "an" (that) and the passive verb, but the correct view is that this is not permitted.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾: from the verses of conciliation (muhadanat) which were abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Then Allah informed him that He had sufficed him against the mockers with calamities that struck them, in which the Messenger did not strive nor exerted any effort. 'Urwah and Ibn Jubayr said: They were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Abu Zam'ah, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; and from Banu Khuza'ah: al-Harith ibn at-Talatilah.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: I said to az-Zuhri, "Ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah disagreed about a man among the mockers: Ibn Jubayr said he was al-Harith ibn 'Aytalah, and 'Ikrimah said he was al-Harith ibn Qays." az-Zuhri said: "Both are right: he is 'Aytalah, and his father is Qays."

ash-Sha'bi mentioned among the mockers Habbar ibn al-Aswad, but this is an error, because Habbar embraced Islam on the day of the conquest (of Mecca) and migrated to Medina.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the mockers were eight; in one narration, instead of al-Harith ibn Qays, 'Adi ibn Qays.

ash-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Bazzah said they were seven: they mentioned al-Walid, al-Harith ibn 'Adi, the two al-Aswads, al-Athram, and Ba'kak, the two sons of al-Harith ibn as-Sabbaq. Muqatil said likewise, except that he said: instead of al-Harith ibn 'Adi, al-Harith ibn Qays as-Sahmi.

The exegetes and historians mentioned that "Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'I have been commanded to suffice you against them.' So he pointed to the leg of al-Walid, and an arrow passed by him and caught his garment; his arrogance prevented him from bending to pull it out, so it struck a vein in his heel." Qatadah and Miqsam said: It was the al-akhal (a vein), so it cut it and he died. He pointed to the sole of al-'As, and a thorn entered it. It was also said that a snake bit him, and his leg swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He pointed to the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he became blind and perished. He pointed to the nose of al-Harith ibn Qays, and he discharged pus through it and died. It was also said that a scorching wind struck him, and he turned black until he looked like an Abyssinian; his family came to him and did not recognize him, and they shut the door in his face, so he kept wandering in the mountain paths of Mecca until he died. There is disagreement about some of what befell these men; and Allah knows best.

Muqatil said: What struck al-Athram or Ba'kak was the boil (dubaylah), and the other had pleurisy (dhat al-janb), and both died.

﴿Then they will know﴾: a threat to them of requital for their mockery, and for making a god with Allah, in the Hereafter as they had allowed in this world.

He used "the chest" as a metaphor (kinayah) for the heart, since it is its locus. He made the cause of constriction what they say, which is what they utter of mockery and slander against what he brought. Then Allah commanded him to glorify Him, exonerating Him from what they attributed to Him of associating partners with Him, accompanied by praise of Him and thanks for what He had bestowed upon him: the blessing of prophethood, messengership, monotheism, and other blessings. This concerns belief and the inner act of the heart.

He commanded him to be ﴿among those who prostrate﴾, and the intended meaning, Allah knows best, is among those who pray; He used prostration as a metaphor for prayer, which is the most noble of bodily acts, and the closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating. Since what proceeds from the mockers is belief, which is an act of the heart, and speech, which is what they say about the Messenger and what he brought, which is an act of the limbs, Allah commanded what corresponds to that: exonerating Allah and prostrating, both of which combine the act of the heart and the act of the body.

Then Allah commanded him with worship (ibadah), which encompasses all kinds of acts by which one draws near to Him. These commands mean: persist in such and such, because he, ﷺ, was always engaged in them; that is: persist in glorification, prostration and worship.

The majority hold that the intended meaning of "certainty" (al-yaqin) is death (p. 471), that is: as long as you are alive, do not neglect worship. This is the explanation of Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about 'Uthman ibn Maz'un at his death: "As for him, he has seen the certainty (al-yaqin)." It is also narrated as "the certainty has come to him." Yet "certainty" is not one of the names of death; rather, knowledge of it is certainty, about which no sane person doubts, so it was called certainty figuratively. That is: the certain matter will come to you, its knowledge and its occurrence.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the meaning is: until the certainty comes to you regarding the victory that you were promised. [End of his words.] Ibn Bahr also said this, saying: The certainty is victory over the disbelievers.

The wisdom of limiting it by "certainty," which is death, is that it requires the continuity of worship as long as one lives, unlike merely commanding worship without a limit, which would be absolute, so one would be obedient by doing it once. The intent is that he not depart from worship until he dies.

(p. 462) ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ ﴿And fear Allah and do not humiliate me."﴾ ﴿They said, "Did we not forbid you from [harbouring] the people?"﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my daughters, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And We made its uppermost part its lowest and rained upon them stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

Their rejoicing (istibsharuhum) is their delight at the guests who came to Lut (peace be upon him). The apparent meaning is that this coming, his dialogue with his people concerning the rights of his guests, and his offer of his daughters to them all took place before he was informed of the destruction of his people and before he knew that the guests were messengers of Allah. For this reason he called them "guests" (dayfan), out of fear of disgrace, because of their engaging in what is not permissible, the ugly act. This is arranged in this order in Hud, but the particle "wa" (and) does not imply order. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that the coming and the dialogue took place after his knowledge of their destruction, and that he conducted that dialogue in a manner of concealment from them, of giving them respite, and of waiting for them." End of quotation.

He forbade them from disgracing him, because whoever wrongs his guest or his neighbour has wronged him. "Do not humiliate me" (la tukhzunī): it is from khizy, which means abasement, or from khazāyah, which means shame. In their saying, "Did we not forbid you," there is evidence that they had earlier forbidden him from hosting anyone, from granting protection to anyone, from defending anyone, or from interceding between them and anyone, for they used to attack everyone. He, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet and upon him, used to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and he would stand between them and those they attacked. So they threatened him that if he did not desist, they would expel him.

The discussion of his words "my daughters" and the meaning of the idafah (possessive construction) in Hud has already been covered. As for "if you are going to act" (in kuntum fa'ilin), it expresses doubt about their acceptance of his words. It is as if he said: "If you do what I say, [these are yours]; but I do not think you will do it." It was also said: "If you intend to satisfy desire in what Allah has made lawful, rather than what He has forbidden."

The lam in la'amruka (by your life) is the lam of inception (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam). The kaf is an address to Lut (peace be upon him). The implied meaning is: the angels said to Lut, "By your life." He referred to error and heedlessness by intoxication (sakrah), meaning that their bewilderment in their heedlessness and error prevented them from perceiving the right course, which would have been to leave the males for the females. It was also said that the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority: Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Hawra', and others. Allah swore by his life, honouring him.

Al-'Amr, with a fatha or a damma on the ayn, means survival (al-baqa'). The grammarians required the fatha for the oath (al-qasam), and it is permissible to omit the lam. Ibn 'Abbas read it as wa 'amruka. Abu al-Haytham said: la'amruka means "your religion, by which you survive." He recited:

"O you who marry Thurayya to Suhayl,
by your life, Allah! How could the two meet?"

That is, your worship of Allah. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I made my Lord survive," meaning I worshipped Him; and "So-and-so is a worshipper for his Lord," meaning he is devoted to Him. He said: It is also said, "I left so-and-so making his Lord survive," meaning worshipping Him. On this basis, la'amruka means "by your worship."

Al-Zajjaj said: They required the fatha for the oath because it is lighter for them, and they frequently swear by la'amrī and la'amruka, so they adopted the lighter form. Its nominative (irtfa'uhu) is due to inception, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "What he swore by."

Some of the scholars of meanings said: it is not permissible to attribute 'amr to Allah, for one does not say 'amr for Allah the Exalted; one says He is eternal (azali). It seems to imply that 'amr is used only of what has an end, and this is not the case with 'amr, which means survival. A poet said:

"When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,
by the life of Allah, their pleasure delights me."

Al-A'sha said:

"And by the life of Him who made the months a sign,
distinguishing from them their deficiency and their completeness."

Al-Nakha'i disliked saying la'amrī (by my life), because it is an oath by the life of the one swearing. Al-Nabigha said:

"By my life, and what is my life to me, is not trivial."

The pronoun in sakratihim refers to the people of Lut. Al-Tabari said it refers to Quraysh, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. He said: Allah created no soul more honourable to Him than Muhammad (ﷺ), and He said to him: "By your life (wa hayatika), indeed they," that is, your people from Quraysh, "are in their intoxication," that is, their error and ignorance, "wandering blindly," that is, wandering about.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is far-fetched, because it is disconnected from what precedes and what follows it."

Al-Ashhab read sukratihim with a damma on the sin. Ibn Abi 'Abilah read sakaratihim in the plural. Al-A'mash read sukrihim without the ta'. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of al-Jahdari, read (annahum) with a fatha on the hamza of annahum.

Al-Sayhah is the shout of destruction. It was also said it is the voice of Jibril (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the shout of horror, and it is not like the shout of Thamud.

Musriqin means entering upon sunrise, which is the rising of the sun. It was said that the beginning of the punishment came at dawn and extended to the sunrise, so that the completion of the destruction took place at that time.

The pronoun in 'aliyaha safilaha refers to the city mentioned earlier. Al-Zamakhshari said it refers to the towns of the people of Lut, though the word "towns" (qura) has not been mentioned before. Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: lil-mutawassimin means lil-mutafakkirin (for those who reflect). Al-Dahhak said: for those who look. A poet said:

"Whenever a tribe came to 'Ukaz,
they sent to their leader to take note (yatawassamu)."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: for those who see clearly. Qatadah said: for those who take warning. It is narrated from Nahshal, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding lil-mutawassimin, that he said: it means the people of righteousness and goodness.

The pronoun in wa innaha refers to the destroyed city, meaning: it is on a clear and evident path for the one who takes warning. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. It was said that it may refer to the signs, and it may refer to the stones. As for His words, labisabilin, it means a established passageway, and it is in a place where people see it and take warning from it; it has not been effaced. This is an admonition to Quraysh, for you pass by them in the morning and at night.

It was also said that it refers to the shout, meaning: indeed the shout is lying in wait for whoever does their deeds, based on His words: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 11:83]. It was also said: muqim means known. It was said: it means lasting transgression. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a destruction whose path endures.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in what We did to the people of Lut, is indeed a sign and a proof for whoever believes in Allah.

﴿And indeed the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿So We took vengeance upon them, and indeed both [towns] are on a clear highway﴾: They are the people of Shu'ayb, and the thicket (al-ayka) to which they were attributed was a tree of doum palm. It was also said: it was the arfaj tree. It was also said: the sidr (lote tree). It was also said: al-Ayka is the name of the region, in which case it is a proper noun. This is strengthened by the reading of those who recited it in al-Shu'ara' and Sad as Layka, without tanwin. They disbelieved, so Allah sent upon them the heat, and they were destroyed by the punishment of the cloud. This will be discussed in full, Allah willing, in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

In (in) the view of the Basrans, it is the light form of the heavy form (in mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah, i.e., "indeed" with the emphatic particle omitted). According to al-Farra', it is a negation, and the lam means "except" (illa). A similar discussion occurred regarding ﴿And indeed it was a great [matter]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143] in al-Baqarah.

The apparent view is that of the majority: that the pronoun in wa innahuma refers to the two towns, the town of the people of Lut and the people of Shu'ayb, meaning: they are on the passageway of the traveller. It was said that it refers to Shu'ayb and Lut, meaning: both are on a clear path (imam mubin), that is, a path of truth that is evident. The imam is the path. It was said: wa innahuma, meaning the stone, that is, the destruction of the people of Lut and the companions of the thicket, is in a clear book (kitab mubin), that is, the Preserved Tablet. Mu'arrij said: the imam is the book in the dialect of Himyar. It was also said: it refers to the companions of the thicket and Madyan, for he was sent to both of them, so the mention of one indicates the other, and the pronoun refers to both.

﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, secure﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at dawn﴾ ﴿And what they used to earn did not avail them﴾: The companions of al-Hijr are Thamud, the people of Salih (peace be upon him). Al-Hijr is a land between the Hijaz and Syria. Its story was discussed fully in al-A'raf. "The messengers" refers to their denial of Salih, for whoever denies one of them is as if he denied them all. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he meant Salih and those believers with him, just as it was said: "the Khubaybiyyun" regarding Ibn al-Zubayr and his companions.

It is narrated from Jabir, who said: "We passed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by al-Hijr, and he said to us: 'Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest what befell them befall you.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged his mount on, and it hastened until he left it behind." In one of its chains it adds: "Then he said: 'These are the people of Salih, whom Allah destroyed, except for a man who was in the sanctuary of Allah, whom the sanctity of Allah protected from the punishment of Allah.'" It was said: "Who is he, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Abu Righal." And the Thaqif tribe is attributed to him.

﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾: It was said: verses from the Book of Allah were sent down to them. It was also said: it refers to the establishment of proofs, but they turned away from them. It was also said: there were five signs in the she-camel: her emergence from the rock, her gestation being near at the time of her emergence, her great size such that no other camel resembled her, the abundance of her milk sufficient for all of them, and it was also said that he had signs other than the she-camel.

Al-Jumhur read yanhitun with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read it with a fatha. He described them with intense focus on the world and on earning from it, and he mentioned as an example their hewing with axes and the like in the stones. As for "secure": it was said: from collapse. It was said: from the accidents of the world. It was said: from death, because of their deception by long lives. It was said: from thieves' breaking in and from enemies. It was said: from the punishment of Allah, they supposing that the mountains would protect them from it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the most correct interpretation is that they felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter, so they did not act according to its requirements, but acted according to the security they felt from it.

Musbihin means entering upon the morning. The apparent meaning of ma in His words fa-ma aghna is a negation particle, though it may also be an interrogative intended to express astonishment. The ma in ma kanu may be a masdariyyah (verbal-noun particle, meaning "what they earned"), but the apparent meaning is that it is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," with an omitted pronoun, meaning: what they used to earn of sturdy houses, wealth, and equipment. Rather, they fell prostrate, dead.

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed the Hour is coming, so overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is the All-Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾ ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers﴾ ﴿And say, "Indeed I am the clear warner"﴾ ﴿Like what We sent down upon the dividers﴾ ﴿Who have made the Qur'an into parts﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿About what they used to do﴾ ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ ﴿Indeed We suffice you against the mockers﴾ ﴿Who set up with Allah another god. But they are going to know﴾ ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ ﴿So exalt your Lord with praise and be among the prostrators﴾ ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾:

Except with truth: that is, a creation intertwined with truth. Nothing of that was created in vain or purposelessly, but so that whoever obeys may obey through reflection on that great creation, and so that one may remember the Hereafter by this first creation. For this reason He alerted whoever is alert with His words: "And indeed the Hour is coming," so that He may reward whoever obeyed and whoever disobeyed. Then He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to pardon, and this implies a truce, which was abrogated (mansukhah, meaning subject to naskh, abrogation) by the verse of the sword, as said by Qatadah. Or it means making the ruling clear to them and overlooking them.

When He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the All-Creator﴾. He used the intensive form because of the abundance of what He created. Or al-Khallaq means: He who grants whatever He wills, for whatever He wills, of happiness or misery.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Khallaq is He who created you and them, and He is the All-Knowing of your condition and their condition, so nothing of what passes between you is hidden from Him. Or: indeed your Lord is He who created you and knew what is most beneficial for you, and He knew that forgiveness today is better than the sword would be.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, and Malik ibn Dinar read: huwa al-Khaliq (with the form of the active participle). Likewise in the codices of Ubayy and 'Uthman. (And) from al-mathani (the oft-repeated).

Al-mathani (the oft-repeated ones) is the plural of mathnat, and al-muthanna is anything that is made into a pair. You say: thaniytu al-shay' thaniyan, meaning I bent the thing and joined another to it. From this the knees and elbows of a beast are called mathani, because it bends at the thigh and the upper arm. The mathani of a valley are its bends.

So the phrase "seven of the mathani" means seven things of the kind that are doubled or repeated. This is unspecified (mujmal), and it cannot be identified except by a separate indicator (dalil munfasil).

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: the seven here are the seven long surahs (al-Tiwal): al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal with Bara'ah, since the two are treated as one surah, and for this reason no basmalah separates them. The long surahs were called mathani because the hudud (prescribed punishments), the fara'id (obligatory duties) and the amthal (parables) are repeated in them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and on his view min is for specifying the genus (li-bayan al-jins).

It was also said: the seventh is Surah Yunus, said by Ibn Jubayr. It was said: Bara'ah alone, said by Abu Malik.

On the view of these and of Ibn 'Abbas in his earlier statement, al-mathani means the Qur'an, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A Book, consistent, oft-repeated﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. It was so named because its narratives and reports are repeated and reiterated within it.

It was also said: the seven are the family of Hamim (Al Hamim), or seven scrolls, which are the sab'at (sets).

It was also said: the seven are the meanings revealed in the Qur'an: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, the coining of parables, the enumeration of blessings, and the reporting of nations. This was said by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam.

'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also (in another report), al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Abi Mulaykah, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and a group said: the seven here are the verses of praise (ayat al-hamd), i.e. al-Fatihah.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they are seven, beginning with bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Others said: seven excluding the basmalah.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: this surah (al-Fatihah) was revealed, and none of the long surahs had been revealed. One should not depart from this view; indeed, departing from it is not permissible, because of the hadith of Ubayy, at the end of which is "it is the seven mathani," and the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is the seven mathani, the Mother of the Qur'an, and the Opening of the Book." It is so named because it is repeated (tuthanna) in every rak'ah.

It was also said: because praise of Allah the Exalted is repeated through it. Al-Zajjaj permitted this.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "In this view there is a problem from the standpoint of morphology (tasrif); (end)."

There is no problem in this, for it is the plural of muthni, with a damma on the mim, a form of af'ala from athna (the quadriliteral), meaning one who gives thanks (muqirr thana'an) to Allah the Exalted; that is, it contains praise of Allah the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas said: because Allah reserved it (istathnaha) for this Ummah and did not give it to any other.

Ibn Abi Mulaykah said something similar.

On this interpretation found in the hadith, min is for specifying the genus, as if it were said: the ones which are the mathani. The same applies to the view of those who made them the sets of the Qur'an, or the seven meanings.

As for those who made them the long surahs or the family of Hamim, min is partitive (lil-tab'id). Likewise for the view of those who made the seven al-Fatihah and the mathani the Qur'an.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is possible that all the Books of Allah are mathani, because they praise Him and because of the repeated admonitions in them, and the Qur'an is part of them.

The majority read: wa al-Qur'an al-'azim, with the accusative (naṣb).

If by the seven he means al-Fatihah or the long surahs, then this is conjunction of the general to the specific (ʿatf al-'amm 'ala al-khass), and the specific is mentioned twice: once in terms of particularity and once in terms of generality. Or because what is less than al-Fatihah or the long surahs is still called Qur'an, since it is a name applied to a part of a thing as it is applied to its whole.

If by the seven he means the sets, then it is conjunction of a thing to itself, in that the meaning is: "We have given you what is called the seven mathani and the great Qur'an," that is, the one combining these two meanings, which are praise, admonition and greatness.

A group read: wa al-Qur'ani al-'azim, with the genitive (khafd), in conjunction with al-mathani.

Whoever went to the view that the waw is superfluous (muqhamah), with the sense "seven of the mathani, the great Qur'an," is far off the mark.

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the blessing He bestowed upon His Messenger (ﷺ) by giving him what He gave him, He forbade him.

We have said that the prohibition does not require actual engagement or proximity, such as the lifting of the eye toward something of the goods of this world. Although this is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), the meaning is that He forbade his Ummah from this, because whoever is given the Qur'an is occupied by reflecting upon it, by carrying out its obligations and understanding its meanings, away from preoccupation with the splendour of this world.

The extending of the eye toward a thing is only for admiring and preferring it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not wish for what We have favoured some of them with of the goods of this world, spouses among them, that is, men with their women, or similar blessings; and there are various opinions about the categories of Jews, Christians and polytheists.

He, the Exalted, forbade him from grieving over them if they did not believe. He was extremely compassionate toward those to whom he was sent, and he loved that they should all believe in Allah, so grief over them would overtake him.

He, the Exalted, forbade him from grieving over those who did not believe, and commanded him to lower his wing (khafd janahihi) toward those who believed. This is a metaphor for gentleness and kindness.

Its origin is that when a bird gathers its chick to itself, it spreads its wing over it and then folds it over its young. The two wings of a human being are his two sides.

Then He commanded him to convey that he is the warner, the clear one, revealing to you what I have brought to you of the punishment if you do not believe, and of the sending down of the terrifying vengeance of Allah upon you.

Al-Kaf (the "ka" of "ka-ma"), al-Zamakhshari said, has two possibilities:

One: that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you﴾, that is: "We sent down to you the like of what We sent down to the People of the Book, who are the muqtasimun (those who divided), ﴿who made the Qur'an into fragments﴾," for they said, out of their obstinacy and hostility: "Part of it is true, agreeing with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false, contradicting them." So they divided it into true and false, and disobeyed it.

It was also said: they used to mock it, and one of them would say: "Al-Baqarah is mine," and another would say: "Al 'Imran is mine."

It is also possible that by the Qur'an is meant what they recite from their books, which they divided by their distortion, and that the Jews acknowledged part of the Torah and denied part, and the Christians acknowledged part of the Gospel and denied part. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the conduct of his people toward the Qur'an, their denial, and their saying "magic," "poetry," and "fables," in that other disbelievers did the same with other books.

The second: that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And say: "I am indeed the clear warner"﴾, meaning: warn the Quraysh with the like of what We sent down of punishment upon the muqtasimin, meaning the Jews. This is what befell Qurayzah and al-Nadir. He made the expected (al-mutawaqqa') equal to the actual (al-waqi'), and this is among the signs of prophethood, for it is a report of what would be and what has been.

It is also possible that "those who made the Qur'an into fragments" is in the accusative governed by "the warner," meaning: "Warn the fragmenters, who divide the Qur'an into magic, poetry and fables, like what We sent down upon the muqtasimin," and they are the twelve who divided the entrances of Mecca during the season, sitting at each entrance dispersed, in order to repel people from believing in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). One of them would say: "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from among us, for he is a magician"; another would say: "He is a liar"; and another: "He is a poet." Allah destroyed them on the day of Badr, and before that by various calamities, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and others.

Or: "like what We sent down upon the group who swore together to attack Salih (peace be upon him) by night." Al-iqtisam here has the sense of al-taqasum (mutual swearing).

(If you say): If you connect His saying "as We sent down" with His saying "And We have certainly given you," then what is the meaning of the interposition of "Do not extend your eyes..." to the end between them? (I say): Since that was a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their denial and hostility, he interposed what supports the meaning of consolation: the prohibition against turning toward their worldly life and grieving over their disbelief, and the command to turn with all his attention toward the believers; end.

As for the first possibility, that "ka" is connected to "atayna-ka," Abu al-Baqa' mentioned it on the basis that it is in the position of the accusative as an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), the estimate being: "We gave you seven of the mathani" as a giving (iya'an) like what We sent down, or as a sending down (inzalan) like what We sent down, since atayna-ka means anzalna 'alayka. As for his saying that the muqtasimun are the People of the Book, this is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid, and al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. As for his saying "they divided the Qur'an," this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas as narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. As for his saying "they divided," some said "Al-Baqarah" and some "Al 'Imran," and so on: this was said by 'Ikrimah. Al-Suddi said they were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Walid, al-'As, and al-Harith ibn Qays, who spoke of the Qur'an, so one said "the gnat is mine," another "the ant is mine," another "the fly is mine," another "the spider is mine," mocking; so Allah destroyed them all.

As for his saying that the Qur'an is an expression for what they recite of their books, to the end, this was said by Mujahid.

As for his saying that "those who made the Qur'an into fragments" may be in the accusative governed by "the warner," meaning "warn the fragmenters," it cannot be in the accusative governed by "the warner" as was mentioned, because the warner is described as "the clear one," and it is not permissible for an adjective to govern a preceding object, according to the Basran school, which does not permit "this is a knowing brave one" in which one separates "knowing" from "knowledge of grammar" by the word "brave." The Kufans permitted it. This is a disputed matter whose proofs are discussed in the science of grammar.

As for his saying "who fragment the Qur'an into magic, poetry and fables," this is related from Qatadah, except that he said "kahanah" (soothsaying) instead of "poetry."

As for his saying "those who divided the entrances of Mecca," this is the saying of al-Sa'ib. In it, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said: "Let some of you say 'he is a soothsayer,' some 'he is a magician,' some 'he is a poet,' and some 'he is a madman'." They were: Hanzalah ibn Abi Sufyan, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu Jahl, al-'As ibn Hisham, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid, Qays ibn al-Fakih, Zuhayr ibn Umayyah, Hilal ibn 'Abd al-Aswad, al-Sa'ib ibn Sayfi, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham, Zam'ah ibn al-Hajjaj, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Aws ibn al-Mughirah. They swore together to deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they were all destroyed.

As for his saying that they are those who swore together to attack Salih, this is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: [the text continues beyond this point].

I am the clear warner, [just as] We sent down [the punishment] upon the dividers (al-muqtasimin). These are far-fetched opinions and forced interpretations. What appears to me is that when Allah commanded him not to grieve over those who did not believe, and commanded him to lower his wing (khafd janah) to the believers, He commanded him to inform the believers and others that he is the clear warner, lest the believers suppose that, because he, peace be upon him, was commanded to lower his wing to them, they were released from the obligation of warning. So Allah commanded him to tell them: "Indeed, I am the clear warner to you and to others," as Allah said:

﴿Indeed, you are only a warner to those who fear it.﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:45]

The kaf (ك) in ﴿كَما أنْزَلْنا﴾ (as We sent down) is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), whose estimated sense is: "And say a statement like what We sent down upon the dividers, that you are a warner to them." Thus the warning to the believers is like the warning to the disbelieving dividers, lest it be thought that your warning to the disbelievers contradicts your warning to the believers. Rather, you are in the quality of warning to them on one level: you warn the believers just as you warn the disbelievers, as Allah said:

﴿a warner and a bringer of good news to a people who believe.﴾ [al-A'raf 7:188]

Apparently, alladhina (الَّذِينَ) is an adjective (sifah) of al-muqtasimin. Others allowed that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and it may be in the accusative as a dispraise (dhamm). The az-Zamakhshari permission for it to be the object of al-nadhir (the warner) was mentioned earlier.

Then: ﴿So by your Lord﴾: Allah swore by His own essence and His lordship, attributing it to His Messenger as a mark of honor. The pronoun in ﴿لَنَسْألَنَّهم﴾ (We will surely question them) apparently returns to the dividers; this is a threat of a questioning meant as reproach. It is also said that it returns to all of them, disbelievers and believers, since both have been mentioned before. The questioning is general for all creation. It is also permissible that the questioning is a metaphor (kinayah) for requital. And ﴿for what they used to do﴾ is general for all deeds.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: He will question the servants about two states: about what they used to worship, and about how they responded to the messengers. Ibn 'Abbas said: It will be said to them, "Why did you do such and such?"

Anas, Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid said: The questioning is about "There is no god but Allah." az-Zuhri mentioned this from the Prophet ﷺ. If that is established, then the meaning is: about fulfilling "There is no god but Allah," and being truthful to its statement, as al-Hasan said: "Faith is not by adornment, nor religion by wishful thinking, but what settles in the hearts and is confirmed by deeds."

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ means: carry it out.

al-Kalbi said: Make it public and manifest it, from al-sadi' (صَدِيع), which is the dawn. A poet said:

*As if the whiteness of its blaze is a dawn.*

As-Suddi said: Speak what you are commanded. Ibn Zayd said: Inform [them] of the delivery. Ibn Bahr said: He made the statement clear in calling to faith. Abu 'Ubaydah reported from Ru'bah: "Nothing in the Qur'an is stranger than His saying ﴿فَاصْدَعْ بِما تُؤْمَرُ﴾." The ma (ما) in (بِما) (with what) means "that which," and the second object is omitted, its estimated form being: "what you are commanded it (bihi)." Its original form was tu'maru bihi (you are commanded with it) from the laws (shara'i'), then the preposition was dropped and the verb became transitive to it. al-Akhfash said: ma is a relative pronoun, and the estimate is: "proclaim what you are commanded with its proclaiming," so he omitted the genitive-governed noun, then the preposition, then the pronoun. az-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that ma be a verbal particle (masdariyyah), i.e., "by your command," a masdar from the passive. [End of his words.] This is based on the position of those who permit that the masdar be expressed by "an" (that) and the passive verb, but the correct view is that this is not permitted.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾: from the verses of conciliation (muhadanat) which were abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Then Allah informed him that He had sufficed him against the mockers with calamities that struck them, in which the Messenger did not strive nor exerted any effort. 'Urwah and Ibn Jubayr said: They were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Abu Zam'ah, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth; and from Banu Khuza'ah: al-Harith ibn at-Talatilah.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: I said to az-Zuhri, "Ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah disagreed about a man among the mockers: Ibn Jubayr said he was al-Harith ibn 'Aytalah, and 'Ikrimah said he was al-Harith ibn Qays." az-Zuhri said: "Both are right: he is 'Aytalah, and his father is Qays."

ash-Sha'bi mentioned among the mockers Habbar ibn al-Aswad, but this is an error, because Habbar embraced Islam on the day of the conquest (of Mecca) and migrated to Medina.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the mockers were eight; in one narration, instead of al-Harith ibn Qays, 'Adi ibn Qays.

ash-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Bazzah said they were seven: they mentioned al-Walid, al-Harith ibn 'Adi, the two al-Aswads, al-Athram, and Ba'kak, the two sons of al-Harith ibn as-Sabbaq. Muqatil said likewise, except that he said: instead of al-Harith ibn 'Adi, al-Harith ibn Qays as-Sahmi.

The exegetes and historians mentioned that "Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'I have been commanded to suffice you against them.' So he pointed to the leg of al-Walid, and an arrow passed by him and caught his garment; his arrogance prevented him from bending to pull it out, so it struck a vein in his heel." Qatadah and Miqsam said: It was the al-akhal (a vein), so it cut it and he died. He pointed to the sole of al-'As, and a thorn entered it. It was also said that a snake bit him, and his leg swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He pointed to the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he became blind and perished. He pointed to the nose of al-Harith ibn Qays, and he discharged pus through it and died. It was also said that a scorching wind struck him, and he turned black until he looked like an Abyssinian; his family came to him and did not recognize him, and they shut the door in his face, so he kept wandering in the mountain paths of Mecca until he died. There is disagreement about some of what befell these men; and Allah knows best.

Muqatil said: What struck al-Athram or Ba'kak was the boil (dubaylah), and the other had pleurisy (dhat al-janb), and both died.

﴿Then they will know﴾: a threat to them of requital for their mockery, and for making a god with Allah, in the Hereafter as they had allowed in this world.

He used "the chest" as a metaphor (kinayah) for the heart, since it is its locus. He made the cause of constriction what they say, which is what they utter of mockery and slander against what he brought. Then Allah commanded him to glorify Him, exonerating Him from what they attributed to Him of associating partners with Him, accompanied by praise of Him and thanks for what He had bestowed upon him: the blessing of prophethood, messengership, monotheism, and other blessings. This concerns belief and the inner act of the heart.

He commanded him to be ﴿among those who prostrate﴾, and the intended meaning, Allah knows best, is among those who pray; He used prostration as a metaphor for prayer, which is the most noble of bodily acts, and the closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating. Since what proceeds from the mockers is belief, which is an act of the heart, and speech, which is what they say about the Messenger and what he brought, which is an act of the limbs, Allah commanded what corresponds to that: exonerating Allah and prostrating, both of which combine the act of the heart and the act of the body.

Then Allah commanded him with worship (ibadah), which encompasses all kinds of acts by which one draws near to Him. These commands mean: persist in such and such, because he, ﷺ, was always engaged in them; that is: persist in glorification, prostration and worship.

The majority hold that the intended meaning of "certainty" (al-yaqin) is death (p. 471), that is: as long as you are alive, do not neglect worship. This is the explanation of Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about 'Uthman ibn Maz'un at his death: "As for him, he has seen the certainty (al-yaqin)." It is also narrated as "the certainty has come to him." Yet "certainty" is not one of the names of death; rather, knowledge of it is certainty, about which no sane person doubts, so it was called certainty figuratively. That is: the certain matter will come to you, its knowledge and its occurrence.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the meaning is: until the certainty comes to you regarding the victory that you were promised. [End of his words.] Ibn Bahr also said this, saying: The certainty is victory over the disbelievers.

The wisdom of limiting it by "certainty," which is death, is that it requires the continuity of worship as long as one lives, unlike merely commanding worship without a limit, which would be absolute, so one would be obedient by doing it once. The intent is that he not depart from worship until he dies.

(p. 462) ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ ﴿And fear Allah and do not humiliate me."﴾ ﴿They said, "Did we not forbid you from [harbouring] the people?"﴾ ﴿He said, "These are my daughters, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And We made its uppermost part its lowest and rained upon them stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

Their rejoicing (istibsharuhum) is their delight at the guests who came to Lut (peace be upon him). The apparent meaning is that this coming, his dialogue with his people concerning the rights of his guests, and his offer of his daughters to them all took place before he was informed of the destruction of his people and before he knew that the guests were messengers of Allah. For this reason he called them "guests" (dayfan), out of fear of disgrace, because of their engaging in what is not permissible, the ugly act. This is arranged in this order in Hud, but the particle "wa" (and) does not imply order. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that the coming and the dialogue took place after his knowledge of their destruction, and that he conducted that dialogue in a manner of concealment from them, of giving them respite, and of waiting for them." End of quotation.

He forbade them from disgracing him, because whoever wrongs his guest or his neighbour has wronged him. "Do not humiliate me" (la tukhzunī): it is from khizy, which means abasement, or from khazāyah, which means shame. In their saying, "Did we not forbid you," there is evidence that they had earlier forbidden him from hosting anyone, from granting protection to anyone, from defending anyone, or from interceding between them and anyone, for they used to attack everyone. He, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet and upon him, used to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and he would stand between them and those they attacked. So they threatened him that if he did not desist, they would expel him.

The discussion of his words "my daughters" and the meaning of the idafah (possessive construction) in Hud has already been covered. As for "if you are going to act" (in kuntum fa'ilin), it expresses doubt about their acceptance of his words. It is as if he said: "If you do what I say, [these are yours]; but I do not think you will do it." It was also said: "If you intend to satisfy desire in what Allah has made lawful, rather than what He has forbidden."

The lam in la'amruka (by your life) is the lam of inception (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam). The kaf is an address to Lut (peace be upon him). The implied meaning is: the angels said to Lut, "By your life." He referred to error and heedlessness by intoxication (sakrah), meaning that their bewilderment in their heedlessness and error prevented them from perceiving the right course, which would have been to leave the males for the females. It was also said that the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority: Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Hawra', and others. Allah swore by his life, honouring him.

Al-'Amr, with a fatha or a damma on the ayn, means survival (al-baqa'). The grammarians required the fatha for the oath (al-qasam), and it is permissible to omit the lam. Ibn 'Abbas read it as wa 'amruka. Abu al-Haytham said: la'amruka means "your religion, by which you survive." He recited:

"O you who marry Thurayya to Suhayl,
by your life, Allah! How could the two meet?"

That is, your worship of Allah. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I made my Lord survive," meaning I worshipped Him; and "So-and-so is a worshipper for his Lord," meaning he is devoted to Him. He said: It is also said, "I left so-and-so making his Lord survive," meaning worshipping Him. On this basis, la'amruka means "by your worship."

Al-Zajjaj said: They required the fatha for the oath because it is lighter for them, and they frequently swear by la'amrī and la'amruka, so they adopted the lighter form. Its nominative (irtfa'uhu) is due to inception, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "What he swore by."

Some of the scholars of meanings said: it is not permissible to attribute 'amr to Allah, for one does not say 'amr for Allah the Exalted; one says He is eternal (azali). It seems to imply that 'amr is used only of what has an end, and this is not the case with 'amr, which means survival. A poet said:

"When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,
by the life of Allah, their pleasure delights me."

Al-A'sha said:

"And by the life of Him who made the months a sign,
distinguishing from them their deficiency and their completeness."

Al-Nakha'i disliked saying la'amrī (by my life), because it is an oath by the life of the one swearing. Al-Nabigha said:

"By my life, and what is my life to me, is not trivial."

The pronoun in sakratihim refers to the people of Lut. Al-Tabari said it refers to Quraysh, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. He said: Allah created no soul more honourable to Him than Muhammad (ﷺ), and He said to him: "By your life (wa hayatika), indeed they," that is, your people from Quraysh, "are in their intoxication," that is, their error and ignorance, "wandering blindly," that is, wandering about.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is far-fetched, because it is disconnected from what precedes and what follows it."

Al-Ashhab read sukratihim with a damma on the sin. Ibn Abi 'Abilah read sakaratihim in the plural. Al-A'mash read sukrihim without the ta'. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of al-Jahdari, read (annahum) with a fatha on the hamza of annahum.

Al-Sayhah is the shout of destruction. It was also said it is the voice of Jibril (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the shout of horror, and it is not like the shout of Thamud.

Musriqin means entering upon sunrise, which is the rising of the sun. It was said that the beginning of the punishment came at dawn and extended to the sunrise, so that the completion of the destruction took place at that time.

The pronoun in 'aliyaha safilaha refers to the city mentioned earlier. Al-Zamakhshari said it refers to the towns of the people of Lut, though the word "towns" (qura) has not been mentioned before. Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: lil-mutawassimin means lil-mutafakkirin (for those who reflect). Al-Dahhak said: for those who look. A poet said:

"Whenever a tribe came to 'Ukaz,
they sent to their leader to take note (yatawassamu)."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: for those who see clearly. Qatadah said: for those who take warning. It is narrated from Nahshal, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding lil-mutawassimin, that he said: it means the people of righteousness and goodness.

The pronoun in wa innaha refers to the destroyed city, meaning: it is on a clear and evident path for the one who takes warning. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. It was said that it may refer to the signs, and it may refer to the stones. As for His words, labisabilin, it means a established passageway, and it is in a place where people see it and take warning from it; it has not been effaced. This is an admonition to Quraysh, for you pass by them in the morning and at night.

It was also said that it refers to the shout, meaning: indeed the shout is lying in wait for whoever does their deeds, based on His words: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 11:83]. It was also said: muqim means known. It was said: it means lasting transgression. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a destruction whose path endures.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in what We did to the people of Lut, is indeed a sign and a proof for whoever believes in Allah.

﴿And indeed the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿So We took vengeance upon them, and indeed both [towns] are on a clear highway﴾: They are the people of Shu'ayb, and the thicket (al-ayka) to which they were attributed was a tree of doum palm. It was also said: it was the arfaj tree. It was also said: the sidr (lote tree). It was also said: al-Ayka is the name of the region, in which case it is a proper noun. This is strengthened by the reading of those who recited it in al-Shu'ara' and Sad as Layka, without tanwin. They disbelieved, so Allah sent upon them the heat, and they were destroyed by the punishment of the cloud. This will be discussed in full, Allah willing, in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

In (in) the view of the Basrans, it is the light form of the heavy form (in mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah, i.e., "indeed" with the emphatic particle omitted). According to al-Farra', it is a negation, and the lam means "except" (illa). A similar discussion occurred regarding ﴿And indeed it was a great [matter]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143] in al-Baqarah.

The apparent view is that of the majority: that the pronoun in wa innahuma refers to the two towns, the town of the people of Lut and the people of Shu'ayb, meaning: they are on the passageway of the traveller. It was said that it refers to Shu'ayb and Lut, meaning: both are on a clear path (imam mubin), that is, a path of truth that is evident. The imam is the path. It was said: wa innahuma, meaning the stone, that is, the destruction of the people of Lut and the companions of the thicket, is in a clear book (kitab mubin), that is, the Preserved Tablet. Mu'arrij said: the imam is the book in the dialect of Himyar. It was also said: it refers to the companions of the thicket and Madyan, for he was sent to both of them, so the mention of one indicates the other, and the pronoun refers to both.

﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, secure﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at dawn﴾ ﴿And what they used to earn did not avail them﴾: The companions of al-Hijr are Thamud, the people of Salih (peace be upon him). Al-Hijr is a land between the Hijaz and Syria. Its story was discussed fully in al-A'raf. "The messengers" refers to their denial of Salih, for whoever denies one of them is as if he denied them all. Al-Zamakhshari said: or he meant Salih and those believers with him, just as it was said: "the Khubaybiyyun" regarding Ibn al-Zubayr and his companions.

It is narrated from Jabir, who said: "We passed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by al-Hijr, and he said to us: 'Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest what befell them befall you.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged his mount on, and it hastened until he left it behind." In one of its chains it adds: "Then he said: 'These are the people of Salih, whom Allah destroyed, except for a man who was in the sanctuary of Allah, whom the sanctity of Allah protected from the punishment of Allah.'" It was said: "Who is he, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Abu Righal." And the Thaqif tribe is attributed to him.

﴿And We gave them Our signs﴾: It was said: verses from the Book of Allah were sent down to them. It was also said: it refers to the establishment of proofs, but they turned away from them. It was also said: there were five signs in the she-camel: her emergence from the rock, her gestation being near at the time of her emergence, her great size such that no other camel resembled her, the abundance of her milk sufficient for all of them, and it was also said that he had signs other than the she-camel.

Al-Jumhur read yanhitun with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read it with a fatha.
